H0.r: Recognition. Elaborate means are employed in folk-literature for the recognition of persons even though they have been separated a very short time. The various means used are detailed in the following discussion.
H0.p: General heading for tests that establish someone's true identity.

H10.p: A person's identity is confirmed because they know something that only the real person would know.

H11.r: Icelandic: *Boberg; Arabian: Burton Nights III 96ff., S V 155, 164, S VI 34f., 476; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: De Vries’s list No. 224.
H11.p: A person is identified when a story is told that both parties already know well, so the teller reveals who they are through shared history.

H11.1.r: *Type 506; Köhler-Bolte II 351ff.; Icelandic: *Boberg; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 19; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H11.1.p: A person is identified by having them recount their own life history, which the listener can check against what they know.

H11.1.1.r: *Type 304; *BP II 255 n. 1, 505; bin Gorion Born Judas I 189, 374; *Chauvin V 90 No. 28 n. 1; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 2.
H11.1.1.p: At an inn, hospital or similar place, everyone present must tell their life history, and this leads to one person being recognized.

H11.1.2.p: A person's life story is painted on a wall, so that viewing the painting reveals who they are.

H11.1.3.p: A person's life history is sung, and the song reveals who they are to someone who knows it.

H11.1.4.r: Greek: Homer Iliad VI 215, Aeschylus Suppliants 290.
H11.1.4.p: A person is recognized by tracing their family line back through their ancestors.

H12.r: Thien Motive 9; Norse: De la Saussaye 137; Lithuanian: Balys Index Nos. *452f.; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “chanson”; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 3 and the legend of Richard Coeur de Leon and Blondel; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Anesaki 359; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 530, 539; New Zealand: Dixon 83; West Indies: Flowers 455.
H12.p: A person is recognized through a song, because only they sing it or only they and the listener know it.

H12.1.p: A missing woman poet is found when she passes a test of her poetic skill.

H12.2.p: A person is recognized by completing or knowing a verse of a song that only they or the listener know.

H12.2.1.p: A person is recognized when a couplet they hold matches another couplet held by someone else, joining the two halves.

H13.r: *Types 313, 533, 706, 870; *BP I 19, III 445ff.; *Fb “hest” I 598b, “ovn” II 774a; **Liungman Jordkulan passim; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 62, 69 Nos. 445*B, 515*; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Thonga): Junod 231.
H13.p: A person who does not dare to reveal themselves directly is recognized after speaking in a way that others overhear, often through an animal or object.

H13.1.p: A person is recognized after overhearing a conversation between animals, where an animal reveals or discusses their identity.

H13.1.1.p: A person is recognized after overhearing a horse speaking about them or their situation.

H13.1.2.p: A person is recognized after overhearing a dog speaking about them or their situation.

H13.1.3.p: A person is recognized after overhearing a cow speaking about them or their situation.

H13.2.r: *Type 870; *BP III 444ff.; Italian: Basile Pentamerone II No. 8; Icelandic: Boberg.
H13.2.p: A hero is recognized when he overhears objects or animals talking about his identity or past deeds.

H13.2.1.p: A bridge speaks and will trip up a wedding party unless the king is marrying someone of equal rank; a disguised princess praises the bridge for recognizing her equality with the king, which reveals her.

H13.2.2.r: *Types 710 870; BP I 19 n. 2; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 62 No. 445B*, Espinosa Jr. No. 114.
H13.2.2.p: A person learns a secret or identity by overhearing a conversation between a stone or other inanimate object, which unwittingly reveals the truth.

H13.2.3.p: A person is recognized after overhearing a plant speaking about them or their situation.

H13.2.4.p: A person is recognized after overhearing a church door speaking about them or their situation.

H13.2.5.p: A person is recognized after overhearing cups or other household utensils speaking about them or their situation.

H13.2.6.p: A heroine reveals herself by comparing her own fate with the fate of flax, which is overheard and recognized.

H13.2.7.r: *Type 533; *BP II 275; *Fb “ovn” II 774a; K. Ranke Festschrift f. W.-E. Peuckert, Berl. 1955, 46.
H13.2.7.p: A person is recognized because they overhear a conversation between objects, such as a stove, that reveals who they are.

H13.3.p: Two sons are recognized as the king's sons after overhearing a conversation between their animals or objects that reveals their identity.

H13.4.p: A person is recognized by overhearing a conversation with a flower-woman that reveals who they are.

H14.p: A person is recognized by watching how another reacts emotionally to something both of them experienced in common.

H14.1.p: A wife recognizes her long-lost husband when she sees him weep at the sight of a bird, which recalls a shared past experience in which the bird was the main character.

H14.2.p: A person is recognized because someone is moved to tears on hearing a retelling of their own heroic deeds.

H15.p: A person's identity is tested or proven by having them recount experiences that only the people involved would know.

H15.1.p: A person's identity is checked by asking them to repeat what they said on an earlier occasion, showing they share the common experience. Only the real person would know what was said.

H15.2.p: A person is recognized because they remember and describe experiences they shared with the other person.

H16.p: A person is recognized because they can describe or make an object that only people with shared knowledge would know about.

H16.1.p: A lost brother builds a clay model of their father's palace, and the king recognizes him as his brother from it.

H16.2.p: A person is recognized by wounds on the lip and finger that they both received during a shared adventure.

H16.3.p: Brothers recognize each other by a bouquet of flowers tied in the way their father's gardener used to tie them.

H16.4.p: A person is recognized because they can describe a bed that is unique and known only to the people involved.

H17.r: Italian: Basile Pentamerone II No. 3; Jewish: Neuman.
H17.p: A person is recognized by being reminded of something that was said between them earlier.

H18.p: A person is recognized because they give or know a secret password that identifies them as one of the group.

H19.p: A miscellaneous category of recognition through shared knowledge that does not fit the other headings in this group.

H19.1.p: A person is recognized because they can identify property that belonged to them or was theirs.

H19.1.1.p: A reincarnated person is recognized because they can identify the weapons they used in a former life.

H19.2.p: A person is recognized by giving the correct answer to a riddle or puzzle that only two people would know.

H20.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “reconnaissance”; Greek: Homer Odyssey IV 144, 150.
H20.p: A person is recognized simply because they look like someone else, through physical resemblance.

H21.r: *Type 881; *BP II 505; Köhler-Bolte I 528; *Chauvin V 92 No. 196, 94 No. 30; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesian: De Vries’s list No. 223.
H21.p: A picture of a lost person is displayed publicly, and seeing it leads to that person being recognized.

H22.p: A person is recognized because of an image, such as a likeness or portrait, that resembles them.

H24.p: A person is recognized because of something seen in a dream.

H30.p: A person is identified through some distinctive trait, habit, or skill that is unique to them.

H31.p: A person is recognized because only they can perform a particular feat of skill or strength.

H31.1.r: English: Wells 43 (Arthour and Merlin); Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Volsunga saga 7; India: Thompson-Balys.
H31.1.p: Only one person can pull a sword out of the stone or tree where it is stuck, and this identifies him.

H31.2.p: Only one person can bend a particular bow, and this identifies him.

H31.3.p: Only one person can swing a particular spear, and this identifies him.

H31.4.p: Only one man can lift a small pot from the ground, and this identifies him.

H31.5.p: A person is recognized because only they can cut or carve a tree and similar objects in a unique way.

H31.6.p: A person is recognized because only they can break an iron apple with the first stone they throw.

H31.7.r: German: Grimm Nos. 76, 89; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Kordofan): Frobenius Atlantis IV 134ff. No. 13.
H31.7.p: A person is recognized because only they can perform a particular magic act.

H31.7.1.p: A person is recognized because only they can make pearls fall from their eyes when they weep.

H31.7.2.p: Only one man can read a magic book, and this identifies him.

H31.8.p: A person is recognized because only they can shoot, swim, and drink in a particular unique way.

H31.9.p: A person is recognized because only they can handle a heavy stone easily.

H31.10.p: A person is recognized because only they can play chess in a particular unique way.

H31.11.p: A person is recognized because only they can read a particular inscription.

H31.12.p: Only one man can pick fruit from a tree, and this identifies him.

H31.12.1.p: Only the bridegroom can pluck a flower from the bride's grave, and this identifies him.

H32.p: A person is identified as the true one because of an extraordinary feat of strength or skill that only they could perform.

H35.p: A person is recognized by the distinctive way they do some everyday action, which no one else does the same way.

H35.1.p: A person is recognized by the unusual way they play the lute, which marks them out as the one who is who they claim to be.

H35.1.1.p: A person is recognized by the unusual way they play the harp, which marks them out as the one who is who they claim to be.

H35.1.2.p: A person is recognized by the unusual way they play the flute, which marks them out as the one who is who they claim to be.

H35.2.r: *Chauvin VI 105 No. 270 n. 1; India: *Thompson-Balys; Icelandic: Boberg.
H35.2.p: A person is recognized by a special dish or way of cooking food that only one particular person could have made.

H35.3.r: *Type 506; von der Hagen I cxxxix; India: Thompson-Balys.
H35.3.p: A person is recognized by a distinctive style of sewing or needlework that only one particular person could have produced.

H35.3.1.p: A false bride is exposed because she cannot finish the weaving that the true bride had left unfinished, showing she does not know the true bride's skill.

H35.3.2.p: A person is recognized by their embroidery, which shows a distinctive style that identifies them.

H35.4.p: A person is recognized by the distinctive way they carve wood chips, and the chips are sent downstream so the one who finds them can identify the carver.

H35.4.1.p: A person is recognized by ogham writing carved on a withe, rod, or tree, which reveals who carved it.

H35.5.p: A person is recognized by the way they throw cakes of different weights into the faces of old uncles, which reveals their identity.

H36.p: A person is recognized because a garment or piece of clothing fits them exactly, showing they are the one it was made or meant for.

H36.1.r: *Type 510; *Cox Cinderella 504ff.; *BP I 187; *Fb “sko” III 288a; Cosquin Contes Indiens 48ff.; Saintyves Perrault 115ff., 156.—Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 6; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 18f.; India: *Thompson-Balys; New Mexican: Rael Mod. Lang. Forum XVIII (1933).
H36.1.p: A person is identified by a slipper that fits only them, as with a lost shoe that proves who the wearer is.

H36.1.1.p: A person is recognized by shoes with which their father once beat them, so the shoes themselves reveal who the person is.

H36.2.p: A garment fits only the true king, so anyone who tries it on who is not the rightful king cannot wear it.

H36.2.1.p: A crown fits only the legitimate heir to the throne, so only the rightful successor can wear it.

H38.p: A person's high or low social rank is revealed by the way they habitually talk, even when they are disguised.

H38.1.p: A disguised king or noble is recognized because of the speech habits typical of their high rank.

H38.2.p: A pretender of humble birth is exposed because his speech habits reveal his low origin.

H38.2.1.p: A tailor who has married a princess gives himself away by asking for his needle and thread, showing he is really a tailor of humble birth pretending to be noble. His old trade slips out in his speech.

H38.2.2.p: A peasant boy pretending to be a prince reveals his true origin through the answers he gives, which a real prince would not give.

H38.2.3.p: A maidservant who has been put in place of the bride is recognized because her everyday way of speaking does not match a lady's.

H38.2.4.p: A weaver who has married a princess gives himself away by talking in his sleep about his trade.

H38.2.4.1.p: A weaver married to a princess is unmasked when, without meaning to, he waves his hands as if weaving and asks for his shuttle.

H38.2.5.p: A low-caste boy substituted for a promised child is detected because he chooses the long way through the jungle, such as swimming across instead of taking the ferry, which shows he is not of noble stock.

H38.3.p: A slave is recognized as not free by his speech, his habits, and his character, which give away his low status.

H41.p: A person of royal birth is identified by personal characteristics or traits that reveal his or her rank.

H41.1.r: *BP III 330; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 575b; Grimm No. 182a; *Fb “seng”; Penzer VI 288ff.; Wirth AA o.s. VII (1894) 367ff.; Arthur Christensen Acta Orientalia XIV 241—257; India: Thompson-Balys.
H41.1.p: A princess is proven royal because she cannot sleep on a bed with a pea hidden under many mattresses, since her delicate nature notices it.

H41.2.r: N. A. Indian (Quileute): Farrand-Mayer JAFL XXXII 253 No. 1, (Chinook): Boas BBAE XX 160, (Nootka): Boas RBAE XXXI 919.
H41.2.p: Spitting high into the air is a test showing that someone is a chief.

H41.3.p: A king or pope is identified because his candle lights itself without anyone touching it.

H41.4.p: Flame coming out of a person's mouth is a sign that he or she is royal.

H41.5.r: Type 920; *De Vries FFC LXXIII 40ff., 323ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Icelandic: *Boberg.
H41.5.p: An unknown prince shows his royal qualities by the way he treats and leads his playmates.

H41.5.1.p: A prince raised by a fisherman spends money in princely ways, showing his true royal taste.

H41.6.p: A prophecy at the birth of princesses says that the one who takes gold in her mouth will marry a prince, and the one who takes hawkweed will marry a peasant.

H41.7.p: A task is set in which whoever rides a certain horse becomes king.

H41.8.p: A test of royalty requires a person to sow, reap, and winnow rice all in one day.

H41.9.r: Irish myth: *Cross; *Nutt Studies in the Legend of the Holy Grail (London, 1888) 81f., 88.
H41.9.p: A king is recognized because only he can sit in a certain seat, known as the Siege Perilous.

H41.9.1.p: In the seat test, a chariot tilts under anyone who is not entitled to the throne, so only the rightful king can sit without it tipping.

H41.10.p: A chief in disguise carries a bundle so large that his rank is recognized by it.

H44.p: A person is recognized by their distinctive perfume or scent.

H45.p: A god or divine being is identified as such by some sign.

H45.1.p: A god is known to be divine because of his supernatural powers.

H45.2.p: Cows give milk spontaneously when they rest under a tree where a deity dwells, showing the deity's presence.

H45.3.r: Oertel Studien z. vgl. Littg. VIII 116; Frazer Pausanias III 336f.; Zs. f. Vksk. II 197, III 89, 448.
H45.3.p: A test of whether someone is a god: when his image is tied up, it breaks free by itself.

H45.4.p: A god in disguise is recognized by marks on his feet and hands.

H45.5.p: A girl found sleeping naked is tested to see whether she is a goddess: a mortal would cover herself when awakened, while a goddess would not.

H46.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Zulu): Callaway 47, 142, (Basuto): Jacottet 4 No. 1, 206 No. 30, (Kaffir): Theal 125.
H46.p: A cannibal is recognized by the cloud of dust raised when they run or move.

H46.1.p: A woman is revealed to be a cannibal when she eats a dead buffalo raw.

H47.p: A demon possessing a corpse is recognized because the body turns into a worm when a stake is driven through it.

H48.p: An animal disguised as a human is recognized for what it is.

H48.1.r: S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 122.
H48.1.p: A fox in human form gives himself away by crying out like a fox while asleep.

H48.2.r: S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 123.
H48.2.p: A fox in human form gives himself away by fetching fox food for his human wife.

H49.p: Miscellaneous recognitions by personal peculiarities that do not fit other headings.

H49.1.p: Abandoned children are betrayed by the unique scent of their rice, which reveals who they are.

H50.p: A person is recognized by bodily marks or physical features such as scars, birthmarks, or brands.

H51.r: (Cf. H56.) *Type 314; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 9, *Rotunda; Greek: Odyssey, books XIX, XXIV; Arabian: Burton Nights I 248; Jewish: *Neuman; Indonesia: De Vries’s list No. 158; Chinese: Werner 281; N. A. Indian (Ponka): Dorsey CNAE VI 606, (Blackfoot): Wissler and Duvall PaAM II 109, (Eastern Cree): Skinner PaAM IX 92.
H51.p: A person is recognized by a scar on the body.

H51.1.r: *Types 400, 850; Dickson 49 nn. 58, 59; cf. Shakespeare’s Cymbeline II, 2, 38; BP II 318, 528; German. Grimm No. 92; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 140; N. A. Indian (Blackfoot): Wissler and Duvall PaAM II 109.
H51.1.p: A person is recognized by a birthmark on the body.

H55.r: *Types 314, 502, 883B; Dickson 41; Chauvin V 152; Tawney I 37, 92; Burton Nights VII 89 n.; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H55.p: A person or animal is recognized by a brand burned into the skin.

H55.1.p: A creature is recognized by a branding mark shaped like a hoofprint.

H55.2.p: A magician brands sacred animals so that they can later be recognized as his property or as those particular animals.

H55.3.p: A person is recognized by a tattoo on the body.

H56.r: (Cf. H51.) *Types 314, 502; *Cosquin Études 447ff.; Dickson 42 n. 41; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 169, 170; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 417.
H56.p: A person is identified by a wound on the body.

H56.1.p: A woman's identity is revealed when a hand is seen with a burn hole in it after she takes off her glove.

H56.2.p: Children's bodies are mutilated so that they can be identified later.

H57.r: *Hartland Perseus III 208f.; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 150, 168, 171.
H57.p: A person is recognized because a body part is missing.

H57.0.1.p: A person brought back to life is recognized because a body part is missing.

H57.1.p: A person is recognized by a broken tooth.

H57.2.r: *Hartland Perseus III 207ff.; Dickson 42 n. 42; Icelandic: Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “doigt”; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. 120, 121.
H57.2.p: A person is recognized because a finger is missing.

H57.2.1.p: A severed finger is found to be evidence of a crime, and the criminal is thereby caught. In one such tale a robber bridegroom is exposed this way.

H57.2.2.p: A murdered person is identified by a fingernail that was cut off.

H57.3.p: A person is recognized because a toe is missing.

H57.4.p: A woman is recognized from a description of her having no hands.

H57.5.p: A person is recognized because he or she has artificial hands.

H58.r: *Type 950; Köhler-Bolte I 200; India: Thompson-Balys; Hindu: Tawney I 15; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 273 n. 1.
H58.p: A secret lover is exposed by marks, left on his skin by his mistress, that show where he has been.

H58.1.p: A disguised mistress is found out because her lover left chalk marks on her back.

H58.2.p: A secret lover is identified by scratches on his face left by a lady.

H61.p: A person is recognized by ornaments that are hidden under the skin.

H61.1.p: Twins are recognized by a golden chain that lies under their skin.

H61.2.p: A person who has been disenchanted is recognized by ornaments under his skin.

H61.3.p: A character is recognized because a ring is found embedded under the skin, having been placed there during a wound. The hidden ring proves who the person is.

H61.4.p: A character is recognized by a grain of gold lodged under the skin. The gold grain serves as proof of identity.

H62.p: A transformed person, who has been turned into an animal, is recognized despite the change of shape. Recognition depends on something that shows who they really are.

H62.0.1.p: A man who has been changed into a horse is recognized as the man he really is. The recognition reveals his true identity despite his equine form.

H62.1.p: A person who has been turned into an animal is recognized for who they are. Their human identity shows through the animal form.

H62.1.1.p: A person changed into an animal is recognized by his eyes. The eyes reveal the human inside the animal.

H62.1.2.p: A person changed into an animal shows they are human by being able to read. Reading ability reveals the hidden human identity.

H62.2.p: A horse recognizes that a kol, a person transformed to look like its master, is not the master. The horse throws the impostor off its back.

H62.3.p: A prince identifies a marvelous horse even though it has taken the form of a miserable, worn-out one. The prince sees through the disguise.

H63.p: Other transformed persons are recognized despite their changed form. This heading covers recognition of transformations not listed under animals.

H63.1.r: Type 407; BP III 259; German: Grimm No. 160.
H63.1.p: A woman transformed into a flower is recognized because the flower lacks dew on its petals. The missing dew reveals that it is really her.

H64.p: A person freed from enchantment is recognized by physical attributes. Bodily features show who they are after the disenchantment.

H64.1.p: A disenchanted man is recognized by a piece of thread caught in his teeth. As a werewolf he had torn a woman's apron and gotten the thread caught in his teeth.

H64.2.p: A werewolf is killed and identified as a man by his clothes under the wolf skin or by a rosary around its neck. The human garments or religious object reveal who he was.

H64.3.p: A person freed from animal form is recognized because they cannot hide their tail. The lingering tail shows what they were.

H64.4.p: A person freed from animal form is recognized because they cannot eat the way humans do. Their animal manner of eating reveals what they were.

H71.r: (Cf. H41, H171.5.) *Type 533; *BP II 275; Köhler-Bolte I 130; India: Thompson-Balys.
H71.p: Physical signs that mark a person as royal. These marks are used to show that someone is of noble or royal birth.

H71.1.r: *Type 707; *BP I 102, II 380, 393; *Fb “stjærne” III 577b, “guldstjærne” I 515a; Köhler-Bolte I 119; Dickson 48; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 311 No. 56; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 137; India: Thompson-Balys.
H71.1.p: A star on the forehead marks a person as royal. The star identifies them as being of royal birth.

H71.1.1.p: A moon on the forehead and stars in the palm of the hand mark a person as royal. Together these signs show royal birth.

H71.2.p: Hairs of gold or silver on a person's body mark them as royal. The unusual hairs show that they are of royal birth.

H71.2.1.p: A boy's body is golden, marking him as royal. Gold hair or silver hair serves as a mark of royal birth.

H71.3.p: Pearls fall or come out of a person's hair, and this marks them as royal.

H71.4.p: Roses come from a person's lips when they speak or laugh, showing they are royal. The note gives the example of a princess who laughs roses.

H71.5.r: Dickson 48f.; English: Wells 14f. (The Lay of Havelok); Icelandic: *Boberg.
H71.5.p: A cross-shaped mark appears between the shoulders, showing that the person is royal or noble.

H71.6.p: A person's eyes shine brightly, marking them as royal or noble.

H71.6.1.p: The face glows with light, showing the person is royal. It is a form of the bright-eyes sign.

H71.6.2.p: The skin or eyes have a golden tint, marking the person as royal. It is a form of the bright-eyes sign.

H71.7.r: *Type 707; BP I 432, II 380ff.; Todd MLN VI 7; Wesselski Märchen 174 No. 64; Wells Manual 96 (Chevalere Assigne).
H71.7.p: A child is born with a chain around its neck, and this marks it as royal.

H71.7.1.p: A girl is born with costly jewels, and this marks her as royal. It is a form of the chain-around-the-neck sign.

H71.7.2.p: A prince is born with a bow of gold and a string of silver, showing he is royal.

H71.8.r: Jewish: Neuman; S. A. Indian (Inca): Alexander Lat. Am. 252.
H71.8.p: Tears shed by a person are blood, and this marks them as royal.

H71.9.p: A person's teeth are red, marking them as royal.

H71.10.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
H71.10.p: A marvelous event occurs that shows a person is royal.

H71.10.1.r: De Vries FFC LXXIII 329; Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
H71.10.1.p: A tree bends down and bows before a prince, showing he is royal.

H71.10.2.p: Water stops flowing and stands still before a prince, showing he is royal.

H71.10.3.p: Frogs croak when a prince commands them, showing he is royal.

H71.10.4.p: The horses pulling a chariot rear up and spring away from anyone who has no right to the throne.

H71.10.5.p: Two blocks of stone move apart to let the chariot of the true king pass through.

H71.10.6.p: A stone screams when the legitimate king stands on it.

H71.10.7.p: Arrows turn aside and miss a prince or king, showing he is royal.

H71.11.p: A person's royal status is revealed when gold is found in their excrement, a sign that they were born or raised as a prince or king.

H75.p: A person is identified or recognized by a hair from their head or body.

H75.1.r: *Type 531; *BP III 31 n. 1. 33; **Golther “Die Jungfrau mit den goldenen Haaren” Studien zur Literaturgeschichte M. Bernays gewidmet (Leipzig, 1893).—N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 355 n. 281.
H75.1.p: A person is identified by a hair found floating on water.

H75.2.p: A person is identified by a hair that a bird has dropped.

H75.3.p: A person is recognized by a hair found inside a fish that swallowed it.

H75.4.p: A person is recognized by golden hair.

H75.5.p: A person is identified by a hair from a wolf.

H75.6.p: A person is recognized because a hair is missing from their head or body.

H75.7.p: Murderers are recognized because they have short hair, which identifies them.

H78.p: A person is recognized by a feather.

H78.1.p: A youth shoots a raven and takes one of its feathers to the raven's sister as a token to prove who he is.

H78.2.p: A hero is identified by a feather that was taken from him when he was turned into a bird.

H79.p: A person is recognized by some physical attribute not covered by the more specific categories.

H79.1.p: A troll's daughter, even after being cooked in a kettle, is recognized by her golden fingernail.

H79.2.p: A man is identified by his little toe.

H79.3.r: Icelandic: Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H79.3.p: A person is recognized by their voice.

H79.4.p: A sultan recognizes a prisoner by his smile, and so frees him because he was formerly one of his aids.

H79.5.p: A man is identified by his skull.

H79.6.p: A woman lying in bed is recognized as not being her husband's wife because of her large breasts.

H79.7.p: A monk is recognized by his large sexual organ.

H79.8.p: A man is identified because one of his teeth is blue, so the blue tooth serves as proof of who he is.

H80.r: Types 300, 301, 304, 306, 873; English: Child V 499 s.v. “tokens”; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 18; Greek: Fox 71; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
H80.p: A person is recognized or proven to be who they claim through a small object or sign given as a token of identity.

H80.1.p: Those who are truly the redeemers are to be recognized by a token that proves their identity.

H81.p: A secret lover is discovered or identified through a token left behind or exchanged.

H81.1.r: *Types 304, 550, 551; *BP II 505; *Fb “sove” III 472a; Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 26; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H81.1.p: The hero lies beside a sleeping girl and leaves an identifying token with her as a sign of his visit.

H81.1.1.r: Type 304; BP II 505; German: Grimm No. 111.
H81.1.1.p: The hero takes a token from the sleeping princess, so she can later recognize or be identified by it.

H81.2.p: A princess secretly visits the hero, but her visit is revealed because of a token she carries.

H81.3.p: A lover secretly visits the queen, but the visit is revealed because of a token.

H82.p: Tokens that identify the sender are sent along with a messenger to prove the message is genuine.

H82.1.p: Tokens are sent to a jailor as proof that the message comes with the king's authority.

H82.2.r: English: Child V 499 s.v. “tokens”; Icelandic: Boberg.
H82.2.p: Marriage tokens are sent to identify a lover.

H82.3.p: Lovers exchange tokens that they use to identify each other.

H82.4.p: A husband sends his wife a ring as a token that he has been baptized and urges her to be baptized too.

H82.5.p: A token is sent as a warning of danger.

H82.6.p: A youth is sent to his relatives with a token so they will take care of him.

H83.r: (Cf. H105, H105.1, H105.2.) *Types 300, 301, 304, 306; *Hartland Perseus III 203ff. (list of tokens).
H83.p: A token is given as proof that the hero has successfully completed a rescue.

H84.p: Objects are brought back as proof of the hero's deeds or exploits.

H84.1.p: Branches are broken from a tree and brought back to prove that a journey was made.

H84.2.p: A cup taken from a feast serves as proof that one was present there.

H84.3.p: A flail serves as proof of a story of having watched threshing in heaven.

H84.4.p: A stolen ring is later shown as proof that the thief carried out a daring theft, so the thief is identified by it.

H85.p: A captive sends a token to his friends or family to show that he is safe and alive.

H86.p: A name written or engraved on an object is used as a token to prove who owns it.

H86.1.p: A sword bears the king's name carved into it, and this name identifies the owner or proves who he is.

H86.2.p: Pieces of clothing with a name embroidered on them are taken as tokens that reveal whose they are.

H86.3.p: A ring has names engraved on it, and these names are used to identify the person who owns it.

H86.4.p: A handkerchief marked with a name is used to recognize or identify its owner.

H87.p: Garlands or wreaths of flowers serve as a token by which a person is recognized.

H88.p: A person is recognized by tokens he has left behind along his route, like a trail of marks or objects.

H90.p: A person is identified by ornaments or jewelry that he or she wears or carries.

H91.p: A person is recognized through a quantity or object made of precious metal, such as gold.

H91.1.p: Gold found in an eagle's nest is used to identify the person who was connected to it.

H91.2.p: Gold wrapped in a mantle or cloak is used to recognize the person who has it.

H91.3.p: A person proves who he is by producing three golden apples.

H92.r: *Types 450, 870, 870A; *BP I 79ff., III 443ff., 445; *Fb “guldkjæde” IV 192a; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 514.
H92.p: A person is identified by a necklace that he or she wears or is known to have.

H93.r: French: Cosquin Lorraine I 220 n.; Hindu: Tawney I 170.
H93.p: A person is identified by a jewel that he or she has or wears.

H93.0.1.p: A person is recognized by the smell of jewels worn around someone's neck.

H94.r: *Types 301, 304, 882; *BP II 348; Thien Motive 33; *Fb “ring” III 60a; *Hartland Perseus III 207ff.; Liungman Två Folkeminnes. 25 n. 1; Saintyves Perrault 204ff.; Irish myth: *Cross, MacCulloch Celtic 26; English: Wells 9ff. (Horn Childe and Maiden Rimnild), 73 (Sir Percyvelle of Galles), 80 (Sir Tristrem); Icelandic: *Boberg; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 181; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 3; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Hindu: Penzer II 76f., Tawney I 142 n., II 620; Chinese: Graham.
H94.p: A person is identified by a ring that he or she wears or is known to have.

H94.0.1.p: A husband learns of his wife's unfaithfulness when he recognizes her ring in the possession of a friend.

H94.1.p: A ring is baked inside a cake and found by a person, and this ring then identifies the person it belongs to.

H94.2.p: A person is recognized because a ring was baked inside a loaf of bread that was shared or given to them.

H94.3.p: A person is recognized because a ring was dropped into a pitcher of wine that they then pour out.

H94.4.r: *Types 400, 506, 510; *Fb “guldring” I 514b, “ring” III 60a; *BP II 348; Wesselski Mönchslatein 111 No. 95; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 53, Beal XXI 320; English: Wells 9 (King Horn), Child V 493 s.v. “ring.
H94.4.p: A person is recognized because a ring was dropped into a glass or cup of wine that they then drink from.

H94.5.r: (Cf. H100.) The two parts of the ring fit together. Type 361, BP II 428; *Fb “guldring” I 514b, “ring” III No. 95; Heptameron No. 24; Köhler-Bolte I 585; Wesselski Mönchslatein 111 No. 95; Icelandic: Boberg; English: Child V 493 “ring”; Filipino: Fansler MAFLS XII 210.
H94.5.p: A person is recognized through a ring that has been broken, with the two halves later matched to prove identity.

H94.6.p: A person is recognized through a ring worn on the arm, which serves as proof of identity.

H94.7.p: A person is recognized when a ring springs off their finger, revealing who they are.

H94.8.p: A person is recognized through a medallion or flat plaque that serves as an identifying token.

H94.9.p: A person is recognized through a ring hidden inside a garland or wreath.

H94.10.p: A person is recognized through a gold ring that has the owner's name engraved on it.

H94.11.p: A person is recognized through a pair of earrings that serve as proof of identity.

H95.p: A person is recognized through a bracelet that serves as proof of identity.

H96.p: A person is identified through an amulet, a charm worn as protection, which serves as proof of who they are.

H100.p: A person is identified when a token that was divided into parts is reunited, with the matching pieces proving identity.

H101.r: English: Wells 80 (Sir Tristrem); Icelandic: Ragnarssaga Loðbrókar 118, Boberg; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 18f.; Indonesia: cf. De Vries’s list No. 163.
H101.p: A person is identified because a broken weapon's missing point, later found, fits the rest of the weapon and proves who they are.

H101.1.r: Africa (Chaga): Stamberg ZsES XXI 296ff., Gutmann 82f. No. 41, (Ganda): Baskerville 1ff.
H101.1.p: A person is identified when a weapon is matched to a wound, showing that the weapon caused it and so revealing who did it.

H102.p: Two people each keep one half of a contract torn in two, and when the halves are fitted together they recognize each other.

H102.1.p: Two people are identified by fitting together two pieces of parchment that were once one document.

H103.p: Pieces cut from flags are used to identify a person by matching them together.

H105.r: *Hartland Perseus III 207; *Hdwb. d. Märchens I 242b. nn. 37—47; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 7; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (Seneca): Curtin-Hewitt RBAE XXXII 343 No. 59.
H105.p: Parts of slain animals are kept as proof that a person did the killing.

H105.1.r: *Types 300, 303; *Hartland Perseus III 203ff.; **Ranke FFC CXIV 251ff.; *BP I 534ff., 548; Fb “tunge” III 893b; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 242a nn. 24—47; Schoepperle I 204 n. 3; Irish myth: Cross; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 7, 18f.; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 63 n. 4; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 323ff.; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 278 No. 90.
H105.1.p: A dragon slayer cuts out the dragon's tongues and later uses them to prove that he was the one who killed it.

H105.1.1.r: *Type 300; *BP I 534ff. and all references to H105.1; *Parsons FL XXXII 194ff.; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H105.1.1.p: An impostor cuts off dragon heads, after the tongues have been removed, and presents them as proof that he killed the dragon.

H105.2.p: A man's tongue is taken and kept as proof that he has been murdered.

H105.2.1.p: The tongue of a slain giant is presented as proof that the giant was killed.

H105.3.p: An arm of a monster is kept as proof that a dog was innocent of wrongdoing.

H105.4.r: Africa (Ronga): Junod Les Chants et les Contes des Ba-Ronga (Lausanne, 1897) 317ff. No. 30.
H105.4.p: The head of a monster is taken and used as proof that its slayer killed it.

H105.4.1.p: A monster's beard is shown as proof that someone visited or confronted it.

H105.5.p: Ears, fingers, and noses of demons are cut off and kept as proof that they were killed.

H105.5.1.p: A tiger-slayer is recognized by the tips of the ears, nose, and tail of the dead tiger.

H105.5.2.p: The teeth and fingernails of a slain cyclops are taken as proof of the killing.

H105.5.3.p: The beak and claws of a slain monster are taken as proof that it was killed.

H105.5.4.p: A son abandoned by his parents in the wild shows the claws and tail of the tiger that was supposed to have killed him, proving he survived.

H105.6.p: Lovers recognize each other by matching a claw and a leg of a dragon.

H105.7.p: The sex organs of an enemy are taken as proof that he was slain.

H106.p: A person is identified by a severed limb that is matched with the rest of the body or with a matching piece.

H106.1.p: A person is identified by a severed hand that is matched or shown as proof.

H106.2.r: Type 507B (H. C. Andersen Rejsekammeraten); Icelandic: *Boberg; Cheremis: Sebeok-Nyerges.
H106.2.p: A severed head is presented as proof that a person was killed.

H110.p: A person is recognized by a piece of cloth or by clothing they wore.

H111.r: *Types 301, 510B, 451; English: Wells 116 (Sir Eglamour of Artois), 126 (Lai le Freine); Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Africa (Benga): Nassau 229 No. 34.
H111.p: A person is identified by a garment they wore or left behind.

H111.1.r: Burton Nights S VII 108; English: Wells 126 (Lai la Freine).
H111.1.p: A person is identified by royal garments, showing they are of noble or royal birth.

H111.2.p: A person is identified by a cloak made of feathers.

H112.p: A hero is recognized as the rightful person when his scarf is produced as proof of identity.

H113.r: *Types 300, 301; *Hartland Perseus III 206ff.; Missouri French: Carrière; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “mouchoir”; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H113.p: A character is identified as a particular person when a handkerchief belonging to them is shown as proof.

H114.p: A character is identified by a glove that belonged to them, which serves as proof of who they are.

H115.p: A character is recognized by a veil that they wore or that belonged to them, used as proof of identity.

H116.p: A character is identified by a girdle, or belt, that belonged to them, used as proof of identity.

H117.p: A piece is cut from a garment and kept, so that the fragment later serves as a token to prove identity.

H118.p: A strip torn from the garment of a rescued princess is used to bandage a wound, and later the cloth identifies her.

H119.p: Miscellaneous recognition tests in which a person is identified by a piece of cloth or clothing.

H119.1.p: A piece of cloth is fastened to a person's back as a guarantee that they will not be eaten on the way.

H119.2.p: A wife who has been abducted leaves a needle in her husband's garment as a sign of where she is or who took her.

H120.p: Miscellaneous recognition tests in which a person is identified by some other object or token.

H121.r: English: Wells 158 (Amis and Amiloun); Italian Novella: Rotunda.
H121.p: A person is identified by a cup that belonged to them or was marked as theirs.

H125.p: Miscellaneous recognition in which a person is identified by a weapon they own.

H125.1.p: A person is identified by a sword that belonged to them.

H125.2.p: A person is identified by a spear that belonged to them.

H125.3.p: A person is identified by a war-club that belonged to them.

H125.4.p: A person is recognized by a dart or arrow that they carry or that is identified as theirs.

H126.p: A person is identified by a coat of arms or heraldic emblem that they bear.

H131.p: A man is recognized by an axe that he carries.

H132.r: Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 46 No. 74; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 131 No. 74.
H132.p: A man who is a werewolf is recognized by a knife that the wolf had carried away.

H133.p: A slave recognizes a calabash (gourd) as a token and so learns that a girl is alive and where she lives.

H134.p: Someone is recognized through books that identify them.

H135.r: (Cf. H35.4.) Child I 40b, 487a; *Schoepperle Tristan and Isolt 301ff.; Irish myth: *Cross.
H135.p: A leaf or chip is floated down a stream to warn someone waiting farther downstream.

H135.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Africa (Nyanja): Rattray Some Folk-Lore Stories (London, 1907) 149ff. No. 24, (Chaga): Stamberg ZsES XXIII 296ff.
H135.1.p: Someone is recognized by a trimmed leaf dropped from a tree where they are hiding.

H135.2.p: Milk is poured into a stream as a signal to someone downstream.

H142.p: Someone is recognized by a mouth-harp (jaw harp) left beside a bed as a token.

H145.p: Someone is identified by a magic hand, a hand with supernatural properties that marks them.

H147.p: Someone is recognized by a tobacco pipe that serves as a token of identity.

H150.p: General heading for the circumstances under which a lost or disguised person is recognized.

H151.p: Someone's attention is drawn to a person or thing, and recognition follows.

H151.1.r: *Type 707; *BP II 380ff.; Italian: Basile Pentamerone Introduction; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H151.1.p: Attention is drawn by magic objects, and this leads to recognition.

H151.1.1.p: Attention is drawn by someone playing marbles with a remarkable jewel, and this leads to recognition.

H151.1.2.p: A gold and silver decorated mouse draws attention; as the princess turns to follow it, a suitor recognizes her.

H151.1.3.p: Someone is recognized by their ability to perform marvels or wonders.

H151.2.p: A helpful animal steals food from a wedding table, drawing attention, and recognition follows.

H151.3.r: *Type 933; *Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 173 (to Gonzenbach No. 85); *Baum PMLA XXXI 562 n. 59; Japanese: Ikeda.
H151.3.p: Parents come to their son, who is a priest or pope, to be confessed, and so he recognizes them.

H151.4.r: *BP I 489; *Fb “sæk” III 720b, “bæger” IV 83a; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 10; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
H151.4.p: A cup is hidden in a sack of men, who are then accused of stealing it, and this leads to recognition.

H151.5.p: A heroine working as a servant drops hints that draw someone's attention, and this leads to her being recognized.

H151.6.p: A heroine in menial disguise is discovered when her beautiful clothes are seen, and recognition follows.

H151.6.1.p: An enchanted heroine is seen briefly restored to her true form, and recognition follows.

H151.6.2.p: A disguised person is recognized because the disguise is imperfect.

H151.7.p: A hero uses his magic power to turn a girl into a carnation, and this display reveals who he is to the people watching.

H151.8.p: A husband is drawn to his wife because of her healing power, and this leads to him recognizing her.

H151.9.p: An abandoned child joins his parents in a game and is recognized by them as their own.

H151.9.1.p: An abandoned child is recognized through a game he is playing.

H151.10.p: Unknown brothers fight each other, and the combat reveals that they are related and leads to their recognition.

H151.11.r: English: Wells 130 (Emare). Cf. Chaucer’s Man of Law’s Tale.
H151.11.p: A hero is waited on at the table by his own son, whom he does not know; this leads to recognition of his wife.

H151.12.r: *Type 533; Köhler-Bolte I 347; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 7.
H151.12.p: Geese reveal the beauty of their mistress by speaking of her, and this leads to her recognition.

H151.13.p: A hero in disguise is discovered when a princess spying on him sees his golden hair.

H151.14.p: Tears falling from above onto someone below show that people are present up on a cliff, in a tree, or similar high place, which leads to their discovery.

H151.14.1.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 77.
H151.14.1.p: A girl who has been abandoned in a tree is recognized when a tear falls down from her onto someone below.

H151.15.p: A seller of trinkets mentions a son's address as the "tiger's son," which leads to the recognition of the true bride.

H152.p: A person is recognized by chance when people happen to meet by accident.

H152.1.p: Poor people are given alms, and one of them turns out to be someone who is recognized.

H152.1.1.p: A woman feeds and hosts every traveler who passes, hoping to find her husband among them.

H152.2.p: A husband who has become poor is recognized while working as a servant to his wife.

H152.3.p: An abandoned wife is recognized among a group of workers.

H153.p: An outcast wife, sometimes with her children, builds a castle exactly like the king's, invites him to it, and is recognized by him.

H154.p: An abandoned child is recognized when the parent comes to him asking for relief from famine.

H155.p: An abandoned queen invites all her persecutors to a forest and serves each of them the food they deserve, and so is recognized.

H157.p: A king finds a note with children, who were sent down a river in a casket, identifying them as his own.

H161.r: Prearranged signals. *Type 313, 325; *BP II 29, 516ff.; *Fb “hest” I 598b; *Köhler to Gonzenbach II 246.—Missouri French: Carrière; Hindu: Keith 142; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 340 n. 224.
H161.p: A person who has been transformed is recognized among others who look exactly alike.

H161.0.1.p: A person who has been transformed is recognized by someone among a group of companions who all look identical.

H162.r: Fb “bi” IV 36b; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
H162.p: A princess in disguise is revealed when a bee settles on her, showing who she really is.

H162.1.p: An insect shows which god is present by landing on the place where he is standing.

H162.2.p: A king is chosen because a cricket lands and sits on his head.

H162.3.p: A disguised princess is recognized when a bull picks her out.

H163.p: A person finds their own cow among a herd of twenty thousand by recognizing it.

H165.p: A father recognizes his son after having earlier thrown him into an oven, the recognition coming from the wounds or marks of that event.

H171.r: *Egerton JAOS XXXIII 158; *Chauvin VI 75 No. 239; Irish: Beal XXI 309.
H171.p: An animal or object shows, by its behavior, who has been chosen to be ruler.

H171.1.r: *Penzer V 175ff.; *Hartland Ritual and Belief (1914) 290ff.; *Christiansen FFC XXIV 124; Paris Zs. f. Vksk. XIII 6 n. 8.—India: *Thompson-Balys.
H171.1.p: An elephant bows to a man, showing that he is to be made king.

H171.1.1.p: An elephant lifts a girl up three times with its trunk, marking her as the future wife of the king.

H171.2.r: *Type 671; *BP I 325; Fb “pave” II 793a; *Loomis White Magic 66; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H171.2.p: A bird shows the election of a king, or in the version given, of a pope, by its action.

H171.3.r: *Howey Horse in Magic and Myth 157; Penzer IV 104, V 176; Herodotus II cap. 84—87; Herbert III 210; Oesterley No. 270.
H171.3.p: A horse shows the election of an emperor by its behavior.

H171.4.p: A man before whom a riderless chariot stops is chosen as king.

H171.4.1.p: A man before whom oxen stop is chosen as king, the oxen pulling a car that halts in front of him.

H171.5.p: A magic stone of destiny roars out when the rightful king stands on it, showing he is the true ruler.

H171.6.p: A chair moves toward a candidate, showing that he is to be chosen pope.

H172.p: An animal will serve or obey only one particular man and no one else.

H172.1.p: A horse will let only one particular man ride it and refuses everyone else.

H173.p: A man in disguise is recognized by his dog, which knows him despite the disguise.

H173.1.p: A disguised chieftain is recognized by a loyal swineherd, who knows him despite his disguise.

H173.2.p: A chieftain is recognized by a man who was once his captive, despite the chieftain's disguise or changed appearance.

H173.3.p: An animal is the first to recognize its master when the master returns, often after being disguised or away for a long time.

H175.r: *Dickson 16f., 69 n. 17; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 86.
H175.p: A person is recognized instantly and seemingly by supernatural means, through an unexplained sign rather than by sight or words, when an unknown family member is present.

H175.1.p: A son is recognized by his mother when milk suddenly gushes from her breasts at the sight of him.

H175.2.p: A child mysteriously recognizes a woman as his mother without being told.

H175.3.p: A sick prince's pulse beats violently when his beloved passes by, revealing who she is to him.

H175.4.p: A cold hearth suddenly bursts into flame when a particular man approaches, revealing his identity or connection.

H175.5.p: The ghost of an unknown child flies over the heads of its parents and bursts in a spray of blood, revealing their relationship.

H181.p: A person is recognized when a disguise or mask is removed.

H182.p: A person is recognized when beating causes them to cry out, and the outcry reveals who they are.

H183.p: A long-missing person is identified by his childhood nurse, who recognizes him from early memory.

H184.p: A person is recognized through the miraculous sight of a seer or saint, who perceives who they really are.

H186.p: A hero spits twice at his wife as a sign by which she recognizes him.

H187.p: A servant recognizes his master and saves him from death by this recognition.

H188.p: A princess appears before a crane, who had demanded her in marriage, and he recognizes her despite her loathly disguise.

H192.p: A person is recognized through a supernatural sign or event rather than by ordinary means.

H192.1.p: A man acceptable to God is shown by a knife that leaps into his hand.

H210.p: A trial or ordeal is used to determine whether a person is guilty or innocent.

H210.1.p: The guilt or innocence of souls is tested by having them cross a bridge.

H211.p: A criminal is exposed when a child is told to hand a knife to him and the criminal's reaction gives him away.

H215.r: Types 451, 710; Irish: Beal XXI 316; German: Grimm Nos. 3, 6, 120; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
H215.p: A supernatural sign at the moment of execution shows that the condemned person is innocent.

H215.1.p: The executioner's sword turns into wood when he tries to behead an innocent person, so the execution cannot go ahead.

H215.2.p: The rope used to hang an innocent person breaks, showing the prisoner did not deserve to die.

H215.3.p: Grass will not grow on the spot where an innocent man was hanged, marking him as innocent.

H215.4.p: A handprint that cannot be removed appears on a place or object, showing that the person it belongs to is innocent.

H216.p: Various signs, such as flowers blooming or a heavenly voice, that show a person is innocent of a charge.

H216.1.p: Flowers suddenly fill a garden when an innocent girl walks into it, showing she is innocent.

H216.2.p: A voice from heaven declares that the accused person is innocent.

H216.3.p: A church door opens by itself to show that the priest accused of a crime is innocent.

H217.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Korean: Zong in-Sob 195; Philippine: Fansler MAFLS XII 137.
H217.p: A dispute is settled by a contest between the parties, the winner being judged right.

H217.1.p: Two army leaders fight a single combat to decide which army wins the war.

H217.2.p: A single combat, called a holmgang, decides which man is to marry a girl.

H217.3.p: A holmgang, or formal duel, is fought to decide who owns a hoard of gold.

H217.4.p: A holmgang, or formal duel, is fought to decide who will become king.

H218.r: Thien Motive 41f.; *Schoepperle II 338ff.; Dickson 74, 77 n. 38, 78 n. 40, 130f., 153, 174, 226; *Ashdown Modern Lang. Review XVII 113ff.; Bell ibid XVIII 22ff.; *Boje 88; *Hibbard 35ff., 132 n. 11.—Irish myth: *Cross; English: Child V 490 s.v. “ordeal”, Wells 97 (Chevalere Assigne); Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; Hindu: Tawney I 396.
H218.p: A dispute of guilt or innocence is settled by a formal combat between the accuser and the accused, or their champions.

H218.0.1.r: Child II 34—48, 508a, 510b. See also most references to H218.
H218.0.1.p: A champion fights in the accused person's place to clear them of the charge, usually when the accused is a noblewoman or king.

H218.1.p: A judicial combat is stopped when friends of the losing fighter interfere and break it up.

H218.2.p: A wrestling match is used to test whether a son is legitimate.

H220.r: **Patetta Le Ordalie (1890). *Hdwb. d. Abergl. III 994ff.; Penzer VIII 196 n.; Keith Encyc. Relig. Eth. s.v. “ordeal”; Basset RTP XVII 397, 597, XIX 156ff., XXIII 182.—Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 317; English: Child V 490 “ordeal”; Icelandic: Boberg; West Indies: Flowers 455.
H220.p: Ordeals are painful or dangerous tests whose outcome is taken to establish whether a person is guilty or innocent.

H221.r: Basset RTP VI 631; Scala Celi 6b, 46b Nos. 38, 259; Herbert III 605f., Alphabet Nos. 69, 221, 434; *Gaster Exempla 191 No. 28.—Irish: O’Suilleabhain 71; English: Child V 490 s.v. “ordeal”; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Hindu: Keith 128; S. A. Indian (Brazil): Ehrenreich Int. Cong. Americanists XIV 661; Am. Negro (Georgia): Harris Nights 248 No. 42; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 238 No. 9.
H221.p: The suspect must walk through fire or leap over it, and the result decides whether they are guilty or innocent.

H221.1.p: A trial by fire in which the accused must pick up or handle burning coals to prove innocence.

H221.1.1.p: The accused carries live coals in a robe or cloak and is proven innocent if neither the garment nor the wearer is harmed.

H221.1.2.p: A person's holiness or innocence is tested by whether they survive being inside a burning house.

H221.1.3.p: Sacred books are thrown into a fire to test whether they are holy; the ones that do not burn are genuine.

H221.2.r: *Penzer VIII 195 n. 3, 196 n.; Basset RTP VII 284, 615, VIII 20, 431, 561; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
H221.2.p: A trial in which the accused must hold or handle red-hot iron to prove innocence.

H221.2.1.p: A virgin pulls on a piece of hot iron and names the men she accuses; both she and the men are burned only if they are guilty.

H221.2.2.p: Druids are said to apply the ordeal of red-hot iron to test the accused.

H221.3.r: Basset RTP VII 282, VIII 20; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 22.
H221.3.p: A trial in which the accused must pass through or touch burning oil to prove innocence.

H221.4.r: Basset RTP VII 281, 616, VIII 561; Irish: *Cross, O’Suilleabhain 50, Beal XXI 318; Icelandic: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
H221.4.p: A trial in which the accused must plunge a hand or body into boiling water to prove innocence.

H221.5.p: A fire ordeal in which spitting on the fire puts it out, and that extinguishing shows the spitter is innocent.

H222.r: *Kittredge Witchcraft 232ff., 536ff.; Penzer VIII 195f.; Basset RTP VII 285; *Fb “svømme” III 695b, “vand” III 999b, “vandprøve” III 1005b; Loomis White Magic 41.—Irish myth: *Cross; Greek: Frazer Pausanias III 388; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3664; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 456.
H222.p: A trial in which the accused is thrown into water, and innocence is shown by the ability to swim.

H222.0.1.p: Druids are said to apply the ordeal by water to test the accused.

H222.1.p: The legitimacy of children is tested by dipping them in a river; the child who is rightfully the father's is accepted.

H222.2.p: An ordeal in which holy water is given to a suspected person; a simpleton who closes his eyes to it is possessed, and one who laughs is merely foolish.

H222.3.p: Guilt or innocence is shown by how enchanted water affects the accused.

H222.4.p: Sacred books are thrown into water to test whether they are holy; the ones that stay intact are genuine.

H223.r: Penzer VIII 196 n.; Basset RTP VI 631, VII 278, 616; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
H223.p: A trial in which the accused must take poison, and survival or the effect of the poison shows guilt or innocence.

H224.r: Basset RTP VII 286; English: Child V 490 “ordeal.”
H224.p: A trial in which the accused is thrown to crocodiles or snakes; being devoured shows guilt, and being rejected shows innocence.

H224.1.p: A trial in which the accused must kiss poisonous snakes to prove innocence.

H225.r: Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 182, (Ekoi): Talbot 402; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 238 No. 9.
H225.p: A trial in which the accused must walk along a rope to prove innocence.

H225.1.p: An ordeal in which a suspect must walk across a ladder laid with knives; surviving without injury proves innocence.

H225.2.p: An ordeal in which a suspect must walk across eggs without breaking them; an unbroken egg shell shows innocence.

H226.p: An ordeal in which the accused is weighed twice; to be proven innocent, he must weigh less the second time.

H227.p: An ordeal in which the accused must carry the blood of a murdered man without spilling any; spilling it indicates guilt.

H228.p: An ordeal in which the suspect must crawl under a turf of sod that is cut loose from the ground, without it collapsing onto him.

H232.r: Declaration: if I am not innocent may I choke on bread and cheese. Kittredge Witchcraft 237f., 543 nn. 85—91; England: *Baughman.
H232.p: An ordeal in which the accused must eat bread and cheese; the food is believed to choke or harm the guilty.

H233.p: An ordeal in which the accused reaches into a bucket and pulls out a stone; the stone's color shows whether he is guilty or innocent.

H233.1.p: A lot-drawing ordeal in which the names of suspects are put in a chalice on an altar, and the person whose name is drawn is judged guilty.

H234.p: A test in which a suspected witch is weighed against the Bible; if she weighs less than the Bible she is judged guilty.

H235.p: An ordeal in which a cock is placed under a pot; if it crows when the suspect touches the pot, the suspect is guilty.

H236.p: An ordeal in which the accused is left out in the open to endure exposure; surviving it is taken as proof of innocence.

H240.p: A general heading for other ways of determining truth that are not ordeals.

H241.r: *Köhler-Bolte I 574f.; Fb “sko” III 288b; Icelandic: Saga och Sed 1940 p. 35, *Boberg; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 114.
H241.p: A person's worn-out shoes are presented as evidence that he has made a long journey.

H242.p: A test in which a messenger proves he was sent by a certain person by showing a sign or token that only that person would know or give.

H242.1.p: A messenger proves he comes from a certain person by riding a speckled horse.

H243.p: A magical test in which nature refuses to bear fruit when a false judgment has been pronounced.

H244.p: A person who speaks falsely is magically disfigured, so that the lie shows on his body.

H245.p: Lots are cast to find the truth, letting chance reveal who is right or guilty.

H245.1.p: A magic spell which, when recited over certain lots, makes them reveal guilt or innocence.

H248.r: English: Child V 3, 6, 498 s.v. “tests”; Africa (Mpongwe): Nassau 16ff. Nos. 1, 3, 3 version 2; (Basuto): Jacottet 14 No. 1.
H248.p: A test to see whether a person is really dead or only pretending to be dead.

H248.1.p: A person pretending to be dead is tested by pouring hot lead on their hand; a real corpse would not react, but a faker would pull away.

H248.2.p: A person pretending to be dead is tested by putting stinging insects down their back; a faker would betray themselves by reacting.

H248.2.1.p: A crocodile pretending to be dead is told to make its flesh quiver, and it obeys, which shows it is only feigning death.

H248.3.p: A person pretending to be dead is tested by pricking them with a pin or sharp object; a faker would flinch.

H248.4.p: To check whether fallen warriors are truly dead, burning wood is put in their mouths; a living man would react.

H248.5.p: A person pretending to be dead is caught because they blink their eyes.

H251.p: A magic object is used to test whether someone is telling the truth or swearing falsely.

H251.1.r: *Bolte Reise der Söhne Giaffers 216; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 8, 206; *Krappe Nuovi Studi Medievali II fasc. I (1925); *Spargo Virgil the Necromancer 207ff.; English: Child I 269, 270 n., cf. Alphabet No. 418; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
H251.1.p: A person swearing an oath puts their hand in the mouth of a carved stone face; if the oath is false, the mouth bites the hand off.

H251.1.1.p: A person swears an oath before a magic lion, and if the oath is false the lier is torn limb from limb.

H251.2.r: Fb “sten” III 554b; *Loomis White Magic 132.—Irish: Plummer clvii, *Cross.
H251.2.p: A magic stone forces whoever stands on it to speak only the truth.

H251.2.1.p: A liar cannot move a magic stone, so the stone shows who is speaking falsely.

H251.2.2.p: A magic stone sheds water when someone swears falsely, revealing the perjury.

H251.2.3.r: “But if (the) oath be true, the stone remains in its proper nature.” Irish myth: Cross.
H251.2.3.p: A stone on which a saint was born pours out water when perjury is committed over it.

H251.3.p: Some other magic object, not a stone or mouth, is used to test the truth.

H251.3.1.p: A tree reveals whether a person is committing perjury.

H251.3.2.p: A thief is found by a diviner's book and key: the closed book with a key inside is held loosely, and when the suspect's name written on the key is spoken and it is the thief's, the book and key turn around.

H251.3.3.r: Charm recited. If sieve trembles when name is called, that person is guilty. Kittredge Witchcraft 198ff. nn. 83—94; England: Baughman; Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn VI (1900) 389ff., (1936) 188ff.
H251.3.3.p: A thief is identified by a sieve balanced on open shears; the sieve turns when the accused's name is named.

H251.3.4.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 248a; *Zachariae Zs. f. Vksk. XXXIII 78; Chauvin II 129; BP IV 323, 389; Jewish: Gaster Exempla No. 121, *Neuman.
H251.3.4.p: A stick containing money breaks when a thief who swears innocence touches it, betraying him.

H251.3.5.p: A person swears an oath before an image; if the oath is false, the image turns around or changes color.

H251.3.6.p: A chain worn around the neck tightens when the wearer speaks falsely.

H251.3.7.p: A magic object placed on water sinks if the person being tested is guilty. It serves as a test of whether someone is lying or at fault.

H251.3.8.p: A magic object sticks to the hand of a guilty person, revealing their guilt.

H251.3.9.p: A magic spring punishes a person who swears falsely by disfiguring them. It exposes perjury through visible injury.

H251.3.9.1.p: A magic spring reveals a person guilty of killing a parent or of worshipping idols by disfiguring them.

H251.3.9.2.p: A well brings sheep up only for their rightful owner. A false claimant cannot get them, so the true owner is identified.

H251.3.10.p: When a judge rules falsely, fruit falls from the tree; when a judge rules justly, the fruit ripens to perfection. The fruit reveals whether the judgment was fair.

H251.3.11.p: A pig that cannot be boiled until four true stories have been told. Only truthful tales allow it to be cooked.

H251.3.12.p: A magic vessel that reveals whether what is said is true or false.

H251.3.13.p: A magic cup that tests whether statements are true or false, showing the difference between truth and lies.

H251.3.14.p: A princess who has been falsely accused is shown innocent when her dead body does not rot. Her accuser is then rejected as a liar.

H252.r: Person asserts a thing as true declaring: “If my words are true, may this or that happen.” W. J. Rees Lives of the Cambro-British Saints 193; J. P. Collier Old Shakespeare Society XIV 82; Alphabet Nos. 35, 486; *Burlingame Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society (July 1917) 429ff.; Fb “ildebrand” II 13.—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys, *Penzer II 31ff., III 179ff., IV 239 n. 3; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 23, 96, 151, 490, 531, 707, 832, II 412, 473, 614, 679, 816, 841, 933, 1060, 1098, 1153, 1258.
H252.p: A test of truth in which a person solemnly declares something true, and the truth of the statement is shown by a supernatural sign.

H252.0.1.p: A test in which a person must tell true stories; the truthfulness of the tales is the proof.

H252.1.p: A person places a hand on their genitals while swearing, and this gesture is taken as a test of whether they speak truly.

H252.2.p: The amount of blood in a person's spittle shows how fully they are under someone's power. The test is incomplete until the spittle is all blood.

H252.3.p: If an oath is false, fruit will fall from the tree as a sign of the lie.

H252.4.p: A person swears an oath with a boy's head as the pledge; if the oath is false, the boy will die.

H252.4.1.p: A boy falls dead when a true statement is made under the oath on his head, yet when a lie is told he is brought back to life. The result is reversed from what one might expect.

H252.4.2.p: Women who swear falsely by their husbands and children have those family members fall dead at once.

H252.5.p: A man who is hanged appeals to God to make an island sink as a sign that he is innocent. The island then sinks into the sea.

H252.6.p: A church clock that has been cursed never keeps correct time, as a sign of the curse.

H253.p: A person is tested for truthfulness by having them swear oaths before gods; the test shows whether they are telling the truth.

H255.p: A test to find out which of two twins is the elder: the younger twin, without thinking, hands the chopsticks to the elder, revealing his lower rank.

H256.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 93a; BP I 203, III 236.
H256.p: An innocence test in which an apple and gold are offered to a person; the innocent one takes the apple rather than the gold.

H256.1.p: A test of a child's innocence in which an onyx stone and a coal of fire are offered; the innocent child takes the stone rather than the burning coal.

H257.p: A holy man's sanctity is tested by asking him to perform miracles to prove it.

H257.1.p: The degree of a holy person's sanctity is tested by a candle: the one whose candle burns down first is the less holy.

H261.p: A man claims to be a great Bible reader, but a king who leaves a coin in his Bible finds it still there on the next visit, exposing the claim as false.

H263.p: A general test to reveal whether a person is sinful.

H263.1.p: A person suspected of sin is tested by being set adrift or exposed in a boat.

H264.p: A dead man is proven to have walked about after death because his footprints are found in manure or dust.

H300.p: A general heading for tests that are part of arranging or winning a marriage.

H301.r: *Chauvin V 63 No. 19 n. 1; Irish myth: Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
H301.p: Impossibly hard demands are made of a suitor to stop the marriage from happening.

H305.p: A suitor must complete a task to win an ogress's daughter as his bride.

H310.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; English: Wells 16 (Guy of Warwick); Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 187; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 324 n. 170, 328 n. 186; S. A. Indian (Tropical Forests): Lowie BBAE CXLIII (3) 55, (Carib): Alexander Lat. Am. 264; Africa: Werner African 153f., (Benga): Nassau 227 No. 34.
H310.p: A suitor is put through severe tests by his prospective bride or her father before he can marry.

H310.1.p: A hero who marries a supernatural or divine wife must pass tests set for him.

H310.2.p: A brother unknowingly passes a test and so qualifies as the bridegroom of his own sister.

H311.r: (Cf. H362, T55.7.) Types 314, 502; BP III 111; Krappe Revue Hispanique LXXXI 5ff.; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 104, *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
H311.p: Suitors for a princess's hand must present themselves for public inspection before being accepted.

H312.r: Penzer III 66; Irish myth: *Cross; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 106 n. 1.
H312.p: Suitors must meet certain physical or mental requirements to be accepted.

H312.1.r: Africa (Mpongwe): Nassau 69 No. 15; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 272 No. 85.
H312.1.p: The successful suitor must have no blotches or skin marks on his body.

H312.2.r: *Fb “tand” III 771a; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 93; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 1.
H312.2.p: The successful suitor must have gold teeth.

H312.3.p: A suitor is chosen by looking only at a part of him, namely his feet, which are the only part of him visible to the one choosing.

H312.4.p: To win the bride, a suitor must have the whitest hands. A blacksmith qualifies because he washes his hands so often that they stay clean.

H312.4.1.p: The successful suitor must have beautiful hands, though not white ones; they are dark, marked with scars, and wearing gold rings.

H312.5.p: The successful suitor must have a particular appearance: cheeks red as blood, skin white as snow, and hair black as a raven's.

H312.6.p: A suitor is tested on whether he can dress correctly.

H312.7.p: A suitor must show he is able to pass through a solid wall.

H312.8.p: The bridegroom-to-be must bring a set of specific strange items: three pecks, three quarts of gold, an animal with a horn on its head pointing up at the sky, and a large red hair.

H313.p: A suitor is tested on whether he is obedient and humble toward the bride.

H313.1.p: The princess agrees to marry whoever gives her anything she wishes for during one month.

H313.2.p: A fairy agrees to marry the king only if he either cuts off his son's head or gives up fasting on the eleventh day.

H314.p: A suitor's sincerity and devotion are tested.

H314.1.r: Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 85 No. 14.
H314.1.p: The suitor's sincerity is tested by telling him the girl has died; all but one of the suitors make excuses for not helping with the funeral.

H314.2.p: The suitor's sincerity is tested by sending him into seven years of banishment to see if he stays faithful.

H315.r: They vie in enticements. *Type 621, 850; Köhler-Bolte I 428f.
H315.p: A suitor is tested by seeing whom the princess turns to. Rival suitors sleep with the princess, and the one she turns to is the one who gets to have her.

H315.1.p: A suitor must make the princess fall in love with him.

H315.2.p: The bride is offered to whichever suitor gives the token showing the greater love.

H316.r: (Often golden apple.) *Type 502; *BP III 111; Cosquin Contes Indiens 317ff.; Chauvin VI 3, *201, VIII 151, *Galtier RTP XIV 65; Fb “guldæble” I 516a; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 93a.
H316.p: The princess shows her choice of suitor by throwing an apple to him.

H316.1.p: The princess shows her choice by throwing an orange or lemon to the chosen suitor.

H316.2.r: Cosquin Contes Indiens 317ff.; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H316.2.p: The princess shows her choice by throwing flowers to the chosen suitor.

H316.3.r: Indonesian: De Vries’s list No. 216; Persian: Carnoy 341.
H316.3.p: The princess shows her choice by throwing a ball, or a goblet, to the chosen suitor.

H316.4.p: A suitor is tested by throwing a garland; whichever man the girl chooses is shown by where the garland lands, so the garland reveals her choice.

H316.5.p: A girl shows her love for a suitor by tossing small pebbles at him.

H317.p: A suitor must serve for a long period of time before he can win the bride.

H317.1.r: Frazer Old Testament II 342—368; English: Wells 149 (The Squyr of Low Degre), Child I 204—6, 255, V 212b; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Cowell Jataka VI 164.
H317.1.p: A suitor must serve the bride's family for seven years before he can marry her.

H317.2.p: A suitor must keep silent for two years before he can marry the bride.

H317.3.p: A gardener's son may marry the princess only if he stays in prison for twelve years.

H317.4.p: The bride's family repeatedly delays the wedding to test whether the suitor's love and patience last.

H318.p: The suitor chosen is the one who will pay a huge sum of money for the bride.

H321.p: The suitor must hide from the princess, but she can see him anyway because she has magic sight.

H322.r: Type 590; Fb “skjule”; cf. Thompson CColl II 393; Filipino: Fansler MAFLS XII 183; Tuamotu: Stimson (z-G. 13/1241); West Indies: Flowers 457.
H322.p: The suitor must find the princess, who is hidden or otherwise hard to locate, to win her.

H322.1.p: The suitor must find an object that the princess has hidden in order to win her.

H322.2.p: The suitor must reach the imprisoned princess within a year to win her.

H322.3.p: The suitor must bring back a leg that fits a dragon's claw left behind by the princess's lover.

H322.4.p: The suitor must bring back a maiden's lost shoe to prove he has found her.

H323.r: Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 45 No. 5.
H323.p: The suitor must learn the girl's name to win her.

H324.r: *Type 554; BP II 28; Irish myth: Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: Dixon 217; Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Ikeda.
H324.p: The suitor must pick out the princess from a group of women dressed exactly alike.

H324.1.p: The suitor must pick out his sweetheart's sedan chair from thirty others that look just like it.

H326.p: The suitor must show a particular skill to be accepted as husband.

H326.1.p: The suitor must show skill at handicrafts, such as making or repairing objects, to win the bride.

H326.1.1.p: The suitor must build a mechanical peacock that moves on its own to win the bride.

H326.1.2.p: A suitor must prove his skill in archery, as one of the handicraft-style tests a would-be husband faces before winning the bride.

H326.2.p: A suitor must eat a pomegranate without letting a single seed fall, showing his skill and care before he can win the bride.

H326.3.p: A suitor must show his skill at hunting to prove himself worthy of marrying the bride.

H326.4.p: A suitor must show his skill at fishing to prove himself worthy of marrying the bride.

H327.p: A suitor must show cleverness and learning, usually by answering hard questions or solving problems, to win the bride.

H328.p: A suitor must show great endurance, enduring some painful or extreme ordeal, to prove he deserves the bride.

H328.1.p: A suitor must drink heavily without getting drunk, showing he can resist intoxication to win the bride.

H328.2.p: A suitor must be swung by his mustache without shedding tears, enduring the pain to prove his worth.

H328.3.p: A suitor must endure a blow from a spear to prove his endurance and win the bride.

H328.4.p: A suitor must stand naked in a river through a winter night to prove his endurance and win the bride.

H328.5.p: A suitor must bathe in boiling water to prove his endurance and win the bride.

H328.6.p: The princess will be given in marriage to whichever man can withstand a twelve-year fight.

H331.r: *Types 513, 514, 900; Philippson FFC L 12f.—Icelandic: Egils saga einhendsa ok Ásmundar Berserkjabana (FAS III) 366; Finnish: Kalevala rune 3; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 9, *Rotunda; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 18f.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Werner 420; Japanese: Ikeda; Oceanic (New Zealand, Tahiti, Cook Group, Society Group): Dixon 61, 64; Eskimo (Aleut): Golder JAFL XXII 17; N. A. Indian: *Thompson-Tales 328n. 186; West Indies: Flowers 457.
H331.p: The bride is offered as the prize in contests that suitors compete in, with the winner gaining her hand.

H331.1.p: Suitors compete in difficult riding feats, and the one who succeeds wins the bride.

H331.1.1.r: *Type 530; *BP III 111 n. 3; Köhler-Bolte I 67; Hdwb. d. Märchens II 627ff.; **Boberg Prinsessen på Glasbjærget (Danske Studier [1928] 16ff.); *Fb “glarbjærg” I 459; Krappe The Glass Mountain (Modern Language Quarterly VIII 139—145); India: Thompson-Balys.
H331.1.1.p: A suitor must ride his horse up a glass mountain to win the bride.

H331.1.2.p: A suitor must ride his horse up to the fourth story of a tower to win the bride.

H331.1.2.1.p: A suitor must make his horse jump over a palace to win the bride.

H331.1.3.r: *BP III 113 n. 3; N. A. Indian (Chilcotin): Farrand JE II 43.
H331.1.3.p: A suitor must ride up a mast or spear to win the bride.

H331.1.3.1.p: A suitor must make his horse jump over a high hedge to win the bride.

H331.1.4.p: A suitor must ride his horse across a pit to win the bride.

H331.1.5.r: *Panzer Sigfrid 110; Krappe Waberlohe (Archiv fur das Studium der neueren Sprachen CLXXII 10ff.); Icelandic: *Boberg.
H331.1.5.p: A suitor must prove himself by riding a horse through fire to win the bride, who is offered as the prize.

H331.1.6.p: A suitor must prove himself by jumping a river on horseback to win the bride offered as the prize.

H331.1.6.1.p: A suitor must jump on horseback over ditches and hedges made of spears to win the bride, a harder form of the river-jumping contest.

H331.1.7.p: A contest in reaping decides who wins the beautiful girl: the best reaper becomes her husband.

H331.2.r: *Type 508; Cosquin Contes Indiens 329ff.; *Liljeblad 39ff.; Dickson 181; English: Wells 147 (Ipomedon); Icelandic: Boberg; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman.
H331.2.p: Suitors compete in a tournament of combat, and the winner gets the bride offered as the prize.

H331.2.1.p: Within the tournament, the suitor who succeeds in battle wins the bride.

H331.2.1.1.p: The bride is given to whichever suitor distinguishes himself most in battle, though the girl loves both suitors equally.

H331.3.r: Told of Joseph in contest for Virgin Mary. *Dh II 265; Jewish: *Neuman.
H331.3.p: The bride goes to the suitor whose staff blooms, that is, whose dead or dry staff sprouts leaves or flowers.

H331.4.r: Icelandic: Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Anesaki 295, Ikeda; N. A. Indian (Kutenai): Boas BBAE LIX 199 No. 64, (Sahaptin): Farrand MAFLS XI 157 No. 9, (Tsimshian): Boas BBAE XXVII 137, (Wichita): Dorsey CI XXI 130 No. 19, Dorsey Contributions to N. A. H331.4.p: Suitors compete in archery or shooting, and the best shot wins the bride offered as the prize.

H331.4.1.p: Suitors compete in shooting against the bride's father, and the winner gets the bride.
