H331.4.2.r: Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 300 n. 3; Japanese: Ikeda.
H331.4.2.p: A suitor wins the bride by bending the bow of the woman's absent husband.

H331.5.r: Dh III 145; Irish myth: Cross; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 23 n. 5, 160 n. 2; India: Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (Salishan): Hill-Tout British North America 229, (Shuswap): Teit JE II 684 No. 22, (Thompson River): Teit MAFLS VI 36 No. 7, (Skykomish): Haeberlin JAFL XXXVII 383 No. 9, (Achomawi): Curtin JAFL XXII 284 No. 2, (Arapaho): Dorsey and Kroeber FM V 105, (Ponca): Dorsey CNAE VI 333, (Menomini): Skinner and Satterlee PaAm XIII 396 No. 25, (California): Gayton and Newman 92; Africa (Vai): Ellis 189 No. 5; West Indies: Flowers 458.
H331.5.p: Suitors compete in a race, and the winner gets the bride offered as the prize.

H331.5.0.1.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 160 n. 2.
H331.5.0.1.p: In a race for the bride, the suitor who loses must die.

H331.5.1.r: *Types 513, 514; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 8; Greek: Fox 59.
H331.5.1.p: A suitor races the princess for her hand in marriage.

H331.5.1.1.r: (Atalanta.) Oesterley Gesta Romanorum No. 60; *BP IV 138; Herbert III 193; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Greek: Fox 59, *Grote I 138.
H331.5.1.1.p: During the race with the bride, someone throws an apple; she stops to pick it up, and the suitor passes her and wins.

H331.5.1.1.1.p: The hero's helper slows the princess down by blowing against her with his extraordinary breath, so she loses the race.

H331.5.2.r: Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 181; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 157 n. 4.
H331.5.2.p: A suitor races against the bride's father to win the bride.

H331.5.3.p: A suitor must win three horse races to earn the bride.

H331.5.4.p: A suitor must win a boat race to earn the bride.

H331.6.r: (Cf. H1562.9.) India: Thompson-Balys Eskimo (Aleut): Golder JAFL XXII 17.
H331.6.p: Suitors compete in wrestling, and the winner gets the bride offered as the prize.

H331.6.1.r: N. A. Indian (Wasco): Curtin PAES II 290 No. 2.
H331.6.1.p: A suitor must win a wrestling match against the bride, who is offered as the prize for the winner.

H331.6.1.1.p: The princess wins the wrestling match against her suitor by showing him her breast, which makes him look away and lose.

H331.7.p: A suitor must win a bride by hitting a target with a thrown or shot object.

H331.8.r: N. A. Indian (Snohomish): Hill-Tout British Assn. Adv. Science (70th meeting) 525.
H331.8.p: A suitor must win a bride by splitting a set of antlers, typically with an axe or sword.

H331.9.r: N. A. Indian (Shoshoni): Lowie JAFL XXXVII 237 No. 18, (Pawnee): Dorsey MAFLS VIII 178 No. 45, (Gros Ventre): Kroeber PaAM I 80 No. 19.
H331.9.p: A suitor must win a bride by catching or snaring animals in a trap.

H331.10.p: A suitor must carry one hundred jugs of water from the sea to the castle within a single day to win the bride.

H331.11.p: The princess is given in marriage to the man who confesses all his treachery.

H331.12.p: A suitor must win a bride by splitting a block of wood.

H331.13.p: A suitor wins the bride by cheating in the contest, and the contest is decided in his favour through deceit.

H331.14.p: A suitor must win the bride by passing a test of physical strength.

H331.15.p: A suitor must win the bride by staging or winning a fight between animals.

H331.15.1.p: A suitor must win the bride by winning a cockfight.

H331.15.2.p: A suitor must win the bride by winning a bullfight.

H331.16.p: A suitor must win the bride by throwing a ball up to her.

H331.16.1.p: A suitor must win the bride by throwing an iron ball up to her.

H331.17.p: A suitor must win the bride by eating one hundred carcasses in one sitting.

H332.p: A suitor must compete against the bride herself or a member of her family to win her.

H332.1.p: A suitor must compete directly against the bride to win her.

H332.1.1.p: A suitor must win a duel against the bride to win her hand.

H332.1.2.p: A suitor must defeat the bride in a game to win her hand.

H332.1.2.1.p: A suitor must beat the bride in a game of dice to win her hand.

H332.1.3.p: A suitor must beat the bride at harp playing to win her hand.

H332.1.4.p: A suitor must win a tournament against the bride to win her hand.

H332.1.5.p: A suitor must win a shooting contest against the bride-to-be to marry her.

H332.2.r: Icelandic: *Boberg; S. A. Indian (Chincha): Alexander Lat. Am. 231.
H332.2.p: A suitor must win a contest against the bride's brother-in-law to gain her.

H332.3.p: A suitor must fight the bride's father-in-law in a duel as a test to marry her.

H332.4.p: The groom and his army must fight the bride's army before he can marry her.

H333.p: A girl demands that her suitor be killed or mutilated as the price of her love.

H333.1.p: At the girl's request, her lover has his head cut off.

H333.2.p: The suitor must bring the girl the severed hands of others as proof of his worth.

H335.r: (For nature of tasks see H1000ff.) *Types 313, 502, 513, 514, 518, 570, 577; BP II 87ff., III 267ff., 424ff.; Hibbard 275ff. (Sir Eglamour).—Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Finnish: Kalevala runes 7, 8, 13, 14, 19; Italian Novella: *Rotunda, Basile Pentamerone II Nos. 5, 7; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 87 n. 3, II 61 n. 3, Fox 107; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesian: De Vries’s list No. 168; Indo-Chinese: Scott Indo-Chinese 290; Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Anesaki 262; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 13/174, 13/203, 13/276, 13/317, 13/441, 13/499, 13/730, 13/243, 13/1241); Easter Island: Métraux Ethnology 57; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 324 n. 170; Africa (Mpongwe): Nassau 31 No. 4, (Benga): Nassau 134 No. 15; West Indies: Flowers 458. Cf. Wünsche Teufel 33 (devil).
H335.p: A suitor is given tasks to perform, and the bride is the reward for completing them.

H335.0.1.r: *Type 313; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; German: Grimm Nos. 92, 113, 121, 196; Italian: Basile Pentamerone II No. 7, Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Ikeda.
H335.0.1.p: The bride gives the suitor help in carrying out the tasks set for him.

H335.0.1.1.p: A otherworld mistress, following her mother's orders, tells the hero how to do his tasks.

H335.0.1.2.p: The bride's supernatural parents secretly help the suitor win the contests.

H335.0.2.r: *De Vries FFC LXXIII 308; Irish myth: *Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Japanese: Ikeda.
H335.0.2.p: The girl herself sets tasks for her suitors to perform.

H335.0.2.1.p: The suitor is assigned to study philosophy for five years.

H335.0.2.2.p: The prince is assigned to learn a trade before he may marry the girl.

H335.0.3.p: The devil, as a suitor, is given tasks to perform.

H335.0.4.p: The tasks a suitor must perform are announced in an inscription on a statue.

H335.0.5.p: A goddess sets a task for her mortal suitor to complete.

H335.1.p: A suitor must avenge the death of the bride's father before he is allowed to marry her.

H335.1.1.p: A suitor must avenge the bride's former fiancé before he is allowed to marry her.

H335.2.p: A suitor must cut open a magic gourd before he may marry the bride.

H335.3.p: A suitor must kill a fierce or dangerous animal before he may marry the bride.

H335.3.1.p: A suitor must kill a dragon to which the princess is to be sacrificed before he can marry her.

H335.3.2.p: A suitor must kill a lion that guards a girl before he may marry her.

H335.3.3.p: A suitor must slay a boar that steals before he may marry the bride.

H335.3.4.p: A suitor must kill a snake that guards treasure and lies around the princess's chamber before he may marry her.

H335.3.5.p: As a task, the hero's servant must kill a giant pig.

H335.3.6.p: A suitor must kill tiger demons before he may marry the bride.

H335.3.7.p: A suitor must kill other monsters before he may marry the bride.

H335.4.p: A suitor must defeat enemies before he may marry the bride.

H335.4.1.p: A suitor must bring back the head of an enemy as proof before he may marry the bride.

H335.4.2.p: A suitor must overcome robbers before he may marry the bride.

H335.4.3.p: A suitor must kill all earlier suitors before he may marry the bride.

H335.4.4.p: A suitor must kill or defeat an unwelcome suitor before he may marry the bride.

H335.5.p: A suitor must bring back food as a marriage gift before he may marry the bride.

H335.6.p: A suitor must make the weather calm before he may marry the bride.

H335.6.1.p: A suitor must control a violent tide before he may marry the bride.

H336.r: *Types 513, 514; Irish myth: *Cross; English: Wells 115 (Sir Eglamore); German: Grimm Nos. 6, 62, 93, 96, 97, 106, 137, 163, 197; Icelandic: *Boberg; Africa (Fjort): Dennett 74.
H336.p: Suitors are given quests that they must complete before they may marry the bride.

H336.1.p: A prospective father-in-law makes a suitor for his daughter's hand travel to a foreign country, possibly the otherworld, as a condition. The purpose is to learn feats of arms.

H336.2.p: A suitor for a girl's hand must catch wild animals to prove himself.

H338.p: A suitor must prove he is faithful, a test of loyalty before he can marry the princess.

H338.1.p: A suitor must prove his loyalty by keeping the princess's secret.

H341.r: *Types 559, 571, 1642; *BP I 59, 61, II 39ff., 454 n. 1; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XXVI 89 n. 1; Italian: Basile Pentamerone Introduction, I No. 3; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H341.p: A suitor must make the princess laugh, since she has never laughed before.

H341.1.p: The princess is made to laugh by seeing people stick together in some awkward way.

H341.2.p: The princess is made to laugh by small animals.

H341.3.r: *Type 571; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XXVI 89 n. 1; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 3.
H341.3.p: The princess is made to laugh by the hero's foolish behavior.

H341.3.1.p: The princess laughs at an indecent display the hero makes during a quarrel with an old woman at a well.

H342.p: A suitor must outwit the princess in a contest of cleverness to win her.

H342.1.p: The suitor must trick the princess into saying "That is a lie."

H343.r: *Type 945; BP III 53ff.; *Gründwald Hessische Blätter f. Vksk. XXX 317; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Yoruba): Ellis 263; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 279 No. 95; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 277 n. 1.
H343.p: A suitor must get a mute princess to speak in order to win her.

H343.0.1.p: The princess will marry the man who can make her speak to him during all watches of the night.

H343.1.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 105 No. 860; India: Thompson-Balys.
H343.1.p: A shepherd insults the mute princess, and this makes her speak.

H343.2.p: The mute princess gives the right answer when the suitor-prince deliberately gives a talking monkey the wrong one.

H344.p: A suitor must enter the princess's bedchamber in a way that wins her, as a test.

H344.1.p: The princess will marry the man who can correctly describe what happened in her bedchamber.

H345.p: A suitor must prove he is stronger than the princess, overcoming her in a contest of strength.

H345.1.p: The suitor must lift the strong princess's giant weapon.

H345.2.p: The suitor must ride the strong princess's horse.

H346.r: *Types 610, 613; *Christiansen FFC XXIV 98; BP III 267ff.; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; S. A. Indian (Chincha): Alexander Lat. Am. 231.
H346.p: A princess is promised in marriage to whichever man can heal her.

H346.1.p: A widowed queen promises to marry the man who heals her sick husband and kills the witch or sorcerer who bewitched him.

H347.p: A suitor must spend a night with the princess without falling asleep; the suitors are secretly given a sleeping potion so they fail.

H351.p: A suitor must survive on only a very small amount of food.

H351.1.p: A suitor must live on as much food as can be piled on a single leaf.

H352.p: A suitor must make a garden bloom in winter as a condition for marrying the princess.

H353.p: A suitor must plunge into a stream as a test before he may marry.

H355.p: A suitor must find some extraordinary object to win the bride.

H355.0.1.p: Several suitors each bring back some marvelous thing, and it turns out all of these objects must be used together to save the girl's life.

H355.1.p: A suitor must find a cow with silver horns.

H355.2.p: A suitor must find a hog with silver bristles.

H355.3.p: A suitor must bring back a marvelous tree.

H355.4.p: A suitor must obtain flowers as a condition of marriage.

H355.5.p: A suitor must get for the bride a necklace like her mother's.

H355.6.p: A suitor must get a wedding dress so fine that it can be drawn through a ring.

H359.p: Other tests set for suitors that do not fit the categories above.

H359.1.p: A suitor must build a causeway as a condition of marriage.

H359.2.p: A suitor must clear a piece of land as a condition of marriage.

H360.p: A test set for the bride, who must prove herself worthy before the marriage.

H361.p: The bride must be the one who possesses a certain ring or jewel, which the hero must have to marry her.

H362.p: A suitor chooses his bride from among the girls gathered at a feast, the choice itself serving as the test.

H363.p: A dead wife's instructions set conditions a man must meet: he will marry only a woman who fits the specifications she left behind.

H363.1.p: As a bride test, the candidate must wear the dead wife's clothes, and only the one whose clothes fit is the right bride.

H363.2.p: As a bride test, the candidate must wear the dead wife's ring, and the right bride is the one on whom it fits.

H365.p: A bride is chosen by the size of her feet, so that only the woman with the right foot size is accepted.

H373.r: *Type 875; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 4; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
H373.p: A suitor must prove herself by performing a set of tasks, and the one who completes them is chosen as bride.

H375.p: The choice of bride is decided by a contest played as a game.

H375.1.p: The hero plays hide and seek with seven princesses, and whoever he finds becomes his wife.

H375.2.p: The man marries the girl who is first to bring him his clothes.

H375.3.r: S. A. Indian (Toba): Métraux MAFLS XL 44, 45.
H375.3.p: The bride is chosen by who gathers food plants in the shortest time.

H381.p: A bride is tested for thrift, meaning careful use of materials and food without waste.

H381.1.p: The bride proves her thrift by making a dress from flax that others would have wasted.

H381.2.r: Type 1452; BP III 236; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 92b.
H381.2.p: A bride is tested for thriftiness by how she cuts a cheese. The first girl eats the rind and all, the second cuts away good cheese, and the third cuts away only as much as needed, and she passes.

H381.2.1.p: The bride proves her thrift by peeling an apple so carefully that almost nothing is wasted.

H381.2.2.p: The bride proves her thrift by scraping the bread tray so cleanly that no dough is wasted.

H382.p: A bride is tested for industry, meaning hard work and diligence.

H382.1.p: A suitor hides a key in the flax on the spinning wheel; a lazy girl fails to find it the next day, revealing her laziness.

H383.p: A bride is tested for housekeeping and cooking skills.

H383.1.p: A bride is tested on her ability to make bread.

H383.1.1.r: Type 1453***; Russian: Andrejev No. 1453*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1454.*
H383.1.1.p: The bride is judged by dough under her fingernails: after three weeks she still has dough there, showing she is a careless or messy cook.

H383.1.2.p: The bride is tested on her skill at cooking griddle cakes.

H383.2.p: A suitor tests whether a prospective bride is good at cloth-making, such as spinning, weaving or sewing.

H383.2.1.p: The bride is tested on spinning and fails because she cannot use a spinning-wheel.

H383.2.2.p: The bride must weave a magic cloth or sew a magic shirt to pass the test.

H383.2.3.p: The bride must sew a shirt for her bridegroom's father as her test.

H383.3.p: The bride is tested on how skillfully and neatly she sweeps.

H383.4.p: The bride is tested on her cooking skill.

H383.4.1.p: The bride is tested on her ability to brew ale.

H383.5.p: The bride must cut up a monstrous fish with scaly hide as her test.

H384.p: A suitor tests whether a bride is kind to others, especially to people in need.

H384.0.1.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 75.
H384.0.1.p: The suitor chooses the bride who is kind, out of several candidates.

H384.1.p: The bride's kindness is tested by her father-in-law, who comes to her disguised as a beggar.

H384.1.1.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; S. A. Indian (Caraja): Métraux MAFLS XL 49.
H384.1.1.p: A wealthy, handsome suitor disguises himself as a beggar to see whether the bride is kind to him.

H384.1.2.p: A prince pretends to be a madman to see what kind of person the bride really is.

H385.p: A suitor tests whether a bride is greedy; her response shows whether she is grasping.

H386.p: A suitor tests whether a bride is obedient to him.

H386.1.p: The bride must submit to being beaten with a shoe as proof of her obedience.

H387.p: A suitor tests whether a bride stays faithful and steadfast to her love.

H387.1.r: English: Wells 151 (The Squyr of Lowe Degre).
H387.1.p: The bride's faithfulness is tested by her mourning for seven years for a lover who is supposed to be dead.

H388.p: A suitor tests whether a bride is wise and clever.

H400.r: *Types 870, 870A; *Bédier Fabliaux 465; Dunlop-Liebrecht 85; Child I 258—71, 507a, II 502, III 503, IV 454a, V 215f., 289a; *Cross MPh X 289; Heinrich von dem Türlin Diu Crone, lines 917f.; Clouston Tales I 173ff.—Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; Arabian: Burton Nights V 271, 278, VII 259, IX 252ff.; India: Thompson-Balys, Penzer I 167, *Tawney I 86 n., 329, 487, *II 601 n.; Chinese: Werner 269; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 516, 535; Samoa: Beckwith Myth 535; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 358 n. 287 m.
H400.p: Various tests are used to check whether a woman, or sometimes a man, is chaste and faithful.

H410.p: A test of a woman's chastity carried out with magic objects or painful trials, used to decide whether she is sexually faithful or pure.

H411.p: A magic object reveals that a woman is unchaste, for example by reacting to her or refusing to accept her.

H411.1.r: At foot of bed: cannot be stepped on by unchaste woman. (Cf. D931.) *Type 870A; Fb “sten” III 554b; English: Child I 269 n.
H411.1.p: A magic stone serves as the test: it shows whether a woman is chaste.

H411.1.1.p: A magic stone breaks apart when an unchaste woman looks at it.

H411.2.p: A magic tree serves as the test: an unchaste woman cannot climb it.

H411.3.p: A magic plant serves as the test of a woman's chastity.

H411.4.r: (Cf. D1171.6.) Unchaste woman cannot drink from cup. *Chauvin VII 167; Bédier Fabliaux 465; Child I 262—273 passim; Penzer I 165; Cross MPh X 289; Irish myth: *Cross.
H411.4.p: A magic drinking horn or cup serves as the test of a woman's chastity.

H411.4.1.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas II 119, 345, *Neuman.
H411.4.1.p: A magic cup test in which the unchaste who drink from it are poisoned by the water.

H411.4.2.p: A magic cup sticks to the hands of an adulterer, revealing the guilt.

H411.5.p: A magic pin serves as the test: if it floats, the woman is chaste.

H411.6.r: (Cf. D1151.2.) Chauvin VII 168; English: Child I 72f., 75.
H411.6.p: A magic chair serves as the test: an unchaste woman cannot sit in it until she is bidden to.

H411.7.r: (Cf. D1053.) *Chauvin VII 168; *Cross MPh X 289, XVI 649; *Child I 260ff., 265, V 289a; Bédier Fabliaux 465; BP IV 138; Oesterley No. 69; Irish myth: *Cross.
H411.7.p: A magic mantle serves as the test: it will not fit an unchaste woman.

H411.8.r: (Cf. D1258.) *Bolte Montanus 631; Chauvin VII 168; Child I 267, 269.
H411.8.p: A magic bridge serves as the test: an unchaste person cannot cross it.

H411.9.p: A magic statue serves as the test: its eyes move when an unchaste woman is present.

H411.9.1.p: A magic idol serves as the test: it turns black in the presence of an unchaste woman and lights up for a chaste one.

H411.10.r: (Cf. D1154.1.) Liungman Två Folkminnesundersökningar 1ff.; English: Child I 64—70 passim.
H411.10.p: A magic bed and pillows serve as the test: they speak and reveal a woman's unchastity.

H411.11.r: (Cf. D927.) Irish myth: Cross; English: Floris and Blanchefleur line 618.
H411.11.p: A magic spring serves as the test: its water wells up if the girl is not a virgin.

H411.11.1.p: An unchaste woman who dips her arm into the magic spring has her skin boiled away.

H411.11.2.p: Two fountains serve as chastity tests: one of clear water and one of muddy water, which reveal the woman's purity.

H411.12.p: A magic harp serves as the test: it plays out of tune when an unchaste girl approaches.

H411.13.p: A magic lamp is used to test a woman's chastity: it will light only for a virgin, and refuses to light for one who is not.

H411.14.p: An apple is used as a magic chastity test: it fades if its owner is not a virgin.

H411.15.p: A magic mirror serves as an indicator of a woman's chastity, showing whether she is unchaste.

H411.16.p: Catching a salmon is taken as proof of a woman's virginity.

H411.17.p: A swan is used as a chastity test, showing whether a woman is a virgin.

H411.18.p: Dust from the Tabernacle is used as a chastity test, revealing whether a woman is a virgin.

H412.p: A woman's chastity is tested by some ordeal, a painful or dangerous trial whose outcome shows whether she is a virgin.

H412.1.r: (Cf. D1254.2.) Irish myth: Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 96.
H412.1.p: A woman must pass under a magic rod as a chastity ordeal; an unchaste woman will bear twins.

H412.2.p: A woman tests her chastity by holding the shaved and greased tail of a bull; the ordeal reveals whether she is a virgin.

H412.3.p: A feather is hung over a door; a girl who enters and blushes is judged not to be a virgin.

H412.4.p: A woman proves her chastity by passing through fire unharmed.

H412.4.1.p: A woman proves her chastity by holding a hot iron; the ordeal shows whether she is a virgin.

H412.4.2.p: A woman swears an oath with her hand in boiling oil as a chastity ordeal.

H412.5.p: A poisonous snake is placed around a girl's neck as a chastity ordeal.

H412.6.p: A woman's lover is drawn out of a wall by a single-thread rope, as a chastity ordeal.

H412.7.p: A woman's chastity is tested by jumping; the outcome of the jump shows whether she is a virgin.

H412.7.1.p: A woman's chastity is tested by jumping over a magic thread; the outcome shows whether she is a virgin.

H412.7.2.p: A woman's chastity is tested by jumping over a pit; the outcome shows whether she is a virgin.

H413.p: A chaste woman is said to have special magic powers, which reveal or prove her purity.

H413.1.p: A chaste woman can blow out a candle with one puff and relight it with another, showing her special power.

H413.2.p: A chaste woman proves her virtue by being able to make a ball out of water.

H413.3.p: A chaste woman proves her virtue by carrying water in a sieve without it leaking out.

H413.4.p: A chaste woman has the special power to lift an elephant that has fallen down.

H413.5.p: A woman's chastity is tested by whether she can throw a certain number on dice.

H413.6.p: A princess who is chaste weighs only as much as five flowers, while an unchaste one weighs normally.

H421.p: Magical tests used to find out whether a lover is truly faithful.

H421.1.p: A valley that no false lover can leave, but that a true lover can enter and leave freely.

H422.p: Magical tests used to find out whether a husband is faithful.

H422.1.p: A crown reveals when husbands have been unfaithful to their wives.

H425.p: Magical tests used to identify men whose wives have been unfaithful to them.

H425.1.p: A cuckold's knife will not be able to carve a boar's head.

H425.2.r: *New English Dictionary V 385c s.v. “horn”; Dunger Germania XXIX 59; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 122.
H425.2.p: Horns grow on the head of a cuckold, a man whose wife has been unfaithful.

H426.p: Tests of chastity applied to holy men and monks, using magic or ordeals.

H430.r: *Type 888; *Penzer I 165ff.; *BP III 517ff.; Clouston Tales II 290ff.; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 110f.
H430.p: Objects that show whether a separated lover or spouse has remained faithful or been unfaithful.

H431.p: A piece of cloth or clothing that shows whether a separated lover or spouse has been faithful.

H431.1.r: D1056.) *Type 888; BP III 517ff.; Penzer I 44, 165; Oesterley No. 69; Herbert III 233; English: Child I 268.
H431.1.p: A shirt that stays white as long as the woman (or man) is faithful to the absent partner.

H431.2.p: A handkerchief or piece of cloth reveals chastity: it stays clean as long as the woman (or man) remains faithful, and soils if they are not.

H431.3.p: Flowers embroidered on a veil fade when worn on the head of someone who is unfaithful.

H432.r: (Cf. D975.) Fb “brudekrans” IV 65b; English: Child I 268; India: *Thompson-Balys, Penzer I 165.
H432.p: A flower that shows whether a separated lover or spouse has been faithful.

H432.1.r: (Cf. D975.2.) G. Paris Romania XXIII 102ff.; Bédier Fabliaux 465; Köhler-Bolte II 444; Penzer I 165.
H432.1.p: A rose that fades when the absent lover or spouse has been unfaithful.

H432.1.1.p: Three roses fall off as a sign that the absent lover or spouse has been unfaithful.

H432.2.p: A lily is used as a test of a woman's chastity: it is taken to show whether she is faithful, as a sign of her purity.

H432.3.p: A lotus flower is used as a test of a woman's chastity, indicating whether she has been faithful.

H432.4.p: A staff or stick that blooms into flower is taken as a sign of a woman's chastity, showing whether she is faithful.

H433.p: An ornament or piece of jewelry is used as a test of a woman's chastity, changing or behaving in a way that shows whether she has been faithful.

H433.1.r: (Cf. D1076.) Penzer I 168; Child I 269; Zingerle Zs. f. Deutsche Myth. und Sittenkunde II (1855) 353.
H433.1.p: A ring is used as a test of faithfulness: its color shows whether the wife has been true to her husband.

H434.p: A fruit is used as a test of a woman's chastity, showing by its condition whether she has been faithful.

H434.1.p: An apple is used as a test of chastity: it keeps shining as long as the woman remains faithful.

H435.p: A weapon is used as a test of a woman's chastity, showing by its condition whether she has been faithful.

H435.1.p: A sword is used as a test of chastity: it will not become stained while the woman remains faithful.

H439.p: Miscellaneous tests of chastity using various objects that do not fit the other categories of this group.

H439.1.r: (Cf. D1266.2.) English: Child I 269; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
H439.1.p: A picture or painting is used as a test of chastity: its color shows whether the woman has been faithful.

H439.1.1.p: A painting is made on a wife's stomach as a test of chastity, its appearance showing whether she has been faithful.

H439.2.p: A drinking-tube is used as a test of chastity: it keeps the taste of another person's lips if the woman has been unfaithful.

H440.p: Other ways of showing whether a woman is chaste that do not fall under the more specific headings of this group.

H451.r: *Taylor MLN XXI 249 n. 2; Gering Hermes LI (1916) 632ff.; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 296 n. 83d.
H451.p: A woman's private parts speak and reveal her unchastity.

H452.p: A bride's chastity is tested by someone who disguises themselves to find out whether she is faithful.

H455.p: A king tests a princess's chastity by weighing her against a flower, the flower's weight showing whether she is pure.

H460.p: Tests of a wife's character and loyalty, undertaken by a husband or others to see how she behaves.

H461.r: Griselda. Children stolen and attendance at wedding to another demanded. *Type 887; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XXXV—XXXVI 290; Hdwb. d. Märchens s.v. “Geduldsprüfung”; **H. Siefkin Das geduldige Weib in der englischen Literatur bis auf Shakespeare (Leipzig, 1903); *Loomis White Magic 118; *Laserstein; Ilse von Stach Griseldis (1922); Köhler-Bolte II 501, 534; *Fb “Griselda” IV 486a; Huet 66; *Cate Studies in Philology XXIX 389ff.; *Hibbard Medieval Romance in Eng. 289 n. 9; Philippson FFC 1 48ff.—Italian Novella: *Rotunda. Cf. also Types 712, 881, 900.
H461.p: A husband tests his wife's patience to see whether she will endure his harsh or unreasonable treatment without complaint.

H461.1.p: A clever wife, disguised, wins a second wife for her husband, and so the husband learns to value her patience.

H465.r: *Type 900; BP I 443ff.; *Philippson FFC L 34ff.; *Fb “tigge” III 793b; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 10.
H465.p: A proud princess is married to a beggar and must endure poverty and hard menial work to prove her devotion to him.

H466.r: *Type 1350; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XIX 92 n. 2; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 144.
H466.p: A husband pretends to be dead to find out whether his wife will remain faithful to him.

H466.1.p: A husband pretends to be dead, or absent, to see whether his wife remains faithful to him.

H467.p: A husband tests his wife's love or faithfulness in various other ways not covered by more specific motifs.

H467.1.p: A husband pretends to be ill, claiming to have lost his genitals, to see how his wife will react.

H467.2.r: Olrik Zs. f. Vksk. II (1892) 254ff.; Icelandic: Boberg.
H467.2.p: A wife's faithfulness is tested when a marriage proposal is sent to her in another man's name.

H472.p: A husband tests whether his wife can keep a secret.

H472.1.r: She tells. When head is dug up it is sheep’s head. *T. Zachariae Zs. f. Vksk. XXXII—XXXIV 77; *De Vries FFC LXXIII 220ff., 224 n. 1; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 25, 275; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H472.1.p: A husband tells his wife he has buried the head of a murdered man, and she must keep this secret; in fact he has buried a sheep's head to test her.

H473.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
H473.p: A husband tests whether his wife will obey his commands.

H473.1.r: Herbert III 18; Crane Vitry 226 No. 228; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 318.
H473.1.p: A disobedient wife puts her finger into a hole where her husband has fixed sharp nails, and is hurt for disobeying.

H473.2.r: Herbert III 19; *Crane Vitry 231 No. 236; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 318; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
H473.2.p: A husband, at his wife's insistence, gives her one command: not to go into the oven while he is away. She disobeys and the oven falls on her.

H473.3.r: Herbert III 24; Crane Vitry 258 No. 284; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 317.
H473.3.p: A husband forbids his wife to eat leeks; although she does not like them, she immediately begins to crave them.

H473.4.r: She does. He cannot understand why; she cannot explain. England: Baughman.
H473.4.p: A man leaving home warns his wife not to wash her face in a puddle in the dunghill, and she is tested by whether she obeys.

H473.5.p: A husband tests his wife's obedience by giving her an instruction about decorating the house.

H474.p: A wife who is overly agreeable to her husband accepts all of his absurd statements without objection.

H476.p: A husband tests a false wife by sleeping with his head on her hair; he has always done this with his true bride.

H479.p: Miscellaneous tests of a wife's worth or loyalty that do not fit under more specific motifs.

H479.1.p: A widow who is to be burned on her husband's funeral pyre (suttee) proves her strength by lifting a heavy stone beside the temple with her little finger.

H480.r: Irish myth: Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “père”, “enfant”; Arabian: Burton Nights S V 236 n.
H480.p: Tests used to determine who the unknown father of a child is.

H481.r: *Type 675; BP I 485; *Fb “barn” IV 27b; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 3; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesian: De Vries’s list No. 208; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 336 n. 212; S. A. Indian (Yunca): Alexander Lat. Am. 228.
H481.p: An infant identifies his unknown father by choosing him from a group of men.

H481.1.r: *Fb “æble” III 1135b, “guldæble” I 516a; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 93b.
H481.1.p: An infant shows who his unknown father is by handing an apple to that man.

H481.1.1.r: S. A. Indian (Chaco): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (1) 369.
H481.1.1.p: A baby identifies his father, who is in disguise among a crowd, by handing him a bow. The baby's choice reveals who the unknown father is.

H482.p: A baby identifies his unknown mother from among a group of women by choosing her. The infant's choice serves as the test.

H483.p: Animals are sent as messengers to call the father of a newborn child, and their voices are tested to decide which one can carry the summons.

H485.p: To find a child's father, a princess has gold laid on the street leading to her. The man who rides over the gold without noticing it is the father.

H486.r: Child tested to see if it is child of certain father. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
H486.p: A general test used to determine who is the true father of a child.

H486.1.r: Oesterley No. 196; Herbert III 191; Zachariae Kleine Schriften 305; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 61, Neuman.
H486.1.p: Paternity is tested by blood: the blood of the real son will stick to the dead father's bones, showing who is the genuine son.

H486.2.r: *Herbert III 206; Oesterley No. 45; Scala Celi 98a No. 526; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 835; Nouvelles de Sens. No 29; Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 28; L. Schmidt Oesterr. Zs. f. Vksk. 1955, 70 ff.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; *Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas II 123, 345, IV 102, 280, *Neuman.
H486.2.p: Several men claim to be a dead emperor's son, and each must shoot at the corpse. The youngest refuses to shoot and is judged the only genuine son.

H490.p: A group of miscellaneous tests of a marriage, other than those tied to paternity, such as tests of love and faithfulness.

H491.p: A test of how much a father and mother love their children, to see which parent will give up a child.

H491.1.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 87, 303, Neuman.
H491.1.p: In a large family, the father is unwilling to sell the children but the mother is willing to sell them.

H492.p: A test of whether a husband and wife are faithful to each other.

H492.1.r: Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 90, 303, Neuman.
H492.1.p: A husband refuses to murder his wife in return for great honors, but the wife agrees to murder her husband for the same reward.

H492.2.p: A husband has a friend court his wife, and she is seduced, showing her unfaithfulness.

H492.2.1.r: blouse of coarse cloth; dress of gold brocade. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
H492.2.1.p: A husband has a friend court his wife, and she is generous only up to a certain point. The husband makes her wear a dress that symbolizes how far her generosity goes.

H492.2.2.p: A husband has a friend court his wife, but the frightened husband steps in and stops the seduction just in time.

H492.3.p: A husband castrates himself in order to test whether his wife is faithful to him.

H493.p: A test of whether a husband is sexually capable or virile.

H494.p: A test of whether a wife can bear a baby within a year of marriage.

H495.p: A test of whether a woman is truly a mother, often decided by which woman a baby recognizes as its own.

H495.1.p: A baby finds its real mother and goes to her to nurse, showing who she is.

H495.2.p: A test of motherhood in which a woman's milk is shown to travel a great distance into a child's mouth, proving she is the true mother.

H495.3.p: An old woman proves she has borne a child by nursing all the babies at her son's circumcision, showing she has milk.

H500.1.p: Sons are tested to see which of them has the most skill.

H501.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys, Penzer VI 74 n.
H501.p: A general test in which someone's wisdom is measured, usually by a challenge or set of questions.

H501.1.p: A wise man sends a ruler magic gems as a test; the ruler admires their beauty but fails to ask what they are good for, showing his lack of wisdom.

H501.2.p: A wise man answers the questions of many people with one single speech.

H501.3.p: Sons are tested for wisdom by being given the same amount of money, and the test is what each will do with it.

H502.p: A general test in which someone's learning is measured.

H502.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
H502.1.p: A test of a person's knowledge of religious teachings or scripture.

H503.p: A general test in which someone's musical ability is measured.

H503.1.r: Contest in singing. Irish myth: *Cross; Eskimo: Alexander N. Am. 282 n. 21.
H503.1.p: A contest in which two singers try to outdo each other in song.

H504.p: A test in which a person's skill in craftwork or handiwork is judged to determine whether they are worthy.

H504.1.p: A general contest in which artists compete to paint the most lifelike picture.

H504.1.1.p: During one artist's absence, a second artist paints a fly on a saint's nose in a picture; when the first returns, he tries to brush the fly away, showing how lifelike the painting is.

H504.1.2.p: One artist paints a mare so realistic that it fools a stallion; the second paints a curtain that fools the first artist.

H504.1.3.p: One artist paints grapes so realistically that birds come to eat them; the second paints a curtain that fools the first artist.

H504.2.p: A contest in which barbers compete to shave a man without waking him.

H505.r: *Type 655; *Chauvin VII 159 No. 438; BP IV 137; Oesterley No. 58; India: Thompson-Balys.
H505.p: A test in which young men must say three wise words, and their answers show remarkable powers of reasoning.

H505.1.p: A variant of the three-wise-words test in which the challenge is to say three truths.

H506.p: A general test in which someone's resourcefulness, or ability to solve a problem by ingenuity, is measured.

H506.1.p: A clever man weighs an elephant by putting it on a boat, marking the water line, then loading the boat with stones until it sinks to that same line, and weighing the stones.

H506.2.p: A test of cleverness where the solver must find out how many people are shut inside a dark, closed room. The room is filled with a foul smell, and the people are made to call each other by name so that their number is revealed.

H506.3.r: Two solutions: (1) (a) take goat over, (b) take wolf over and goat back, (c) take cabbage over, (d) take goat over; (2) (a) take goat over, (b) take cabbage over and goat back, (c) take wolf over, (d) take goat over. *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XXXIII—XXXIV 38; Fb “ulv” III 970a, “kål” II 354b.
H506.3.p: A riddle-test in which a man must ferry a wolf, a goat, and a cabbage across a stream in a boat that holds only himself and one of them at a time. He must arrange the trips so the wolf cannot eat the goat and the goat cannot eat the cabbage.

H506.4.r: Greek: Frazer Apollodorus II 141 n. 1 (Daidalus); Zachariae Kleine Schriften 59, 108ff.; Japanese: Ikeda.
H506.4.p: A test of cleverness in which the solver must thread a string through the coiled chambers of a snail shell. The string is tied to an ant, which pulls it through the spiral.

H506.5.p: A test of cleverness in which the solver must swing seventy girls until they are all tired out.

H506.6.p: A test of cleverness in which the solver must avoid sitting at the foot of a couch. A servant solves it by placing a lemon on the couch to show which end is the head and which is the foot.

H506.7.p: A test of cleverness in which the solver must eat the food inside a tied cloth without untying it. The solver tears a hole in the cloth to get at the food.

H506.8.p: A test of cleverness in which a melon must be removed from a jar without breaking the jar. The melon is planted inside a jar made of unbaked clay, and the jar is wrapped in a wet cloth so that it collapses and the melon can be taken out.

H506.9.p: A test of cleverness in which the solver must cook rice without a fire, using only hot sand to do the cooking.

H506.10.p: A test of cleverness in which three sticks are placed in a vessel of water. How far each one sinks shows which part of a tree it came from, which reveals the relationships among the sticks.

H506.11.p: A test of cleverness in which the solver must work out the ages of three horses. Water is dropped on each one: one jumps only fifteen paces, another twenty, and the last bounds into the air and gallops off, showing its relative age.

H507.r: Test in repartee. Type 1093; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Finnish: Kalevala rune 3; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H507.p: A contest in which two people compete by trading clever replies, insults, or arguments until one is defeated.

H507.1.r: *Type 853; BP I 201; *Wesselski Der Islam XXII (1934) 114 n. 4; Japanese: Ikeda.
H507.1.p: A princess promises to marry any man who can beat her in a battle of clever replies.

H507.1.0.1.r: E. g., Hero: What red lips you have!—Princess: There is fire inside.—Hero: Then boil this egg (producing egg). Type 851; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 414ff.
H507.1.0.1.p: The princess is beaten in a battle of clever replies when the man uses objects he happened to pick up to answer her.

H507.1.0.2.r: Boy: “Who would give a man a bath, feed him his rice, and then bring him the tamal-pan to chew?” King: “No one but a wife.” Boy claims minister’s daughter. India: Thompson-Balys.
H507.1.0.2.p: A king is beaten in a battle of clever replies by a boy, who thereby wins the girl as his bride.

H507.1.1.p: A princess promises to marry any man who can beat her in an argument.

H507.2.r: King brought to say, “What is the sense in that?” Anderson FFC XLII 357; Japanese: Ikeda.
H507.2.p: A test in which the challenger must make nonsensical remarks that the other person must somehow answer or match.

H507.3.p: A contest in which rivals try to outdo each other by making wishes.

H507.3.1.p: Three brothers compete in wishing, and the third brother wishes for everything the other two have wished for.

H507.4.p: Three sisters compete in wit to win a larger dowry, giving clever replies to their husbands when the husbands notice that they were pregnant before marriage.

H507.5.p: A contest of insults and scolding between two people that comes before they fight.

H507.6.p: In a contest of wits, the rival who is first left speechless loses. A false teacher answers with nonsense syllables, and the true scholar, unable to reply, is silenced and so loses.

H508.r: Irish myth: Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
H508.p: A general category of tests in which a person must find the answer to a particular question to win something, such as a throne or a bride.

H508.1.p: A king asks his sons questions to decide which of them will inherit the kingdom; whoever answers correctly becomes the successor.

H508.2.r: *Type 306; BP I 198ff.; Wesselski Märchen 211; Malone PMLA XLIII 399; Irish myth: Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
H508.2.p: A bride is offered as the prize to any man who can find the answer to a given question.

H509.p: A miscellaneous group of tests that check someone's cleverness or skill in various ways that do not fit other categories.

H509.1.p: A guest at a convent is offered a choice of nuns to marry. The next morning he must thread a needle three times; if he succeeds he is rewarded, and if he fails his belongings are taken.

H509.2.p: A contest in which the hero makes the onlookers' mouths water by using a particular berry that always has this effect.

H509.3.p: A chess game is used as a test of a person's ability or cleverness.

H509.4.p: A general category of tests in which a person's skill at writing or understanding poetry is examined.

H509.4.1.p: A poetry test in which the person must supply the missing half of a stanza.

H509.4.1.1.p: In a poetry contest, a rival adds a verse to the first poet's stanza in a way that makes that poet look foolish.

H509.4.2.p: Riddles are set as a test of a person's poetic ability.

H509.4.3.p: A poem is given to a person, who is tested on whether he correctly understands its meaning.

H509.5.p: A test of skill in telling a lie that is convincing.

H509.5.1.p: A person must tell five lies so close to the truth that the tester ends up believing them himself.

H510.p: A general category of tests in which a person must guess correctly to succeed.

H511.r: *Type 621; BP III 483; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 5; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H511.p: A princess is offered as the prize to any man who makes the correct guess.

H511.1.r: Alphabet No. 412; Scala Celi 20b No. 127; Oesterley No. 251; Dunlop-Liebrecht 462 n. 74; *Wesselski Märchen 213 No. 18; India: Thompson-Balys; S. A. Indian (Carib): Alexander Lat. Am. 264; Africa (Angola): Chatelain 121 No. 10, (Benga): Nassau 219 No. 33.
H511.1.p: A princess is promised to the man who correctly chooses one of three caskets.

H511.1.1.p: The suitor must choose between two sword sheaths; one holds a gold shaft protruding from it and the other a silver one, and he must pick correctly.

H511.1.2.p: The suitor must show that he prefers the princess herself to the treasures on offer; choosing the wealth means failure.

H511.2.p: A test in which someone must guess which of several veiled sisters has golden hair. The guesser who answers correctly wins the princess as a reward.

H512.p: A guessing contest in which the loser forfeits his life. Failing to guess correctly means death.

H515.p: A contest of guessing between two kings, each trying to outdo the other by naming or identifying something the other cannot.

H516.p: A test in which a person saves their own life by guessing the names of trolls. Knowing the trolls' names is the only way out.

H517.p: A curse is avoided when a person guesses names written in magic writing. Discovering the names breaks the spell.

H521.p: A test in which a person must guess the name of someone who sets the challenge, and that person's identity is unknown to the guesser.

H521.1.p: A test in which a person must guess the age of an unknown challenger. It is a variant of the guessing-the-name test.

H522.p: A test in which a person must identify an unknown animal or plant by guessing what it is.

H522.1.p: A test in which a person must guess where a certain skin came from.

H522.1.1.r: Louse (flea) is fattened and its skin made into coat (drum, etc.) *Type 621; BP III 484; *Taylor MPh XV 224 n. 2; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “bète”; Italian: Basile Pentamerone I No. 5; India: *Thompson-Balys; Filipino: Fansler MAFLS XII 114.
H522.1.1.p: A test in which a person must guess what kind of skin it is, here identified as the skin of a louse.

H522.1.2.p: A test in which a person must guess what kind of skin it is, here identified as the skin of a wolf.

H522.1.3.p: A test in which a person must guess where an animal's lungs came from. The lungs belong to a fattened lizard, which are further inflated.

H522.2.p: A test in which a person must guess what kind of plant something is. The plant grew from scrapings of princesses' bodies.

H522.3.p: A test in which a person must identify what type of rice is inside a sack, without looking.

H523.p: A test in which a person must guess the nature of objects belonging to the devil.

H523.1.p: A test in which a person must guess the nature of the devil's horse.

H523.2.p: A test in which a person must guess the nature of the devil's cloth.

H523.3.r: Answer: cup of pitch. *Type 812; BP III 12ff.
H523.3.p: A test in which a person must guess the nature of the devil's gold cup.

H523.4.p: A test in which a person must guess the nature of the devil's roast meat.

H523.5.p: A test in which a person must guess the nature of the devil's spoon.

H523.6.p: A test in which the person must guess the true nature of the devil's wine glass, a magical object belonging to the devil.

H523.7.p: A test in which the person must guess the true nature of the devil's plate, a magical object belonging to the devil.

H523.8.p: A test in which the person must guess the true nature of the devil's purse, a magical object belonging to the devil.

H524.r: *Anderson FFC XLII 219ff.; Fb “konge” II 264b, “gjætte” I 452a, “liv” II 438b; Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
H524.p: A test in which a person must correctly guess what another person is thinking.

H524.1.p: The challenger asks what the other is thinking, and the answer is that he is thinking he is the priest. In this way a youth disguised as a priest is revealed.

H525.p: A test in which a suitor must guess the hidden birthmarks on a princess's body in order to win her.

H526.p: A question asking the other to guess what is hidden under the questioner's cloak. The answer is a branch of blackthorn laden with berries.

H527.p: A guessing test asking whether there is more of a certain stone above ground or below it. It is set by a heathen king to a saint.

H528.p: A guessing test in which the person must predict whether an unborn child, or an unborn animal, will be male or female.

H528.1.p: A test in which the person must foretell the sex of the offspring of a cow and a mare.

H530.r: **J. B. Friedreich Geschichte des Räthsels (Dresden, 1860); **Taylor English Riddles in Oral Tradition (Berkeley, 1951), A Bibliography of Riddles (FFC CXXVI); R. Petsch Das deutsche Volksrätsel (Strassburg, 1917); *Anderson FFC XLII 3ff.; *Chauvin VI 42 No. 207; Jewish: *Neuman. A classification of riddles will be found in Lehmann-Nitsche Zs. f. Vksk. XXIV 240ff. and in Von Sydow and Christiansen Iriska gåtor (Folkminnen och Folktankar, II 65—80, VI 120—48).
H530.p: Riddles in general. This category covers only riddles that appear within tales, ballads, myths, or similar stories.

H540.p: The act of posing a riddle to someone, usually as a test or challenge within a story.

H540.1.r: (See also H541.1.1, H543, G681.) Child I 13ff., 484, II 495; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H540.1.p: A supernatural being poses riddles to a person.

H540.2.p: A queen poses riddles to someone.

H540.2.1.r: *Penzer VI 74; FL I 349ff.; Anderson FFC XLII 237 n. 2; Hertz Gesammelte Abhandlungen (1905) 412ff.; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 32, 297f., *Neuman; *Frazer Old Testament II 564.
H540.2.1.p: The Queen of Sheba poses riddles to King Solomon.

H540.3.p: A king poses riddles to someone.

H540.3.1.p: King Hiram sends riddles to Solomon to be solved.

H540.4.p: A saint poses riddles to someone.

H540.5.p: A bridegroom poses riddles to his guests at the wedding feast.

H541.p: A riddle is posed with a penalty for anyone who fails to answer it.

H541.1.r: (Cf. H512.) *Type 922; **Anderson FFC XLII 252; *BP III 230; *Oertel Studien zur vgl. Littgsch. VIII 121; Malone PMLA XLIII 398f.; Fb “bejler” IV 31b; English: Child V 493 “riddles”; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
H541.1.p: A riddle is posed on pain of death: whoever cannot answer it will be killed.

H541.1.1.r: **Laistner Rätsel der Sphinx; Fb “menneske” II 578a; Gascon: Bladé I 3 No. 1; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 349 n. 1; Persian: Carnoy 335; Hindu: Penzer IX 143.
H541.1.1.p: A sphinx-like creature poses a riddle to a traveler, under threat of death if the riddle is not answered correctly.

H541.2.p: A riddle is set where failing to answer it means losing one's property.

H541.2.1.p: The penalty for failing to solve a riddle is a fine.

H541.3.p: A riddle is set where failing to answer it means losing one's official position or office.

H542.r: ; **F. J. Norton FL LIII 27—57; Köhler-Bolte I 46; Penzer I 51, 51n.; Malone PMLA XLIII 407; Icelandic: Boberg; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 112 No. 927*A.
H542.p: A condemned person saves himself from execution by posing a riddle that the king or judge cannot solve.

H542.1.p: A riddle is given to the defendant in a lawsuit, and if he solves it he wins the case.

H543.r: *Type 812; BP III 12ff.; Fb “spørgsmål” III 524b; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 754; Jamaica: *Beckwith MAFLS XVII 275 No. 86.
H543.p: A person escapes from the devil by answering the riddles the devil asks.

H543.1.r: St. Andrew the Bishop, and the Devil. The Devil, in form of beautiful maiden visits a holy bishop. St. Andrew appears as a pilgrim, answers the questions through which the devil seeks to keep him at a distance and discomfits the devil. (Cf. B302.22.3.) Anderson FFC LXII 353; Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 45; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
H543.1.p: The devil is kept away from a person as long as that person can answer the devil's riddles.

H543.2.p: A child lying in a cradle guesses the devil's riddle, and as a result everyone is saved.

H544.p: Riddles asked along the way are answered by finding the solutions in the other world.

H548.r: *BP II 370; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 435b n. 150; Frazer Old Testament II 564; Child I 405; *De Vries FFC LXXIII 43ff.; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 427, 458.
H548.p: A contest in which two parties pose riddles to each other to see who can solve more.

H548.1.p: A king and a rabbi pose riddles to each other in a contest of wits.

H551.r: *Types 725, 851, 900; BP I 188ff., 200; Philippson FFC L 22; *Chauvin V 192, 192 No. 113; Fb “bejler” IV 31b; Malone PMLA XLIII 414; von der Hagen Gesammtabenteuer III *lxi; Child V 493 s.v. “riddles”.—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 851A*; India: Thompson-Balys; Filipino: Fansler MAFLS XII 278; Africa: Werner African 356.
H551.p: A princess is offered in marriage to any man who can outdo her in riddling.

H551.1.p: A man wins a wife by coaching her on how to answer the riddles her mother asks.

H551.2.p: A woman gives herself in marriage to whoever solves her riddles.

H552.r: Child V 493 s.v. “riddles”; Irish myth: Cross.
H552.p: A man marries a girl who is able to guess his riddles.

H561.p: A general heading for characters who are skilled at solving riddles.

H561.1.r: *Type 875; **De Vries FFC LXXIII 52ff.; *Hdwb. d. Märchens I 195a; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
H561.1.p: A clever peasant girl is questioned with riddles by the king.

H561.1.0.1.p: A clever peasant wife poses riddles to the king.

H561.1.1.r: De Vries FFC LXXIII 65ff.; India: Thompson-Balys.
H561.1.1.p: A dispute between a peasant and a nobleman is settled by having each answer riddles, and the peasant's daughter solves them.

H561.1.1.1.p: A clever daughter of a peasant explains the puzzling statements of a king or nobleman, so that the dispute between them is settled.

H561.1.2.p: A peasant finds a mortar in his field and takes it to the king, who also demands the pestle. The peasant regrets not following his daughter's advice, and the king summons her to answer.

H561.2.r: *Type 922; **Anderson FFC XLII; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 55; Fb “hyrde” I 719; India: Thompson-Balys; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
H561.2.p: A king sets a abbot three riddles to answer on pain of death, and a herdsman disguises himself as the abbot and answers the questions.

H561.3.r: *BP II 359 n. 2; Fb “Salomon”; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 317 No. 146.
H561.3.p: A witty exchange of questions and answers takes place between a young man and a servant, with King Solomon and the servant Marcolf as the famous pair.

H561.3.1.p: King Solomon is portrayed as the greatest solver of riddles.

H561.4.r: *Type 921; **De Vries FFC LXXIII 111ff., 308ff.; Anderson FFC XLII 356 n. 2; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H561.4.p: A king asks questions and a clever young man answers them with riddling replies.

H561.5.r: **De Vries FFC LXXIII 365ff.; *Encyc. Rel. Ethics s.v. “Ahiqar”; *Marc Studien zur vgl. Littgesch. II 393f., III 52; **Meissner Das Märchen vom weisen Achikar (Leipzig, 1917); Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H561.5.p: A king poses riddles and questions to his clever minister, who must answer them.

H561.6.p: A king and a peasant compete by asking each other riddling questions and giving riddling answers.

H561.6.1.p: A king gives riddling questions to a peasant, who always answers correctly. The king sends him a fowl to pluck, and gives the same questions to his courtiers, who cannot answer and pay the peasant for the answers. The peasant then tells the king he has plucked the fowl, meaning he has taken the courtiers' money.

H561.7.p: A druid, a member of the ancient Celtic priesthood, is able to solve riddles.

H561.8.p: A churchman or member of the clergy is able to solve riddles.

H561.9.p: A clever prince works out the meaning of puzzling or enigmatic statements.

H561.10.p: A saint is able to solve riddles.

H562.p: A riddle-solver's home bears the inscription "I have no care," showing he is untroubled because he can answer any riddle.

H565.p: On the way to a riddle contest, a young man notices things that give him ideas for his own riddles.

H565.1.p: Things that happen before a feast give Samson the clue for his riddles.

H570.p: Ways of solving riddles, the methods a clever person uses to find the answer.

H571.r: *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 275 No. 299; Wesselski Arlotto I 215 No. 59; Anderson FFC XLII 346; Japanese: Ikeda.
H571.p: A riddle is answered with a counter-question that shows the riddle's logic to be absurd.

H571.1.r: What is difference between you and a cushion.” *Wesselski Hodscha Nasreddin I 228 No. 74.
H571.1.p: A riddle is answered by asking what the difference is between the person and a donkey.

H572.r: BP II 372; Chauvin VI 39 No. 207 n. 4.
H572.p: A riddle is answered by an absurd counter-example: asked why his mare is restless when the stallions of Babylon neigh, the hero beats a cat for strangling a cock in Babylon, which is impossibly far away.

H573.p: A riddle is answered by means of a trick or deception rather than by genuinely working out the solution.

H573.1.r: Malone PMLA XLIII 400; Irish myth: Cross.
H573.1.p: A riddle is solved because a hidden person secretly gives the answer to the one who must solve it.

H573.2.p: Someone asks why a certain person cannot sleep, and the puzzle is solved by a trick rather than by reasoning.

H573.3.p: A riddle is solved by listening to the person who posed it while he talks in his sleep, which reveals the answer.

H574.p: Riddles are solved with the help of the wife of the person who posed them, who reveals the answer.

H575.p: The answer to a riddle is found by accident, without the solver intending or working it out.

H580.r: *Wesselski Märchen 197; **De Vries FFC LXXIII; Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo II 389, *Boberg; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 122 No. 1358; Jewish: *Neuman; Arab: Azov 411f.; India: *Thompson-Balys; Batak: Voorhoeve 163 No. 169.
H580.p: Strange or seemingly meaningless remarks or actions are understood figuratively and turn out to be wise.

H580.1.p: A girl is given puzzling commands and gets out of trouble by doing the opposite of what she was told.

H581.p: Three young men who are arrested state who they are in puzzling words, and their words reveal their identities.

H581.1.p: An arrested man reveals who he is through a riddling statement about his father, who must bow his head and give blood and money; the father is a barber.

H581.2.p: An arrested man reveals who he is through a riddling statement that his father's hospitable fire is sought; the father is a bean merchant.

H581.3.p: An arrested man reveals who he is through a riddling statement that his father throws himself into the ranks and holds them; the father is a weaver.

H581.4.p: An arrested farmer reveals his sons' trades in riddling terms: one son is a thief, another a beggar, and the third a murderer, described as priest, teacher, and doctor.

H582.r: ; Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 59 (to Gonzenbach No. 1); *Wesselski Märchen 197.
H582.p: Riddling answers reveal that someone has committed theft or adultery.

H582.1.p: A riddling answer exposes a theft.

H582.1.1.r: *BP II 361; Köhler Zs. f. Vksk. VI 59; Arab: Azov 401f.; Africa (Sahel): Frobenius Atlantis VI 79—86.
H582.1.1.p: A prince sends a servant with a tart, cakes, and a capon, and asks a clever girl riddling questions about the moon, the date, and a crowing cock. She answers in riddles that show the servant has stolen half the tart, half the cakes, and the capon.

H582.2.p: A riddling answer exposes an act of adultery.

H582.2.1.r: (Cf. T411.) Woman, recognizing cleric as her son by her father (Fiachna), gives him a drink of milk and says, “I give drink to my brother; he is Fiachna’s son, he is Fiachna’s grandson; his mother is Fiachna’s daughter.” The son’s reply shows that he understands the situation. Irish myth: *Cross.
H582.2.1.p: A riddling answer exposes an act of incest.

H582.3.p: A woman disguised as a man asks her husband how many men she had in one night; the question is really about how many helpers he had, and he answers by lifting ten fingers.

H583.p: A clever youth or maiden answers a king's questions entirely in riddles.

H583.1.r: (Himself, the legs of the king on horseback in the door, and the horse’s head.) *Köhler-Bolte I 84, 87, 151ff.; *Basset 1001 Contes II 41.
H583.1.p: A clever youth or maiden answers the king's question "What do you see?" with a riddle, "one and a half men and a horse's head."

H583.1.1.r: (Two legs of the king and the forefeet of his horse.) *Köhler-Bolte I 84, 87.
H583.1.1.p: Asked by the king whether he is alone at home, the clever youth answers with a riddle: he sees the halves of two four-legged animals.

H583.2.r: (He prunes vines and sometimes cuts good and sometimes lets bad ones stay.) *Köhler-Bolte I 84, 87.
H583.2.p: A king asks a youth what his father is doing, and the youth answers in riddles: the father is in the vineyard doing both good and bad.

H583.2.1.r: (Closes up a path; this causes another to be opened.) *De Vries FFC LXXIII 116ff.
H583.2.1.p: Asked what his father is doing, the youth riddles that his father makes an evil greater, referring to his work in the vineyard.

H583.2.2.p: Asked what his father is doing, the youth riddles that his father makes many things out of few, referring to his work in the vineyard.

H583.2.3.p: Asked what his father is doing, the youth riddles that his father makes better things from good ones, referring to his work in the vineyard.

H583.2.4.r: (To pay old debts.) *De Vries FFC LXXIII 116ff.
H583.2.4.p: Asked what his father is doing, the youth riddles that he cuts wood which was burnt last year, referring to his work in the vineyard.

H583.2.5.r: (Eggplant garden fenced with thorns.) India: Thompson-Balys.
H583.2.5.p: Asked what his father is doing, the youth riddles that he fences thorns with thorns, referring to his work in the vineyard.

H583.3.r: (Hunts for lice on his body.) *De Vries FFC LXXIII 128ff.; Wesselski Mönchslatein 120 No. 102; Missouri French: Carrière.
H583.3.p: Asked what his brother is doing, the youth riddles that he hunts, throwing away what he catches and carrying with him what he does not catch.

H583.3.1.p: Asked what his brother is doing, the youth riddles that he runs back and forth.

H583.3.2.p: Asked what his brother is doing, the youth riddles that he sits between heaven and earth.

H583.4.r: (Lays out a corpse.) *De Vries FFC LXXIII 124ff.
H583.4.p: Asked what his mother is doing, the youth riddles that she does for another what that other cannot do for her.

H583.4.1.r: (Assists at a birth.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 124ff.
H583.4.1.p: Asked what his mother is doing, the youth riddles that she shows the light of the world to one who has not yet seen it.

H583.4.2.r: H583.2.4.) *De Vries FFC LXXIII 124ff.; Köhler-Bolte I 85, 87.
H583.4.2.p: Asked what his mother is doing, the youth answers that she is baking the bread they ate last week, which is a way of paying back borrowed bread.

H583.4.3.r: (Kills chickens to feed her sick mother.) Köhler-Bolte I 85, 87.
H583.4.3.p: Asked what his mother is doing, the youth riddles that she cuts off the heads of the well to cure the sick.

H583.4.4.r: (Drives away the hungry hens and stuffs the geese.) Köhler-Bolte I 85, 87.
H583.4.4.p: Asked what his mother is doing, the youth riddles that she drives away the hungry and forces the full to eat.

H583.4.5.p: Asked what his mother and father are doing, the girl answers that her mother is separating earth, as a midwife would, and her father is mixing earth, as at a funeral.

H583.4.6.p: Asked what her mother is doing, the girl answers that she has gone to turn one into two, meaning to split peas.

H583.5.r: (Nurses child, the fruit of last year’s love affair.) *De Vries FFC LXXIII 133ff.
H583.5.p: Asked what his sister is doing, the youth riddles that she is mourning last year's laughter.

H583.6.r: (Beans which keep rising and falling in water.) *Types 875, 921; De Vries FFC LXXIII 115.
H583.6.p: Asked what he is doing, the youth riddles that he boils those things which come and go.

H583.7.r: (Between wagon and sleigh.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 254.
H583.7.p: Asked where he should tie his horse, the maiden riddles that he should tie it between summer and winter.

H583.8.r: (No child at window nor dog in yard to announce king’s approach: he therefore finds her not dressed to receive him.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 252.
H583.8.p: A clever maiden answers a king's question with a riddle: the house has neither eyes nor ears. The riddle must be solved to pass the king's test.

H583.9.r: (A slaughtered hen or milk.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 254; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1465*; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 877*.
H583.9.p: A clever maiden answers the king's question with a riddle about whether she will feed him with loss or gain.

H583.10.p: A girl tells the king, in riddling words, that if the flood comes she will not come, and if it does not come she will come.

H584.p: Miscellaneous riddling answers given to a king's or other person's question, where the answer is itself a puzzle.

H585.p: A king and a peasant talk in riddles, each speaking in puzzling words the other must interpret.

H585.1.r: (Focus.) King: What do you do with the four coins you earn? Peasant: First I eat (feed self); second I put out at interest (give my children); third I give back (pay debts); fourth I throw away (give my wife.) Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 161 (to Gonzenbach No. 50); BP IV 137; Oesterley No. 57; cf. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 8; Anderson FFC XLII 356 n. 1.—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 921A*; Russian: Andrejev No. 921 I*; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Swahili): Steere 295.
H585.1.p: A riddling exchange between a king and a peasant in which four coins are central to the puzzle.

H585.2.p: The king asks why the peasant did not marry so that sons could help him, and the peasant replies that he did marry, three times, but God did not will him to have sons.

H586.r: De Vries FFC LXXIII 43ff.; *Wesselski Märchen 197 No. 7; India: Thompson-Balys.
H586.p: A traveling companion makes riddling remarks along the way, and a girl or man at the journey's end explains what they meant.

H586.1.p: A man helps a traveler by giving him food, sharing his coat in the rain, and carrying him over a stream. He then scolds him for travelling without a mother, house, or bridge, meaning without food, shelter, or a horse.

H586.2.r: (What has become of the girl he left in the city to await his return.) Köhler-Bolte I 197; Nouvelles de Sens No. 3.
H586.2.p: A traveler says he is going to the city to see what has become of the seed he sowed in the street.

H586.2.1.p: A traveler says he is going to seek a hind he saw in the woods ten years earlier.

H586.2.2.r: lady has had lovers.) English: Child I 191 n.
H586.2.2.p: A traveler says he must check his net to see whether it has caught fish. The underlying meaning is that he left his lady seven years earlier, having pledged to be faithful, and his net has taken fish.

H586.3.r: (Let us tell tales and amuse ourselves on the way.) *Wesselski Märchen 197 No. 7; Nouvelles de Sens Nos. 3, 8; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H586.3.p: One traveler tells another that they should carry each other to shorten the way.

H586.4.r: (Belongs to spendthrift who has already spent the money.) Wesselski Märchen 197 No. 7.
H586.4.p: One traveler tells another that a field, still uncut, has already been harvested.

H586.5.r: (Has left good property.) Wesselski Märchen 197 No. 7.
H586.5.p: Two travelers see a corpse being carried by, and one says the man is not entirely dead.

H586.6.r: (Found a ford with an ashen staff.) Wesselski Märchen 197 No. 7; Nouvelles de Sens No. 8.
H586.6.p: Asked how he crossed a stream with no bridge, a traveler replies that he crossed on an ashen bridge.

H586.7.r: (Is your daughter married or not?) India: Thompson-Balys.
H586.7.p: One traveler asks another whether a cup is valuable or not, a riddling question about its worth.

H586.8.p: A boy says travelers should catch the mares, meaning the walking sticks that grow in the jungle.

H587.p: A king gives a puzzling order to his minister, whose meaning must be worked out.

H587.0.1.p: A king sends an enigmatic letter that must be correctly explained, under penalty of death.

H587.1.r: Minister: The lamp sells at eight for a pice and gives more light than any ruby; the water is the real nectar; and the dog is worthless and faithless lover because he follows anyone who feeds him. India: Thompson-Balys.
H587.1.p: A king gives his minister a riddling order to bring three odd things: a ruby worth eight for a pice, nectar worth eight for a pice, and a faithless creature worth one-eighth of a pice. The minister must solve the puzzle to carry it out.

H588.r: Icelandic: Hervarar saga 36—39, 116—18, *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys, (Kashmir): Knowles 243; Indonesia: De Vries’s list No. 232; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 256 No. 200.
H588.p: A father gives his children or heirs advice in riddling words. Taken literally it causes trouble, but properly understood it is valuable wisdom.

H588.0.1.p: A father-in-law gives his daughter-in-law a riddling permission to go home, which she must interpret correctly.

H588.1.r: (Attend to business, rising early and retiring late.) India: Thompson-Balys.
H588.1.p: The father advises his son never to walk in sunshine on the way from his house to his shop. The advice is meant figuratively, not literally.

H588.2.p: The father advises his son to make pilav (a rice dish) his daily food. The words are meant in a non-literal sense.

H588.3.r: (Do not see your wife too much.) India: Thompson-Balys.
H588.3.p: The father advises his son to marry a new wife every week. The advice is riddling and must be understood figuratively.

H588.4.r: (Stench in vat so great that desire for wine is turned to loathing.) India: *Thompson-Balys.
H588.4.p: The father advises that when you want to drink wine, go to the wine vat and drink from it. The phrase has a hidden meaning.

H588.5.r: (If you see how wretched professional gamblers are you will not want to gamble.) *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 376; India: Thompson-Balys.
H588.5.p: The father advises that if you want to gamble, you should gamble only with experienced gamblers. The advice is riddling.

H588.6.r: (Plant the road with fruit trees and betel between the trees.) India: *Thompson-Balys; Batak: Voorhoeve 164f. No. 169.
H588.6.p: The father advises his son to dress up tree trunks and cover the road. The instruction is riddling and must be interpreted to reveal its sense.

H588.7.r: (Sons dig everywhere and thus loosen soil of vineyard, which becomes fruitful.) Wienert FFC LVI 82 (ET 490), 126 (ST 346); Halm Aesop No. 98; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 914*; India: Thompson-Balys.
H588.7.p: The father tells his heir that treasure is to be found within a foot of the ground. The words are a riddle that conceals a hint about where wealth lies.

H588.8.r: Three empty and one full (3 sons and father). Full one can fill the three empty but the three when full cannot fill the one when empty (sons when scattered will not support the father). India: Thompson-Balys.
H588.8.p: The father gives his sons advice about four wells, speaking in riddling terms whose meaning must be worked out.

H588.9.r: not outlets of rice-field as son-in-law thinks). India: *Thompson-Balys.
H588.9.p: The father advises his heir to dam up the outlets, which is a riddling way of saying to keep expenditures down.

H588.10.p: The father warns his son not to stay too late with a concubine and not to tell her any secret. The advice is riddling and must be understood figuratively.

H588.11.r: (Working diligently, your bread will be as sweet as honey.) Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 915A*.
H588.11.p: The father advises his son always to eat bread with honey. The word honey is used in a riddling, non-literal sense.

H588.12.r: (Start your work the earliest, so that not you but others may greet you.) Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 915A*.
H588.12.p: The father advises his son never to greet anyone. The instruction is riddling and must be interpreted rightly.

H588.13.r: (Walk the fields bare-footed, wearing your shoes only when nearing the town.) Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 915A*.
H588.13.p: The father advises his son always to wear new shoes. The words are a riddle with a hidden meaning.

H588.14.p: The father advises his son to have a black look, meaning to frown. The phrase is riddling and must be understood figuratively.

H588.15.p: The father advises his son to bite the ear, meaning to conduct state affairs secretly. The phrase is a riddle.

H588.16.p: The father advises his son to take people by the locks, meaning to use influence to make people subservient. The phrase is riddling.

H588.17.p: The father advises his son that if he must visit a prostitute, he should go early in the morning. The advice is riddling and must be understood figuratively.

H588.18.p: A father gives the cryptic advice to eat your breakfast before going to the bazaar, and the riddle is solved only by experience or reflection on its meaning.

H588.19.p: A father gives a cryptic saying that a father should always check up on his children and never forgive them, while a mother should always forgive and never check up on them.

H588.20.p: A father gives the cryptic advice not to plant a thorny tree, a saying whose meaning must be worked out.

H588.21.p: A father's cryptic advice is to eat only salt and water as food, a saying whose meaning must be worked out.

H591.p: Someone performs a strange action that seems foolish, and a clever person explains the reason behind it.

H591.1.r: (He cannot see what he is walking on.) India: Thompson-Balys.
H591.1.p: A man puts on his shoes only when he has to wade across a river, and the odd habit is explained by the need to keep his feet dry or his shoes unspoiled until then.

H591.2.r: (To protect self from falling branches and bird droppings.) India: Thompson-Balys.
H591.2.p: A man carries and opens an umbrella while walking under trees, a seemingly odd act that has a sensible explanation.

H591.3.p: A man cuts hooks as part of avenging his father, a deed that seems strange until its purpose is revealed; this version is linked to Shakespeare's Hamlet.

H592.p: A puzzling statement becomes clear only when the listener later lives through an experience that reveals its meaning.

H592.1.r: *Type 923; *BP III 305 n. 2, IV 407; *Hartland FLJ IV 309; *DeCock Studien en Essays 4f.; Cosquin Contes Indiens 103ff.; Köhler Aufsätze 14; India: *Thompson-Balys. Cf. Shakespeare’s King Lear.
H592.1.p: A girl says she loves her father like salt; he is offended, but later learns the meaning of salt's value from experience and understands her love.

H592.1.1.p: A wife says her love is like wind in the hot sun; her husband is offended at first but later learns what she meant.

H592.2.p: A wife secretly betrays her husband to his enemies, so what seemed sweet like nectar turns out to be poison.

H592.3.p: A mistress who seemed harmful, like poison, actually saves her lover, so the poison proves to be nectar.

H592.4.p: A man's friends, who look like dogs in human form, seduce his wife, a statement understood only through experience.

H592.5.p: A donkey is shown ruling a kingdom, and the king is shown unjustly condemning a man, a scene that reveals the meaning of a riddling statement.

H593.p: Suitors ask for a girl's hand and receive one-word answers that, when arranged in a particular order, reveal that she accepts them.

H594.p: A host who has been inhospitable is rebuked through a riddling or indirect statement rather than directly.

H594.1.r: (Else it would give the beggar shelter.) India: Thompson-Balys.
H594.1.p: A cryptic remark is made that the roof has no eaves, a hint rebuking a host who gave no shelter or hospitality.

H594.2.r: (Else you would have given the beggar fish to eat.) India: Thompson-Balys.
H594.2.p: A cryptic remark says that the pond or tank does not belong to the person, a rebuke for refusing hospitality or water to a traveler.

H594.3.r: (Else you would have given the beggar milk and curds.) India: Thompson-Balys.
H594.3.p: A cryptic remark says that the flocks are only rocks and grass, a rebuke for a host who refused to share.

H595.p: A host's words of welcome sound rude or inhospitable on the surface, but when properly understood they mean the guests are truly welcome.

H595.1.p: A host's invitation is worded as a symbol that promises the guest will keep being generously treated.

H596.p: Relatives other than a father give advice or counsel in riddling, cryptic words that must be decoded to be understood.

H596.1.p: A brother gives advice in cryptic words that must be interpreted to be understood.

H596.1.1.r: Answer: A measured mouth, a close purse, and a knot on the trouser’s fly. Spanish: Childers.
H596.1.1.p: A younger brother asks an older brother, who stays unusually healthy and vigorous in old age, for his secret; the older brother answers in riddling words.

H599.p: Other enigmatic or riddling statements that do not fit the more specific categories of this section.

H599.1.p: A girl refuses to drink water that has no father or mother, meaning stagnant water that has no source or flowing origin.

H599.2.p: A man pretends to be mad and speaks in riddling words to hide his true purpose, as Hamlet does.

H599.3.p: A flatterer compares a lord to a full moon and his sovereign to a new moon, implying the lord is past his peak while the sovereign is just beginning to grow.

H599.4.r: (To shave his head, put some hairs under his arm, etc.) India: Thompson-Balys.
H599.4.p: A man is asked to do impossible-sounding feats, such as killing thousands or pressing hundreds under his arm, and answers with a clever reply or interpretation.

H599.5.p: A ruler gives a cryptic counsel to uproot old trees and plant new ones, which means he should dismiss old officials and appoint new ones.

H599.6.r: (Request for chickens for breakfast.) Jewish: Neuman.
H599.6.p: A riddle answer describing impossible or contradictory images: coals made orange, a glimmer of gold spread across the sky like heaven, and two heads made of darkness.

H600.p: Riddles or puzzling sayings are solved by finding a symbolic meaning hidden in the words, objects or actions involved.

H601.r: Clever person divides it symbolically: head to head of house, neck to wife, wings to daughters, legs to sons; keeps rest for himself. *Type 875; *BP II 360 n. 1; *Taylor JAFL XXXI 555; Köhler-Bolte II 645ff.; Scala Celi 37a No. 205; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 58.—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1580*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1580*; Livonian: Loorits FFC LXVI No. 1533*; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman; Filipino: Fansler MAFLS XII 63, 253, 351.
H601.p: A wise person cuts up a fowl in a way that symbolically answers a question or riddle, showing cleverness in the carving.
