H601.1.p: A wise person divides a goat in a clever, symbolic way, similar to the carving of a fowl.

H602.p: Numbers, letters and names are given symbolic meanings that serve as the clever answer to a riddle or test.

H602.1.p: Numbers are given symbolic meanings that answer riddles or tests.

H602.1.1.r: E.g. One: sun; two: Moses’ tablets; three: three Maries; etc. *Type 812; *BP III 15 n. 1; Irish myth: Cross; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 156 No. 2045*; Japanese: Ikeda.
H602.1.1.p: The numbers one through seven, and also ten and twelve, are each given a symbolic meaning used to answer a riddle.

H602.2.p: Individual letters of the alphabet are given symbolic meanings that serve as clever answers.

H602.3.p: Names are interpreted symbolically, so that the meaning of a name provides the clever answer.

H603.r: Ace: one God, one Faith, one Baptism; 2: old and new Testaments; 3: Trinity; 4: evangelists; 5: wise virgins; 6: days of creation; 7: sabbath; 8. Noah’s family; 9: ungrateful lepers; 10: commandments; knave (jack): Judas; queen (of Sheba); king: God; 12 face cards: 12 months; etc. *Type 1613; **Bolte Zs. v. Vksk. XI 376ff., XIII 84; Penzer IV 240 n. 1.
H603.p: A soldier scolded for playing cards during church replies that the cards are his prayerbook and calendar, since each card symbolizes something religious or time-related.

H604.p: A tongue that is spiced and bitter, served at a dinner, is given a symbolic meaning that someone must work out. The puzzle is about what the dish stands for, not about eating it.

H605.r: Works and prays where monk can see him. (Cf. H604, H606.) Spanish Exempla: Keller.
H605.p: An angel explains symbolically how much work is worth compared with prayer. The explanation is given through a symbol rather than plain speech.

H606.p: A priest explains sin through a symbol: he drags a heavy sack of sand behind him, showing how men drag their sins along with them.

H607.r: Sign language. *Penzer I 80f. n.; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 32; W. Coland Zs. f. Vksk. XXIV 88; Hertel ibid. XXIV 317; Loewe ibid. XXVIII 126; *Bolte Reise der Söhne Giaffers 206; Irish myth: Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H607.p: Two people hold a conversation using only symbols or gestures instead of words. Their meaning is understood only by reading the signs.

H607.1.r: *Anderson FFC XLII 354 n. 4; Köhler-Bolte II 479ff.; *Loewe Zs. f. Vksk. XXVIII 126; Penzer VI 249; Irish myth: Cross; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 922A*; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
H607.1.p: A priest and a Jew talk to each other using symbolic gestures. For example, the priest raises three fingers for the Trinity, and the Jew raises one arm for one God.

H607.2.p: Two poets or sages argue in deliberately obscure, poetic language that only the initiated can follow.

H607.2.1.p: A learned professor from one university tests a professor from another university using signs, and the second turns out to be a humble tradesman such as a shoemaker or miller.

H607.3.p: A princess tries to declare her love to someone through sign language, but her message is not understood.

H607.4.p: A saint entering a holy town is sent a cup filled to the brim with milk, meant to show that the town has no room for more holy hermits. The saint floats a flower on the milk and returns the cup, answering that there is still room.

H608.p: The parts of official robes are given symbolic meanings, so that each garment or detail stands for something.

H608.1.p: The points or peaks of a bishop's hat are given symbolic meanings.

H611.p: A young man asks for a branch of a tree and is offered the root instead, a reply that carries a hidden symbolic meaning.

H611.1.r: Iraq: Ethel Stevens Folk Tales of Iraq (London, 1931) 60.
H611.1.p: Ripe and overripe melons stand for girls who are ready for marriage, and the comparison is used in a riddling exchange.

H611.2.p: A girl sends a message to a prince she loves using signs, and the prince's friend interprets the meaning for him.

H611.3.p: A chief asks another man for cuttings of yams to complete his yam patch, which is a veiled request for a daughter in marriage. The reply is that the seed yams are shrivelled and old and it is too early for seedlings, meaning his daughters are too young or too old.

H614.p: A puzzling natural or strange occurrence is given an explanation, usually a symbolic one that reveals a moral point.

H614.1.p: A strange sight is explained as a man who gathers not only firewood but everything lying in his path, meaning a miser.

H614.2.p: A large pond drains into several smaller pools, explained as a man who spends money and gets nothing back.

H617.p: The meanings of dreams are interpreted symbolically, so that each dream image stands for some other event or fact.

H619.p: Symbolic interpretations that do not fit any of the more specific categories above.

H619.1.p: A riddle-type test in which the chairs in heaven are given a symbolic meaning rather than their literal one.

H619.2.p: A test of cleverness in which a church and the image inside it are explained symbolically, not literally.

H619.3.p: The roots and branches of the World-tree are given a symbolic explanation in a riddle-like test.

H619.4.p: A symbolic riddle in which a thatching of a house that does not work and a fire built in the otherworld are explained as hidden meanings.

H619.5.p: A symbolic riddle in which a fight between a one-legged bird and a twelve-legged bird is interpreted: the one-legged bird stands for innocence and the twelve-legged bird for guilt.

H620.p: A tale that deliberately ends with a puzzle or unanswered question, leaving the listener to solve it.

H621.r: (Answer sometimes given: her father, her mother, or her husband). *Type 945; *BP III 53ff.; Tille FFC XXXIV 254; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: De Vries’s list No. 199; Africa (Fjort): Dennett 33 No. 3; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 112 No. 39.
H621.p: Skilled companions each make part of a woman (one carves her body, one clothes her, one gives her speech), and the tale asks who she should belong to.

H621.1.p: Skilled companions bring a dead girl back to life, and the tale asks who she should belong to.

H621.2.p: A girl is rescued by skilled companions, and the tale ends by asking who she belongs to.

H625.p: A race in which a hare and a pig both try to cross a ditch, each failing in his own way, with the pig coming in behind the hare.

H630.p: Riddles that ask what is the strongest, mightiest or greatest thing in the world.

H631.r: *Types 461, 875, 922; *BP II 357; *De Vries FFC LXXIII 84, Aarne FFC XXIII 129; Japanese: Ikeda.
H631.p: A riddle asking what is the strongest thing in the world.

H631.1.r: *De Vries FFC LXXIII 85; Arab: Azov JPASB II 415f.
H631.1.p: The riddle answer to what is the strongest thing is a horse.

H631.2.p: The riddle answer to what is the strongest thing is God.

H631.3.r: Type 875; De Vries FFC LXXIII 85; *BP II 357; Köhler-Bolte I 457f.
H631.3.p: The riddle answer to what is the strongest thing is the earth.

H631.4.r: Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas I 23, 360, Neuman.
H631.4.p: The riddle answer to what is the strongest thing is woman.

H631.5.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: Neuman; Japanese: Ikeda.
H631.5.p: The riddle answer to what is the strongest thing is truth.

H631.6.p: The riddle answer to what is the mightiest thing is rain.

H631.7.p: The riddle answer to what is the strongest thing is necessity.

H631.8.p: The riddle answer to what is the strongest thing is wine.

H631.9.p: A riddle asks what is strongest, and the answer given is the king.

H632.p: A riddle asks what is the swiftest thing in the world.

H632.1.p: A riddle asks what is swiftest, and the answer given is thought.

H632.2.p: A riddle asks what is swiftest, and the answer given is the eye.

H632.3.p: A riddle asks what is swiftest, and the answer given is the sun.

H633.p: A riddle asks what is the sweetest thing in the world.

H633.1.p: A riddle asks what is sweetest, and the answer given is sleep.

H633.2.p: A riddle asks what is sweetest, and the answer given is peace in heaven.

H633.3.r: De Vries De Sage van het ingemetselde Kind (Nederlandsch tijdschrift voor volkskunde XXXII 192ff); BP III 43; Krappe Balor 165ff.; India: Thompson-Balys.
H633.3.p: A riddle asks what is sweetest, and the answer given is a mother's breast.

H633.4.p: A riddle asking what is sweetest, with the answer being one's own interest.

H633.5.p: A riddle asks what is sweeter than sugar, and the answer given is a princess's speech.

H634.p: A riddle asks what is the sweetest song.

H634.1.p: A riddle asks what is the sweetest song, and the answer given is the song of angels.

H635.r: Anderson FFC XLII 233; De Vries FFC LXXIII 90; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
H635.p: A riddle asks what is the sweetest sound.

H635.1.r: Anderson FFC XLII 233; De Vries FFC LXXIII 91; BP II 357.
H635.1.p: A riddle asks what is the sweetest sound, and the answer given is the ringing of bells.

H635.2.p: A riddle asks what is the sweetest sound, and the answer given is God's Word.

H636.r: Types 461, 875; BP III 357; Aarne FFC XXIII 129.
H636.p: A riddle asks what is the richest thing.

H636.1.p: A riddle asks what is richest, and the answer given is autumn.

H637.p: A riddle asks what is the hardest thing.

H637.1.r: *De Vries De Sage van het ingemetselde Kind (Nederlandsch tijdschrift voor volkskunde XXXII 192ff.); BP III 43; *Krappe Balor 165ff.
H637.1.p: A riddle asks what is hardest, and the answer given is a parent's heart, said by a child who is being sacrificed.

H637.2.p: A riddle asks what is the hardest thing, and the answer given is death.

H638.p: A riddle asking what is the costliest thing in the world. The answer is given in the entries below it.

H638.1.p: The answer to the riddle of the costliest thing is the earth.

H641.p: A riddle asking what is the most beautiful thing. The answers are given below it.

H641.1.p: The answer to the riddle of the most beautiful thing is spring.

H641.2.p: Another answer to the riddle of the most beautiful thing is the earth.

H642.p: A riddle asking what is the highest thing. The answer is given below it.

H642.1.p: The answer to the riddle of the highest thing is the sun, moon, and stars.

H643.p: A riddle asking what is the deepest thing. The answer is given below it.

H643.1.r: De Vries FFC LXXIII 92; BP II 358.
H643.1.p: The answer to the riddle of the deepest thing is the heart of man.

H644.p: A riddle asking what is the longest thing. The answer is given below it.

H644.1.p: The answer to the riddle of the longest thing is the way through the world.

H645.p: A riddle asking what is the heaviest thing. The answer is given below it.

H645.1.p: The answer to the riddle of the heaviest thing is lead.

H646.p: A riddle asking what is the greenest thing. The answer is given below it.

H646.1.p: The answer to the riddle of the greenest thing is the month of May.

H647.p: A riddle asking what is the most beloved thing. The answers are given below it.

H647.1.p: The answer to the riddle of the most beloved thing is life.

H647.2.p: Another answer to the riddle of the most beloved thing is health.

H648.r: De Vries FFC LXXIII 95; *Krappe Revue Celtique XLVII 401ff.
H648.p: A riddle asking what is the best thing. The answer is given below it.

H648.1.r: De Vries FFC LXXIII 95; BP II 358.
H648.1.p: The answer to the riddle of the best thing is God.

H648.2.p: A riddle asks what is best, and the answer given is water, which is the best thing in the world.

H651.p: A riddle form in which the solver must name the brightest thing in the world.

H651.1.p: A riddle asks what is brightest, and the answer is the sun.

H651.2.r: (Cf. H662.) De Vries De Sage van het ingemetselde Kind (Nederlandsch tijdschrift voor volkskunde XXXII 192ff.).
H651.2.p: A riddle asks what is brightest, and the answer is a mother's eyes.

H652.r: De Vries FFC LXXIII 87; BP II 358.
H652.p: A riddle form in which the solver must name the softest thing in the world.

H652.1.r: (In order to lie soft one places his hand between the head and the pillow.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 88; BP II 358.
H652.1.p: A riddle asks what is softest, and the answer is the hand.

H652.2.r: De Vries De Sage van het ingemetselde Kind (Nederlandsche tijdschrift voor volkskunde XXXII 192ff.)
H652.2.p: A riddle asks what is softest, and the answer is a mother's bosom.

H653.p: A riddle form in which the solver must name the fattest thing in the world.

H653.1.r: De Vries FFC LXXIII 77; BP II 357f.; Anderson FFC XLII 232 n. 3.
H653.1.p: A riddle asks what is the fattest, and the answer is the earth.

H659.p: A miscellaneous group of riddles asking for the superlative, such as the oldest, hardest, or best of something.

H659.1.p: A riddle asks what is oldest, and the answer is God.

H659.1.1.p: A riddle asks what is oldest, and the answer given is God.

H659.2.p: A riddle asks which four things are hardest to hold onto.

H659.2.1.p: The answer to the riddle of four things hardest to hold: a wolf is hardest to hold by its eyebrows, a bear by its claws, a snake by its tail, and a hawk by its beak.

H659.3.p: A riddle asks which stones are the best and which are the worst.

H659.3.1.r: Anderson FFC LXII 228; BP III 220 n. 3; De Vries FFC LXXIII 95.
H659.3.1.p: The answer to the riddle of best and worst stones: the best are the altar, whetstone, and millstone; the worst are the hailstone, a stone in the eye, and a gallstone.

H659.4.p: A riddle asks which is the best fowl.

H659.4.1.p: The answer to the riddle of the best fowl is the goose, because it makes the cabbage sweet and the bed soft.

H659.5.p: A riddle asks whether the Christian or the Mohammedan religion is best.

H659.5.1.p: The answer to the question of which religion is best, Christian or Mohammedan, is that they are equally good: as both eyes are equally dear to you, so both religions are equally dear to God.

H659.6.p: A riddle asking what kind of work occupies most men. It is a test of cleverness posed as a question with a surprising answer.

H659.6.1.p: Asked what work occupies most men, the answer given is healing, because every sick man practices it.

H659.7.p: A riddle asking what is the greatest thing. It is a test of cleverness whose answer is a surprising single word.

H659.7.1.p: Asked what is greatest, the answer given is fame.

H659.7.2.p: Asked what is the greatest, the answer given is a sense of shame.

H659.7.3.p: Asked what is the greatest, the answer given is charity.

H659.7.4.p: Asked what is the greatest villainy, the answer given is stealing.

H659.8.p: Asked what is the moistest thing, the answer given is the south wind. It is a playful superlative riddle.

H659.9.p: A riddle asking what is the wisest thing. It is a test of cleverness posed as a superlative question.

H659.9.1.p: Asked what is wisest, the answer given is time.

H659.10.p: A riddle asking what is the most general or widespread thing. It is a test of cleverness posed as a superlative question.

H659.10.1.p: Asked what is most general, the answer given is hope.

H659.11.p: A riddle asking what is the most useful thing. It is a test of cleverness posed as a superlative question.

H659.11.1.p: Asked what is most useful, the answer given is excellence.

H659.12.p: A riddle asking what is the most shameful thing. It is a test of cleverness posed as a superlative question.

H659.12.1.p: Asked what is most shameful, the answer given is cowardice.

H659.13.p: A riddle asking what is the most pleasant thing. It is a test of cleverness posed as a superlative question.

H659.13.1.r: (In spite of childbirth pains women continue becoming pregnant.) Arab: Azov JPASB II 415f.
H659.13.1.p: Asked what is most pleasant, the answer given is love.

H659.14.p: A riddle asking what is the easiest thing. It is a test of cleverness posed as a superlative question.

H659.14.1.p: Asked what is easiest, the answer given is the natural thing, that which comes without effort.

H659.15.p: A riddle asking what is the hardest thing to skin. It is a bawdy riddle about superlatives, posed as a test of wit.

H659.15.1.p: The answer to the riddle of what is hardest to skin is the male member, a bawdy joke answer.

H659.16.p: A riddle asking who the best painters are, with the answer that women are, since they excel at painting faces with make-up.

H659.17.p: A riddle asking what the best time to eat is. The answer is that for the rich it is whenever they wish, and for the poor it is whenever they have food.

H659.18.p: A riddle asking which things are the most accursed or unfortunate, posed as a test of cleverness.

H659.18.1.p: The answer lists as the most accursed things a thriftless wife, a bald daughter, a sour-faced daughter-in-law, a crooked axle, and a field lying across the village road.

H659.19.p: A riddle asking what is the hardest thing to find and also the hardest to lose. The answer is the truth.

H659.20.p: A riddle asking who is truly irresistible, with the answer that meat and drink are.

H659.21.p: A riddle asking who is truly meek, with the answer that cows and daughters are.

H659.22.p: A riddle asking which is better, married domestic life or a life of ascetic renunciation. The answer is that domestic life is best when one has a good wife.

H659.23.p: A riddle asking which is the best of flowers, with the answer cotton.

H659.24.p: A riddle asking what the finest jewel is.

H659.25.p: A riddle asking what is the most faithful thing in the world.

H659.26.p: A riddle asking what is the most faithless thing in the world.

H660.r: Boberg Danske Studier 1945, 1ff., and Øst og Vest, Afhandlinger til Arthur Christensen (Kbhvn. 1945) 192.—Irish myth: Cross.
H660.p: A category of riddles that ask for comparisons, such as which of two things is swifter, dearer, whiter, sweeter, or softer.

H661.p: A riddle asking whether the wind or lightning is swifter than a bird. The answer is the eye, which is swifter than both.

H662.p: A riddle asking what is dearer than gold. The answer is mother's love.

H663.p: A riddle asking what is whiter than a swan. The answer is an angel.

H671.p: A riddle asking what is sweeter than honey.

H672.p: A riddle asking what is softer than swan down.

H673.p: A riddle asking what thing is harder than stone; the answer is given as a comparison that the listener must work out.

H674.p: A riddle asking who is greater than God, with the answer that man's purpose is what the riddle is really about.

H680.p: A general heading for riddles that ask how far apart things are, whether on earth or between earth and heaven.

H681.p: A general heading for riddles about distances on the earth, such as how far across it or how deep it goes.

H681.1.p: A riddle asking how far it is from one end of the earth to the other, going east to west.

H681.1.1.p: The answer to the earth-width riddle is one day's journey, because the sun travels across the whole earth in a day.

H681.2.p: A riddle asking how deep the earth is, or how far it is down to the lower world.

H681.2.1.p: The answer to the earth-depth riddle is that the earth is very deep, since the speaker's grandfather went down into it, died years ago, and has not yet come back.

H681.2.2.p: The answer to the earth-depth riddle is that the speaker's father went down years ago to measure it, died, and will report the result when he returns.

H681.3.p: A riddle asking where the exact center of the earth is.

H681.3.1.p: The answer to the earth-center riddle is that the center is right where the questioner stands, and the listener may measure it to check.

H681.3.2.p: The answer to the earth-center riddle is that the center is right here, because the earth is round and any point can serve as its center.

H681.4.p: A riddle asking how deep the sea is.

H681.4.1.p: The answer to the sea-depth riddle is that it is only a stone's throw deep.

H681.4.2.p: The answer to the sea-depth riddle is that the water starts knee-deep, then rises to waist-deep and neck-deep, and beyond that is over the head.

H682.p: A general heading for riddles about distances between earth and heaven.

H682.1.r: *Type 922; BP III 231; Anderson FFC XLII 113; Jewish: *Neuman.
H682.1.p: A riddle asking how far it is from earth to heaven.

H682.1.1.r: *Anderson FFC XLII 119; Wesselski Bebel I 36 No. 75.
H682.1.1.p: The answer to the heaven-distance riddle is a day's journey, since Christ went up to heaven in one day; a note adds that a half-day's journey is also given, for a similar reason.

H682.1.2.p: The answer to the heaven-distance riddle is a day's journey, because there is no inn on the way to stop at.

H682.1.3.p: The answer to the heaven-distance riddle is a specific height given as so-and-so high, with the questioner telling the listener to measure it to check.

H682.1.4.p: A riddle asks how far it is from earth to heaven, and the answer is that the distance is as far as you can see. The joke is that the question has no measurable answer.

H682.1.5.p: A riddle asks how far it is from earth to heaven, and the answer is that it is as far as from heaven to earth. The answer is a circular joke that gives no real measurement.

H682.1.6.p: A riddle asks how far it is from earth to heaven, and the answer is that it is not far, because thunder heard in heaven can be heard on earth.

H682.1.7.r: *Anderson FFC XLII 121; BP III 231; cf. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 96; Fb “kalvehale”.
H682.1.7.p: A riddle asks how far it is from earth to heaven, and the answer is the length of a calf's or fox's tail, if the tail were long enough. The joke is that the answer is an absurd measure.

H682.1.8.p: A riddle asks how far it is from earth to heaven, and the answer is a leg's length, because scripture says heaven is God's throne and earth is his footstool.

H682.1.9.p: A riddle asks how far it is from earth to heaven, and the answer is one step, since a man who is near death is said to have one foot in the grave and one in heaven.

H682.1.10.p: A riddle asks how far it is from earth to heaven, and the answer is that the devil knows the distance because he fell it when he was cast out of heaven.

H682.2.p: A riddle asks how wide heaven is. It is a question posed as a test of cleverness, with the expected answer given in the sub-entries.

H682.2.1.p: A riddle asks how wide heaven is, and the answer is a certain width, with the challenge that the listener can go and measure it themselves if they doubt it.

H682.3.p: A riddle or test asks how many ways out of paradise there are. It is a question about the number of exits from the garden of Eden or heaven.

H685.p: A riddle asks how far it is from happiness to misfortune, a question about how quickly a person's fortune can change.

H685.1.p: A riddle asks how far it is from happiness to misfortune, and the answer is one day, since a man can be a herdsman one day and an abbot the next. The point is how quickly fortune can change.

H690.p: A heading for riddles that ask about weight or measurement, such as how heavy the moon is or how big a distance is.

H691.p: A heading for riddles that ask about weight, such as how much the moon or the earth weighs.

H691.1.p: A riddle asks how much the moon weighs. It is a question posed as a test of cleverness, with the answer given in the sub-entries.

H691.1.1.r: *Type 922; BP III 232; *Anderson FFC XLII 173; Köhler-Bolte I 458.
H691.1.1.p: A riddle asks how much the moon weighs, and the answer is one pound, because the moon has four quarters.

H691.1.2.p: A riddle asks how much the moon weighs, and the answer is a certain amount, with the challenge that the listener can go and weigh it themselves if they doubt it.

H691.2.p: A riddle asks how heavy the earth is. It is a question posed as a test of cleverness, with the answer given in the sub-entry.

H691.2.1.p: A riddle asks how heavy the earth is, and the answer is to take away all the stones and then the speaker will weigh it.

H696.p: A heading for riddles that ask about measurement, such as how far or how big something is.

H696.1.p: A riddle asking how much water the sea holds. It is a test of cleverness, since the answer must be an unexpected, witty reply rather than a real measurement.

H696.1.1.p: The answer to the sea-water riddle: stop all the rivers flowing into the sea, and then you can measure what is left.

H696.1.2.p: A witty answer to the sea-water riddle: give a figure, and challenge the questioner to go and measure it to check.

H696.1.3.p: The answer to the sea-water riddle: a tub full of water, provided the tub is big enough to hold the sea.

H696.1.4.p: A riddle asking how many measures of water the river holds, which is answered with a clever reply rather than a real count.

H700.p: A group of riddles whose questions ask for a number, such as how many stars, hairs, or leaves there are, and whose answers are clever rather than exact.

H701.p: A riddle asking how many seconds are in eternity, a question with no real answer that tests the wit of the one replying.

H701.1.r: (Cf. D791.1.2, H1583, X950.2, Z61.) *Type 922; BP III 232; *Anderson FFC XLII 232.
H701.1.p: The answer to the eternity riddle: a bird carries one grain of sand from a mountain each century, and the first second of eternity has passed when the whole mountain is gone.

H702.r: *Type 922; BP III 231; Anderson FFC XLII 162ff.; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 116 No. 970.
H702.p: A riddle asking how many stars there are in the heavens, answered with a witty figure instead of a count.

H702.1.p: The answer to the star riddle: as many as there are grains of sand, and the questioner is challenged to count them to check.

H702.1.1.p: A star-riddle answer giving the figure of two million stars, with a challenge to the questioner to count them.

H702.2.p: The answer to the star riddle: as many as there are hairs on the head, and the questioner is challenged to count them.

H702.2.1.p: A star-riddle answer comparing the stars to the hairs on a goatskin, or on a donkey.

H702.3.p: The answer to the star riddle: as many as there are points on a sheet of paper, and the questioner is challenged to count them.

H703.p: A riddle asking how many hairs are on the head, answered with a clever reply rather than an actual count.

H703.1.p: The answer to the hair riddle: as many hairs as are in a donkey's tail, with a counter-challenge to pull out and count the hairs of the questioner's beard and the donkey's tail.

H704.p: A riddle asking how many drops of water are in the sea, a test of wit with a clever rather than exact answer.

H705.r: Anderson FFC XLII 175; West Indies: Flowers 459.
H705.p: A riddle asking how many leaves are on a tree, answered with a witty reply rather than a count.

H705.1.p: The answer to the leaf riddle: as many leaves as there are stems for them to grow on.

H705.2.p: The answer to the leaf riddle: a stated number given with a challenge to the questioner to go and count the leaves.

H705.3.r: (Cf. H702.) Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 116 No. 970.
H705.3.p: A riddle that answers a question about leaves on a tree with a counter-question about how many stars there are in the sky, a clever way of posing an unanswerable count.

H706.p: A riddle asking how many days have passed since the creation of Adam, the first man in the Bible.

H706.1.p: The answer to the riddle about days since Adam: the number is given as seven, the days of the week, meaning the count is always the same week cycle.

H707.p: A riddle in which the answer is a date or a particular day in time.

H707.1.p: A riddle asking when someone was born, described as having a beginning like its end and a top like its bottom; the date given is 1691.

H708.p: A riddle asking whether there are more men or more women in the world.

H710.p: Riddles that ask what something is worth, testing the solver's wit with a clever monetary answer.

H711.r: Anderson FFC XLII 194; cf. Aarne FFC XXIII 129.
H711.p: A riddle in which a king asks how much he is worth, and the solver must give a clever price for him.

H711.1.p: The answer to the king's worth riddle is twenty-nine pieces of silver, because Christ was sold for thirty, so the king is worth one less.

H712.r: *Type 875; De Vries FFC LXXIII 160; BP II 359.
H712.p: A riddle in which a king asks how much his beard is worth, and the solver must give a clever answer.

H712.1.p: The answer to the king's beard riddle is the months July, August and September, a clever pun on the word for a value that is three months' worth.

H712.2.r: De Vries FFC LXXIII 161; Köhler-Bolte I 456.
H712.2.p: Another answer to the king's beard riddle is a May rain, or three rains in summer, a clever figurative price.

H713.p: A riddle asking how much a golden plow, throne, crown or palace is worth, which the solver must answer cleverly.

H713.1.p: The answer to the golden plow riddle is a rain in May, a clever figurative price for something precious.

H715.p: A riddle asking how much the sun earns for his daily work, which the solver must answer cleverly.

H715.1.p: The answer to the sun's earnings riddle is a day's wages, the pay for one day of work.

H716.p: A riddle asking how much a certain crucifix is worth, answered with twenty-nine pieces of silver.

H720.p: Riddles that describe something indirectly through comparisons or figures of speech rather than plainly.

H721.p: A riddle describing the year through images, such as a tree with branches and leaves that stand for months and days.

H721.1.p: A riddle describing the year as a tree with twelve branches, each bearing thirty leaves, black and white, standing for the months and the days and nights.

H721.2.p: A riddle describing a tree whose leaves are white on one side and black on the other; the answer is the year, with its nights and days.

H721.3.p: A riddle describing twelve cypress trees, each with thirty boughs; the answer is the year, with its twelve months and thirty days.

H721.4.r: Year, months, days, hours. *Chauvin VI 40 No. 207.
H721.4.p: A riddle describing a palace of 8760 stones and twelve trees with thirty branches, each bearing a cluster of black and white grapes; the answer is the year, counted in hours, days and months.

H722.p: A riddle whose answer is the day and night, usually posed as a puzzle about two opposite figures.

H722.1.r: (Day and night.) Köhler-Bolte I 116; Gascon: Bladé I 9 No. 1.
H722.1.p: A riddle about a white brother and a black sister who every morning seem to kill each other, yet never die; the answer is day and night.

H722.2.p: A riddle about black and white horses chasing each other; the answer is night and day.

H725.p: A riddle whose answer is the path or course of the sun across the sky.

H725.1.p: A riddle about a bird that nests on one cypress in the morning and on another in the evening; the answer is the sun.

H726.p: A riddle asking who the real travellers are; the answer is the sun and the moon, which never stop moving.

H731.p: A riddle about a king and his courtiers, whose answer depends on how they are dressed or colored.

H731.1.r: (Sun and its rays.) Chauvin VI 39 No. 207 n. 1.
H731.1.p: A riddle where the king wears red and the courtiers wear white; the answer turns on those colors.

H731.2.r: (Moon and stars.) Chauvin VI 39 No. 207 n. 1.
H731.2.p: A riddle where the king and the courtiers are all dressed in white; the answer turns on that sameness.

H731.3.r: (Spring and flowers.) Chauvin VI 39 No. 207 n. 1.
H731.3.p: A riddle where the king wears red and the courtiers wear many different colors; the answer turns on that contrast.

H734.p: A riddle asking what mother devours her children once they grow up; the answer is a riddle-answer about a mother's fate.

H741.p: A riddle describing a white field with black seed; the answer is writing on paper.

H742.p: A riddle about things with two legs, three legs, and four legs; the answer is a human being, who crawls, walks upright, and uses a cane in old age.

H743.r: (Cow’s teats, feet, eyes, tail.) (Other answers: cat, dog, horse, hog, etc.) **Aarne FFC XXVII 60ff.
H743.p: A riddle describing four things hanging, four walking, two showing the way, and one wagging behind; the answer is a cow.

H744.p: A riddle describing a creature with six legs, four ears, two faces and similar odd features; the answer is a strange animal or thing.

H746.p: A riddle describing a white bill, horns on the feet, and a knob on the head; the answer is a rooster.

H751.p: A riddle asking who has a fourfold beard and a blue foot and ruddy neck; the answer is an arrow.

H761.r: (Man, who crawls as a child, walks in middle life, and walks with a stick in old age.) **Aarne FFC XXVII 3ff.; **Laistner Rätsel der Sphinx; Gascon: Bladé I 10 No. 1.; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 349 n. 1 Köhler-Bolte I 115; Fb “menneske” II 578a.
H761.p: The Riddle of the Sphinx: a riddle about a creature that walks on four legs in the morning, two at midday, and three in the evening. The answer is a human, who crawls as a baby, walks upright as an adult, and uses a staff in old age.

H761.1.p: A riddle answer saying that two legs are better than three: a person walking on two legs is preferred to one who needs a staff in old age.

H762.p: A riddle asking what creature is found in every country, is loved by all the world, and has no equal. The answer is not given here in the headline.

H763.p: A riddle describing a father who is not yet born and a son who is already at the top of the house. It is a paradox-style puzzle to be solved by guessing its hidden meaning.

H764.r: (Snow falls on bare tree.) **Aarne FFC XXVIII 1ff.
H764.p: A riddle about a bird without feathers flying in a tree without leaves. It is a nonsense-seeming puzzle whose answer is a hidden image.

H765.r: If you rub lids with it, tears come.) Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas III 32, 297f., *Neuman.
H765.p: A riddle in which a wooden spring and an iron bucket produce stones from which water flows; the note indicates the answer involves a metal stick removing a stone from an eye. The headline is garbled in the source, so the exact wording is uncertain.

H767.p: A general heading for allegorical riddles, in which the answer is hidden behind symbolic or indirect description.

H767.1.r: (The field of youth; the mountains of youth, etc.) Irish myth: Cross.
H767.1.p: A riddle asking what is that which one passes over with haste. It is an allegorical puzzle in which the answer is something briefly crossed or traversed.

H768.p: A riddle asking what house gives no hostages, cannot be burned, and cannot be attacked. The answer is a fairy stronghold, here named as the fairy mound of brugh na Boinne.

H770.p: A general heading for riddles that explain why things are the way they are, by asking for a reason behind a natural or common fact.

H771.r: (It is twenty years older.) *Wesselski Arlotto II 270 No. 222.
H771.p: A riddle asking why a person's hair turns gray before the beard does.

H772.r: (The moon turns some nights into days.) Chauvin V 38 No. 365.
H772.p: A riddle asking why there are more days than nights.

H773.r: (There are some of the dead of whom we still speak.) Chauvin V 38 No. 365.
H773.p: A riddle asking why there are more living people than dead ones.

H774.r: (Some women make women [i.e., weaklings] of their husbands.) Chauvin V 38 No. 365.
H774.p: A riddle asking why there are more women than men.

H790.p: A general heading for riddles whose answers depend on odd or unusual circumstances, such as unusual births or family relationships.

H791.r: (Man eats magic fish and becomes pregnant; a girl is taken from his knee.) *Type 705; *Fb “fisk” I 297; Norse: Christiansen Norske Eventyr 96.
H791.p: A riddle describing a speaker whose father was a fish and whose mother was a human. The answer is a figure with an unusual origin.

H792.r: He rides on a colt which has been taken from a dead mare’s body.) *Type 851; BP I 196; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 112 No. 927*B; Africa (Swahili): Werner African 356.
H792.p: A riddle about someone unborn who carries his mother on his hands, and whose horse is also unborn. The note tells of a boy taken from his dead mother's body who digs up her body and makes gloves from her skin.

H793.r: (A horse’s head in which a bird’s nest is found with seven birds in it.) *Type 927; Köhler-Bolte I 46; *Fb “hestehoved”.
H793.p: A riddle about a head that has seven tongues. It is a puzzle whose answer is not given in the headline.

H795.p: A riddle whose answer depends on working out family relationships that result from unusual marriages between relatives.

H797.p: A riddle asking what God does. It is a question puzzle whose answer is a clever or surprising reply.

H797.1.p: A riddle asks what God does: he humbles the proud and raises the humble. The answer is given by a shepherd disguised as a bishop to a king who has swapped places with him.

H797.2.p: A riddle answer to 'what does God do?': God is astonished that the speaker sits on a horse while the king rides an ass. This is a variant of the swapped-places riddle.

H802.r: (Horse is poisoned; raven eats of him and dies; twelve robbers eat raven and die.) *Type 851; BP I 188ff.; *Fb “hest” I 598b, “ravn” III 23a; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 172 No. 34; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 284 No. 116.
H802.p: A riddle about someone who killed no one yet caused twelve deaths.

H803.r: Snake can’t get out of its hole. India: Thompson-Balys.
H803.p: A riddle about three kinds of death caused by sleepiness, anger, and greed. In the tale an elephant sleeps by a snake's hole, the snake bites and kills it, and a jackal eats into the elephant's body and is trapped inside.

H804.r: (Swarm of bees and honey in lion’s carcass.) Jewish: Judges 14:14.
H804.p: A riddle whose answer is that meat came out of the eater and sweetness out of the strong. It is a paradox puzzle, like the riddle of Samson's lion and honey.

H805.r: (Queen has cup made from skull of her murdered lover; ring with one of his eyes; she carries two of his teeth in her boots.) *Type 851; *BP I 196, II 361; Köhler-Bolte I 350, 372; India: Thompson-Balys.
H805.p: A riddle about a murdered lover, asking what thinks, drinks, sees, carries, and walks. The note's answer lists the body parts: the head, the eyes, and the feet, which the riddle describes as drinking, carrying, and walking.

H806.r: (Stork took bunch of grapes to nest; boy makes wine from them.) Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 112 No. 927B*.
H806.p: A riddle asking someone to drink wine that a bird carried off to its nest.

H807.r: (Girl has nursed her imprisoned father through a crack in the prison wall.) Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 111 No. 927*A.
H807.p: A riddle about a woman who was once a daughter and is now a mother, whose son is also the husband of her mother. The answer is a family puzzle in which the relationships seem to contradict each other.

H810.p: A heading for riddles whose questions and answers rely on stories from the Bible or from legend.

H811.p: A riddle asking who first spun thread, and when.

H812.p: A riddle asking what clothes Adam and Eve wore.

H813.p: A riddle asking who, having had neither father nor mother, is dead.

H814.p: A riddle asking who, having had a father and a mother, is not dead.

H815.r: (Lot’s wife.) Chauvin V 195 No. 114; Scala Celi No. 821.
H815.p: A riddle asking who, having had a father and a mother, is not dead like other mortals.

H817.p: A riddle asking who, while on earth, has had two names.

H821.r: (Jonah and the whale.) Chauvin V 194 No. 114; Jewish: *Neuman.
H821.p: A riddle asking what the walking tomb with a living tenant was.

H822.r: (The bottom of the Red Sea during the passage of the Israelites.) Chauvin V 194 No. 114; Jewish: *Neuman.
H822.p: A riddle asking what land has seen the sun only once.

H822.1.r: (The land on which the waters were gathered after the creation.) Jewish: Neuman.
H822.1.p: The question form of the riddle about which land has seen the sun only once.

H823.p: A riddle asking what tree became flesh.

H824.r: (Moses’s staff, which became a serpent.) Chauvin V 194 No. 114.
H824.p: A riddle asking what drinks water to stay alive and eats after it is dead.

H825.r: (The idol Bel surrounded by the priests of the god.) Chauvin VI 39 No. 207.
H825.p: A riddle asks what a king surrounded by his nobles is like, and the answer is a comparison drawn from the story's setting. The riddle is a test of the solver's cleverness.

H826.r: Answer: entered into his thirty-first. (Cf. H865.) Italian Novella: Rotunda.
H826.p: A riddle asks what Christ did in his thirtieth year, a test drawn from Bible or legend. The solver must find the clever answer.

H827.r: Punishes the bad people. India: Thompson-Balys.
H827.p: A riddle asks what the king of the world of the Devas (divine beings in Indian belief) does. The solver must give the clever answer.

H828.p: A riddle asks which three beings not born of a male and female parent ate and drank on earth. The answer is a figure from legend or scripture.

H831.r: (Philistines in the building demolished by Samson.) Jewish: Neuman.
H831.p: A riddle asks which house was full of dead people. The solver must find the clever answer.

H832.p: A riddle asks what thing was never born yet was given life. The solver must find the clever answer.

H840.p: A general heading for riddles that do not fit the other riddle groups in this part of the index.

H841.p: A heading for riddles about how much an animal is worth, asked by comparing its value alive and dead.

H841.1.p: A riddle asking what animal is alive yet not dead, with the answer concerning the animal's worth. Used as a test of cleverness in riddle contests.

H841.2.p: A riddle asks which animal is good when dead but not when alive. The solver must name the animal.

H841.3.p: A riddle asks which animal is good both while living and when dead. The solver must name the animal.

H841.4.p: A riddle asks which animal is good neither living nor dead. The solver must name the animal.

H842.p: A heading for riddles about the special qualities of animals.

H842.1.p: A riddle asks which animal living in sea water would drown if taken out of it. The solver must name the animal.

H842.2.p: A riddle asks which animal living in fire would burn if taken out of it. The note identifies this creature as the salamander, earlier called tegillus.

H842.3.r: (Ibis, from whose carcass musical instruments are made.) Jewish: Neuman.
H842.3.p: A riddle asks which animal has one voice while living and seven voices when dead. The solver must name the animal.

H851.r: (Heaven and earth; sun and moon; night and day; soul and body; life and death.) Chauvin V 195 No. 114.
H851.p: A riddle asks what the two fixed things, two moving things, two joined things, two divided by jealousy, and two eternal enemies are. The solver must name them.

H852.p: A riddle asks which two trees do not fade until they wither. The solver must name the trees.

H853.p: A riddle asks what goodness man found on earth that God did not find. The solver must give the clever answer.

H861.r: (The bull and the buffalo.) Chauvin V 194 No. 114.
H861.p: A riddle asks what two combatants are that have no hands, feet, or words. The solver must name them.

H862.p: A riddle asks what is neither a man, a jinn (spirit), a beast, nor a bird. The solver must name the thing.

H865.p: A riddle asking what crows do when they reach five years old; the answer is that they begin their sixth year.

H871.r: (Sowing salt, mowing pebbles, drinking from an empty jug, making signs to a blind man, wooing at mealtime, playing a harp in a mill.) Anderson FFC XLII 227, *228 n. 1.
H871.p: A riddle asking which six things are not worth doing.

H871.1.p: The answer to the riddle about six things not worth doing: three foolish things men do, given in various versions.

H875.p: A riddle asking what the difference is between a poor man and a rich man.

H878.p: A riddle asking what a person buys that they neither want nor use.

H881.p: A group of riddles whose answer is "none" or nothing.

H881.1.p: A riddle asking how many dead mice attend a feast, with the answer being none, since dead mice cannot come.

H882.p: A riddle asking which of the two ends of a staff is the top and which is the bottom.

H883.p: A riddle asking where the root of the floor is.

H885.r: Taylor English Riddles from Oral Tradition (Berkeley, California, 1951) 250; Jewish: *Neuman.
H885.p: Riddles about flax, the plant used for linen fibre.

H886.p: Riddles about naphtha, a flammable liquid fuel.

H900.r: *Penzer X 330 s.v. “tests”; *Chauvin VI 200 No. 372.—Irish myth: *Cross; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “épreuves”; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 184 n. 1 (Hercules), Fox 80ff. (Hercules), ibid. 98 (Theseus); N. A. Indian: **Lowie The Test Theme in North American Mythology (JAFL XXI 97ff.).
H900.p: A hero's strength or skill is tested by being given tasks, usually impossible or very hard, that he must perform either to avoid punishment or to win a valuable reward.

H901.r: Types 306, 851; BP I 188; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 53, 83—84, 179, *Boberg; French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
H901.p: A hero is given a task under threat of death if he fails to carry it out.

H901.0.1.p: A task is imposed under threat that a relative, friend or hostage will be put to death if the task is not done.

H901.0.2.p: A bird is ordered to bring an orphan to the king, on pain of the bird being killed if it fails.

H901.1.r: *Types 329, 507A; *BP III 368; *Taylor Romanic Review IV 21ff.; *Brown Iwain 137 n. 1; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Greek: Fox 119, Frazer Apollodorus II 160 n. 2; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
H901.1.p: Heads of unsuccessful youths are beheaded and set on stakes; the hero sees them when he sets out to do his own task.

H902.p: A task is assigned to the hero by the gods.

H910.p: Tasks are assigned to a person because someone suggests it.

H911.r: *Types 328, 501, 531, 725; BP I 109, III 18ff.; Köhler-Bolte I 430; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 22; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 59 No. 425D; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 7, IV No. 5, Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 459.
H911.p: Tasks are assigned at the urging of jealous rivals who hope the hero will fail or die.

H911.1.p: A quest is assigned at the suggestion of a jealous co-wife.

H912.r: *Type 408; Köhler-Bolte I 468; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 49 No. 328*A, Espinosa Jr. No. 81; India: Thompson-Balys; S. A. Indian (Inca) Rowe BBAE CXLIII (2) 317; West Indies: Flowers 460.
H912.p: A hero or heroine is given an impossible or dangerous task because jealous brothers or sisters urged it on the person who assigns it.

H913.p: A hero or heroine is given a difficult task because a jealous parent suggested it.

H913.1.p: A difficult task is set because a jealous mother suggested it.

H913.1.1.p: A prospective bride is given a task at the suggestion of her jealous mother, usually to keep her from marrying.

H913.1.2.p: A task is suggested by a mother's jealous co-wife, a rival wife who is also the mother's co-spouse.

H913.2.p: A difficult task is assigned because a jealous father suggested it.

H913.2.1.p: A prospective bride is given a task at the suggestion of her jealous father, usually to keep her from marrying.

H914.r: *Type 500, 501; BP I 490, 109; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 4.
H914.p: A mother boasts foolishly to a king that her daughter can do something impossible, such as spinning enormous amounts, and so the daughter is given that task.

H915.r: *Type 501, 1525; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 460.
H915.p: A girl or boy is given a difficult task because of their own foolish boast that they could do it.

H915.1.p: A person is given difficult tasks because of a foolish boast they made themselves.

H916.p: A task is imposed on someone at the suggestion of their spouse or sweetheart.

H916.1.p: A task is imposed because a wife foolishly boasted about her husband's abilities.

H916.1.1.r: *Crane Vitry 231f. No. 237; *Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. XXVI 89 n. 1; Herbert III 19; Japanese: Ikeda.
H916.1.1.p: A jealous wife tells the authorities that her husband is a famous doctor, so he is ordered to cure the princess, though he is not a real doctor and faces danger if he fails.

H916.2.p: A task is imposed on someone because a girl foolishly boasted about them.

H916.3.p: A task is assigned at the joint suggestion of a wife and her lover.

H917.p: Someone is given a task because of a suggestion they made without realizing it would lead to that task. The example given is Jason being sent for the Golden Fleece.

H918.p: A task is assigned because of a suggestion written in a letter that the victim carries unknowingly.

H919.p: Miscellaneous cases in which tasks are assigned in response to someone's suggestion, not covered by the more specific headings.

H919.1.r: Icelandic: Herrmann II 583ff., *Boberg; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
H919.1.p: Tasks are assigned at the suggestion of treacherous servants who wish harm to the person given the task.

H919.1.1.p: A barber suggests a task, and it is assigned on his advice.

H919.2.p: Tasks are assigned at the suggestion of a religious person, such as a priest, monk, or holy figure.

H919.3.p: A task is given to a hero because a parrot suggests it. The parrot's advice is what leads to the assignment of the task.

H919.4.p: A plaintiff, as proof of his claim, sets the defendant an impossible task. The task is assigned on the plaintiff's own suggestion.

H919.5.p: A task is assigned to a hero because a treacherous soldier suggests it, with the aim of harming the hero.

H919.6.p: Tasks are assigned to a hero at the urging of a queen who is secretly an ogress. She suggests the tasks, which are part of her plot against him.

H920.p: A general heading for characters who assign tasks to others as tests. It introduces the kinds of people who set such tasks.

H921.r: *Type 920; De Vries FFC LXXIII 40ff., 323ff.; India: *Thompson-Balys; S. A. Indian (Tupinamba): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 132.
H921.p: A king, who is the father of a young man he does not yet know, assigns him tasks. The tasks test the young man so the king can recognize him.

H921.1.p: A king sets his sons a task to decide which of them will inherit the kingdom. The one who succeeds becomes heir.

H922.p: A husband leaving on a journey gives his wife tasks to perform while he is away. The tasks test or occupy her.

H923.p: Before a man can go to the spirit world to rescue his wife, he is given tasks to perform.

H923.1.p: Before a wife can rescue her husband from a supernatural power, she is given tasks to perform.

H924.r: De Vries FFC LXXIII 309, 313; India: Thompson-Balys; Icelandic: *Boberg.
H924.p: A prisoner is given tasks to perform so that he may escape punishment if he completes them.

H924.1.p: Tasks are set as the price of a prisoner's release, to be paid as ransom.

H927.p: A general heading for tasks that are set by a god or other deity. It introduces the cases where divine beings assign such tests.

H927.1.p: Gods set tasks to test the courage or skill of a mortal.

H927.2.p: An angel is sent to assign a task, following a command from God.

H928.p: Tasks are imposed on a people or person as tribute, a payment owed to a ruler.

H928.1.p: Tasks are imposed as a fine, a penalty for an offense.

H931.r: *Types 428, 461; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Icelandic: *Boberg; Greek: Grote I 110; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Anesaki 357, Ikeda.
H931.p: Tasks are assigned to a hero with the purpose of getting rid of him, so that he will die or fail while attempting them.

H931.1.r: *Type 465.—Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: De Vries’s list No. 170; Japanese: Ikeda.
H931.1.p: A jealous prince, who envies the hero's wife, assigns the hero tasks in order to remove him.

H931.1.1.p: A husband is assigned tasks by a king who has stolen his wife. The tasks are meant to keep him from getting her back.

H931.2.p: The hero is given unpleasant tasks that are meant to make him disobey so that he can be punished or killed. The assigner's real aim is to get rid of him.

H932.p: A devil or ogre sets the hero tasks to perform.

H933.p: A princess sets the hero tasks he must complete, usually as a condition for winning her.

H933.1.p: The princess throws her handkerchief high into a tree and asks the hero to fetch it back.

H933.2.p: A maiden who is a queen gives the hero three dangerous tasks, which are meant to free her sisters from enchantment.

H933.3.p: The princess orders the hero to bring her rings belonging to another princess.

H933.4.p: A princess who has been scorned gives the hero a quest to complete.

H933.5.p: The Queen of the Sea gives the hero tasks to perform.

H934.p: A relative of the hero gives him tasks to perform.

H934.1.p: A wife gives her husband tasks to perform.

H934.2.p: The hero's sisters-in-law impose tasks on him.

H934.3.p: The hero's stepmother gives him tasks to perform.

H934.4.p: The hero's elder brothers impose a task on him.

H935.r: Type 480, *Roberts; BP I 207; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1137A*.
H935.p: A witch gives the hero tasks to perform.

H936.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 4; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
H936.p: A pregnant woman's cravings lead to tasks being assigned to get what she longs for.

H937.p: A dying child gives a task that must be carried out.

H938.p: A fairy gives the hero tasks to perform.

H939.p: Tasks are assigned by other kinds of beings or people not covered by the more specific headings.

H939.1.p: A druid, a priest of the ancient Celtic religion, gives the hero tasks to perform.

H939.2.p: A man who wants to win a woman as his lover sets her tests to perform.

H939.3.p: Cruel sisters-in-law give a hero a series of difficult tasks in the hope of getting rid of him or his tigress wife. The tasks are a test of his strength and ability.

H939.4.p: A giant gives a hero a task to perform as a test of his prowess.

H939.4.1.p: A serpent king, acting as a giant-like assigner, gives a hero a task to perform.

H940.p: A miscellaneous group of motifs in which tasks are assigned to a hero, with no more specific category.

H941.r: *Cosquin Contes indiens 474ff.; Chauvin VI 109 No. 274 n. 3; Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 109 n. 4; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H941.p: A hero is given a second task that must be done before he can complete the first, so the tasks form a chain.

H942.p: A person loses a bet or gambling game and must then perform a task as payment.

H945.p: A hero takes on a difficult task of his own free will rather than being ordered to do it.

H945.1.p: Warriors go out to meet a strong enemy because of a boast they made earlier.

H945.2.p: A hero travels north voluntarily to fight trolls.

H946.p: A task is given to a hero because of a misunderstanding of what was said or meant.

H946.1.p: A hero is sent to search for a prince named Sabr, a name meaning wait, because of a misunderstanding of the word.

H950.p: A hero avoids carrying out an assigned task by using a clever trick or excuse.

H951.r: (Cf. H691.2.1, H1021.1.1, H1021.3, H1021.6.1, H1021.6.2, H1022.2.1, H1022.3, H1022.9, H1023.1.1, H1023.1.2, H1023.2.2.1, H1023.9.1, H1023.10.1, H1142.3, H1146.) *Types 531, 875; *BP I 221, II 367, 369, III 18ff.; *De Vries FFC LXXIII 43ff., 145ff., 150ff., 154, 232ff., 241f., 249; *Chauvin VIII 61 No. 26; Zachariae Kleine Schriften 98; *Child V 497 s.v. “tasks”; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Ikeda.
H951.p: The hero agrees to do an assigned task only if the assigner first does another task of the hero's choosing, turning the demand back on the assigner.

H952.r: (Cf. H1023.3.1, H1024.1.1.1.) *Type 821B; BP II 368 n. 1; Child I 10f., 13; De Vries FFC LXXIII 265, 269 n. 2; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: De Vries’s list No. 237; Chinese: Graham.
H952.p: When given an impossible task, the hero answers with an equally absurd counter-task that shows how ridiculous the original demand is.

H960.p: A miscellaneous group of motifs in which a hero performs assigned tasks through wit or intelligence rather than strength.

H961.r: *M. Bloomfield in Penzer VII x; S. A. Indian (Quiché): Alexander Lat. Am. 174.
H961.p: A hero completes an assigned task by using cleverness rather than force.

H962.p: A hero completes a task by carefully observing and noticing a hidden trick.

H962.1.p: The hero is told to sit on eggs without breaking them, and he succeeds because he notices the trick in the task.

H963.r: *Type 613; *Christiansen FFC XXIV 96ff.; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Ikeda.
H963.p: A hero completes a task using secrets he overhears from birds or others speaking in a tree.

H970.p: A hero receives help from a helper, such as an animal or magical being, in carrying out a task.

H971.p: A hero is helped to complete a set task by an old person who does the work for him or guides him through it.

H971.1.r: Types 306, 510, 566, 567; Irish myth: *Cross; Scotch: Macdougall and Calder 160; German: Grimm Nos. 9, 14, 29, 122, 125, 133, 181, 186; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Japanese: Ikeda.
H971.1.p: A set task is completed with the help of an old woman.

H971.2.p: A set task is completed with the help of several little old men.

H972.p: A set task is completed with the help of dead people who are grateful for past kindness shown to them.

H972.1.p: Tasks are performed by spirits of the dead who are held captive and are freed or rewarded for helping.

H973.p: A set task is completed with the help of helpful spirits of the forest.

H973.1.p: A set task is completed by a fairy who helps the hero.

H973.2.p: A set task is completed with the help of four demons who are bound in a ring.

H973.3.p: A set task is completed by dwarfs who help the hero.

H974.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Greek: Grote I 219; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Anesaki 357, Ikeda.
H974.p: A set task is completed with the help of a supernatural wife, usually one who is not human.

H974.1.p: A set task is completed with the help of a mistress, a supernatural woman who helps the hero.

H975.p: A set task is performed by a deity, a god or divine being, on the hero's behalf.

H975.0.1.p: A deity performs a set task in answer to the hero's prayer.

H975.1.p: A set task is performed with the aid of a goddess.

H976.p: A set task is performed by a mysterious stranger who appears and helps the hero, then vanishes.

H981.p: A set task is completed with the help of the hero's brother.

H982.p: Animals come to a man's aid and help him complete a difficult task he has been set.

H982.1.p: Pigeons spread their wings to block the sun and make the night last six months, giving the hero enough time to finish his task in a single night.

H983.p: A set task is completed with the help of an angel.

H984.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 69 No. 515.
H984.p: A set task is completed with the help of a saint, a holy person.

H984.1.p: A set task is completed with the help of a Brahmadaitya, a spirit of a Brahmin who died unnaturally and became a ghost.

H985.p: A hero is set a task that is accomplished with the help of a druid, a magic helper figure.

H986.p: A task is performed with help from invisible hands, which do the work unseen.

H987.p: A task is accomplished with the aid of a magic object that does the work or makes it possible.

H990.p: A miscellaneous category of tales in which a task is performed with help that does not fit the other headings in this group.

H991.p: The least promising hero is the last to attempt a task, such as rescuing someone from an animal, and he succeeds where the others failed.

H1010.r: *Type 428; *Child V 498 s.v. “tasks”; Burton Nights VI 204ff., S VI 4ff.; Hdwb. d. Märchens I s.v. “Aufgaben, schwierige”; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: De Vries’s list No. 168; Chinese: Graham.
H1010.p: General heading for tasks that cannot be done at all, set as impossible or absurd challenges.

H1020.p: General heading for tasks that go against the laws of nature, so they could not really be done.

H1021.p: A task requires building or making something out of a material that is impossible to work with in that way.

H1021.1.r: *Type 1174; *De Vries FFC LXXIII 154, 155 n. 1; BP III 16; *Fb “reb” III 25b; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 431b n. 45; Chauvin VI 40 No. 207 n. 2.—Icelandic: Boberg.
H1021.1.p: The hero is asked to make a rope out of sand, which cannot be done.

H1021.1.1.p: A rope of sand is demanded as a task, and in answer the other party first shows how the pattern is to be made, so the task is turned back.

H1021.2.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “corde”; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1021.2.p: The hero is asked to make a rope out of chaff, which cannot be done.

H1021.3.r: De Vries FFC LXXIII 150ff.; Indonesia: De Vries’s list No. 235.
H1021.3.p: The hero is asked to make a ship out of stone, which cannot be done.

H1021.4.p: The hero is asked to make a knot out of spilled brandy, which cannot be done.

H1021.5.p: The hero is asked to tie an invisible knot using an egg, which cannot be done.

H1021.6.p: The hero is asked to weave a silk shirt out of hair, which cannot be done.

H1021.6.1.p: A silk shirt is demanded from hair, and in answer the other party asks for a loom made from shavings, so the task is turned back.

H1021.7.p: The hero is asked to take a stick out of the body, which cannot be done.

H1021.8.p: The hero is asked to spin gold, which cannot be done.

H1021.9.p: The hero is asked to sew a shirt out of stone, which cannot be done.

H1021.9.1.p: A stone shirt is demanded, and the task is answered by asking for a shirt sewn from flower petals, which is equally impossible.

H1021.10.p: A task impossibly demands that ale be brewed from sweet milk, a material that cannot yield it. The hero is tested with this absurd request.

H1021.11.p: A task asks the hero to make a peacock out of silk, a clearly impossible request to build a living bird from the wrong material.

H1022.p: A general category of tasks in which the hero must build or make something from an impossibly small amount of material.

H1022.1.p: The hero must weave cloth using only two threads, an impossibly small amount of material.

H1022.2.r: Köhler-Bolte I 459, 566; *Hdwb. d. Märchens II 151a nn. 503—521.
H1022.2.p: The hero must make enough shirts to clothe a whole army from a single hank of flax or wool, an impossible quantity from so little.

H1022.2.1.p: The hero must clothe an army from one hank of flax; the matching counter-task is to make horseshoes for cavalry from a single needle.

H1022.2.2.p: The hero must weave a shirt from a single piece of thread; the counter-task is to make a loom from a rod.

H1022.3.p: The hero must make ship sails from one bundle of linen; the counter-task is to make a spindle and loom from one stick of wood.

H1022.4.r: Oesterley Gesta Romanorum No. 64; Herbert Catalogue III 206.
H1022.4.p: The hero must make a shirt from a piece of linen only three inches square, an impossibly small piece of cloth.

H1022.4.1.p: The hero must make a shirt from a single flax seed, an impossibly small starting material.

H1022.4.2.p: The hero must weave a mantle from the wool of a single sheep, an impossibly small amount of wool for such a garment.

H1022.4.3.p: The hero must make shawl cloth one hundred cubits long from a single silk cocoon, an impossible quantity from one small cocoon.

H1022.5.p: The hero must feed an entire army from one measure of meal, an impossibly small amount of food.

H1022.5.1.p: The hero must make broth enough for an entire army, a variant of feeding an army from very little food.

H1022.6.p: The hero must make many kinds of food from a single small bird, an impossibly small amount of meat.

H1022.6.1.p: The hero must brew ale from a single grain of corn, an impossibly small amount of grain.

H1022.7.p: The hero must make a boat from splinters of a spindle and shuttle, an impossibly small amount of wood.

H1022.8.p: The hero must brew an impossibly large amount of ale from a single grain of corn.

H1022.9.p: The hero must bring a quantity of mosquito bones within a month; the counter-task is to furnish scales using wind as beams and heat as pans.

H1023.p: A general category of tasks that demand the nature of an object be changed or reversed, which cannot happen in the real world.

H1023.1.p: A hero is given the impossible task of hatching boiled eggs, which cannot hatch because they have been cooked.

H1023.1.1.r: (Cf. H951, H952.) *Types 821B, 875; *De Vries FFC LXXIII 242; *BP II 368 n. 1.
H1023.1.1.p: The hero is asked to hatch boiled eggs, and in return he must sow cooked seeds and harvest a crop from them, an equally impossible counter-task.

H1023.1.2.r: (Cf. H951, H952.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 242; Köhler-Bolte I 459.
H1023.1.2.p: The task is to hatch eggs at once, and the counter-task is to sow seeds and bring in the crop the next morning, both impossible.

H1023.2.r: *Types 480, 1180, Roberts 138, 165; *BP I 5, 215, III 16, 477 n. 1; *Fb “såld” III 750a; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 354; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; S. A. Indian (Ackawoi): Alexander Lat. Am. 269.
H1023.2.p: A hero or heroine is ordered to carry water in a sieve, which cannot hold water, as an impossible task.

H1023.2.0.1.r: *BP I 5, 215, III 477 n. 1; England: Baughman; American Negro (Georgia): Harris Remus 107 No. 22.
H1023.2.0.1.p: The sieve is stuffed with moss so that the water can be carried, making the impossible task possible.

H1023.2.0.2.p: A pious child is able to carry water in a sieve, accomplishing the impossible task through piety.

H1023.2.1.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “cruche”; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa (Mpongwe): Nassau 32 No. 4; (Zulu): Callaway 16, (Basuto): Jacottet 15 No. 10, 202 No. 30, (Kaffir): Theal 15, (Angola): Chatelain 163, 171, 179 No. 21.
H1023.2.1.p: The task is to carry water in a leaky vessel, which lets the water run out.

H1023.2.1.1.p: The leaky vessel is mended with clay or gum so the water can be carried.

H1023.2.1.2.p: A frog sits in the hole of the leaky vessel, plugging it so the water can be carried.

H1023.2.2.p: A hero tells his wife to fill a water bottle while its spout is turned downward, an impossible task meant as a test.

H1023.2.3.p: The impossible task is to fill a grain bin through the hole in its bottom.

H1023.2.4.p: The task is to fill a water tube that has no bottom, so the water always runs out.

H1023.2.5.p: The task is to fill pots that have outlets underground, so the water drains away beneath.

H1023.3.r: *Type 403B, 480, *Roberts 134; BP I 99ff., II 232; *Saintyves Perrault 20; De Vries FFC LXXIII 269 n. 2; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Eskimo (Greenland): Rink 159; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 313 n. 126c.
H1023.3.p: A hero is asked to bring berries, fruit, or roses in winter, when they are not in season.

H1023.3.1.r: Reductio ad absurdum: father is sick from snake-bite (impossible in winter). (Cf. H952.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 269 n. 2.
H1023.3.1.p: The task is to bring berries in winter, when none grow.

H1023.3.1.1.p: The task is to get a cuckoo to sing in winter, when cuckoos are not heard.

H1023.3.2.p: The task is to make withered flowers green again.

H1023.4.r: Type 1175; BP III 15; Lithuanian: Balys Legends No. 636; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 314 No. 113, 329 No. 45; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H1023.4.p: The impossible task is to straighten a curly hair.

H1023.4.1.p: The impossible task is to make a dog's curly tail straight.

H1023.5.p: The impossible task is to pump out a leaky ship so it does not sink.

H1023.6.r: Type 480; *Roberts 165; *Fb “får” I 406b, “hvid” I 700b, “skjorte” III 268a, “sort” III 467b; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 314 No. 113, 328 No. 10.
H1023.6.p: A hero is set the impossible task of washing black wool, cloth, or cattle until they are white.

H1023.6.1.p: A hero must wash a large, heavy quilt smeared with ghee and oil, with no soap or other cleaning aid.

H1023.7.p: A hero is set the impossible task of sewing together a broken millstone.

H1023.7.1.p: A hero is set the impossible task of sewing together a broken egg.

H1023.7.2.p: A hero is set the impossible task of sewing together a broken ship.

H1023.8.p: A hero is set the impossible task of fitting the two pieces of a broken sword back together.

H1023.9.r: De Vries FFC LXXIII 249; Jewish: Neuman.
H1023.9.p: A hero is set the impossible task of mending a broken jug.

H1023.9.1.p: A hero is set to mend a broken jug, and the answer is to turn it wrong side out the way one turns a shoe, a countertask that makes the impossible task absurd.

H1023.10.p: A hero is set the impossible task of skinning a stone.

H1023.10.1.p: A hero is set to skin a stone, and the countertask is to first make the stone bleed, a clever reply that turns the task back on the setter.

H1023.11.p: A hero is set the impossible task of putting a large whole squash into a narrow-necked jar.

H1023.12.p: A hero is set the impossible task of catching a noise.

H1023.13.p: A hero is set the impossible task of catching a man's broken wind, meaning a fart.

H1023.14.p: A hero is set the impossible task of splitting a hair using a blunt knife.

H1023.15.p: A hero is set the impossible task of turning fruit into gold.

H1023.16.p: A hero is set the impossible task of making the sun and moon shine in the north.

H1023.17.p: A hero is set the impossible task of sowing rye and bringing the crop in by the next morning.

H1023.18.p: A hero is set the impossible task of putting peaches back on the tree.

H1023.19.p: A hero must bring a bundle of faggots (firewood) without any rope to tie them. A helpful snake coils itself around them to bind them.

H1023.20.p: A hero must fetch water from a well in a bucket without any rope to draw it up.

H1023.21.p: A hero is given the impossible task of gathering a necklace of rubies from the sea. Tasks like this test a suitor's prowess by asking for something nature does not allow.

H1023.22.p: A hero is set the impossible task of catching a sunbeam. It is a test of prowess that asks for something contrary to the nature of light.

H1023.23.p: A hero is asked to tie the sun up with a chain made of stone. It is an impossible task used to test a suitor.

H1023.24.p: A suitor is told to bathe in a huge cauldron of boiling water without making the water lukewarm. It is an impossible test that asks him to defy the nature of water.

H1023.25.r: Types 1045, 1650; Zachariae Kleine Schriften 93; India: Thompson-Balys.
H1023.25.p: A hero is asked to bring a well, pond, or lake to the king. It is an impossible task, and in the tale the hero asks for another lake to be tied to it, which overawes the king.

H1023.25.1.p: A hero is asked to bring a well to the king, and in reply he sends his own well along with it as a counter-task. It is a clever answer to the impossible demand of moving a well.

H1024.p: A heading for impossible tasks that go against the natural behavior of animals. Tasks under it ask a hero to make animals do things they cannot do.

H1024.1.r: De Vries FFC LXXIII 43ff.; Fansler MAFLS XII 63; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H1024.1.p: A hero is asked to milk a bull, something no bull can produce. It is an impossible task that tests the hero's cleverness or prowess.

H1024.1.1.p: A hero is asked to make a bull give birth to a calf. It is an impossible task, a more specific form of milking a bull.

H1024.1.1.1.r: Reductio ad absurdum: have a man prepare for childbirth. (Cf. H952.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 265; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H1024.1.1.1.p: A hero is asked to make a bull give birth to a calf. This is the same impossible task listed again under the bull-milking heading.

H1024.2.p: A hero is asked to place frogs in a tree. It is an impossible task because frogs do not live or climb there.

H1024.3.p: A hero is asked to chase a hare into every trap set in a high tree. It is an impossible task that goes against how hares and trees behave.

H1024.4.r: Anderson FFC XLII 357 n. 1; cf. Type 1675.
H1024.4.p: A hero is asked to teach a donkey to read. It is an impossible task because asses cannot learn to read.

H1024.5.p: A hero is asked to sow dragon's teeth. It is an impossible task of the kind used in tests of prowess.

H1024.6.p: A hero is asked to get a bird that is out of its season. It is an impossible task because the bird cannot be had at that time of year.

H1024.7.p: A hero is asked to teach an animal to speak. It is an impossible task because animals cannot talk like people.

H1024.7.1.p: A hero is asked to teach a horse to speak. It is a specific form of the impossible task of teaching an animal to talk.

H1024.8.p: A hero is asked to spin wool while it is still on a goat's back. It is an impossible task because the wool cannot be spun before it is sheared.

H1025.p: A hero is asked to get bacon or fat from a pig that was never born. It is an impossible task that asks for something no living swine could provide.

H1026.p: A hero is asked to change the course of time. It is an impossible task that goes against the laws of nature.

H1026.1.p: A task set for a hero is to name things that have not yet happened, which is impossible for anyone to do. It appears among tasks that defy the laws of nature by trying to change the course of time.

H1026.2.p: A task requires someone to bring the past back into the present, which is impossible. It is one of the tasks that try to change the course of time.

H1030.p: A general heading for impossible tasks that do not fit the more specific groups, such as tasks set to test a hero's prowess.

H1033.p: A task requires someone to show a picture of a voice, which cannot be done because a voice is sound and cannot be pictured.

H1035.p: A task requires someone to eat the moon, which is impossible.

H1036.p: A task requires someone to build a castle suspended between heaven and earth, which is impossible.

H1038.r: (Cuts roots of tree.) Africa (Mpongwe): Nassau 32 No. 4.
H1038.p: A task requires someone to pick fruit from the top of a tall tree without cutting the tree down, which is impossible.

H1041.p: A task requires someone to bring a plantain leaf from the garden without tearing it, which is impossible.

H1042.p: A task requires someone to recall a dream that another person has had, which is impossible.

H1045.p: A task requires someone to fill a sack with lies, or with truths, which is impossible.

H1045.1.p: A task requires someone to go and fetch nothing and bring it back, which is impossible because nothing cannot be carried.

H1046.p: A task requires someone to carry a woman across a river without wetting their feet, which is impossible.

H1046.1.p: A task requires someone to dip water out without getting the dipper wet, which is impossible.

H1046.2.p: A task requires someone to cut and bring leaves from a thorn thicket without tearing any of them at all, which is impossible.

H1046.3.p: A task requires someone to drink beer without touching the pot, which is impossible.

H1047.p: A task requires someone to bring a melon 12 cubits long together with its seed 13 cubits long, which is absurd because the seed is larger than the fruit.

H1049.p: A miscellaneous group of impossible tasks that do not fit the more specific headings.

H1049.1.p: A task requires someone to bring the foam of the ocean in a large piece of cloth, which is impossible.

H1049.2.p: A task requires someone to grow oil seed on stony ground, where it cannot grow.

H1049.3.p: A task requires someone to turn the sun back in its course, which is impossible.

H1049.4.p: A task set to a hero that is impossible to carry out, here stopping the rain. Such tests of prowess are often set by a rival or suitor who expects the hero to fail.

H1050.r: *Type 875; *BP II 362; *Gruffydd Math vab Mathonwy (U. of Wales Press, 1928) 307ff.
H1050.p: A group of tasks that are set up as contradictions, asking the hero to do something that seems logically impossible, such as being in two states at once.

H1051.r: (Comes in the rut or the ditch at side of the road.) *Type 875; BP II 349ff.; De Vries FFC LXXIII 195f.
H1051.p: A task in which the hero must arrive somewhere neither on the road nor off it, so that the test seems impossible.

H1052.r: (Forefeet of horse inside, hind feet outside.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 198; BP II 362.
H1052.p: A task in which the hero must stand neither inside nor outside a gate, a paradox that the hero must solve to pass the test.

H1053.r: *Type 875; *BP II 362; Köhler-Bolte I 446ff.; *De Vries FFC LXXIII 186ff.; Fb “kjöre”, “ridende”; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 423; Filipino: Fansler MAFLS XII 63.
H1053.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must arrive neither riding a horse nor walking on foot.

H1053.1.r: (Comes on another animal.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 187; Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière.
H1053.1.p: A variant of the paradoxical task of arriving neither on horseback nor on foot, the hero being tested with the same impossible condition.

H1053.2.r: (Comes sitting on animal but with feet reaching ground.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 188; Irish myth: Cross.
H1053.2.p: Another variant of the task of arriving neither on horseback nor on foot, a paradox the hero must meet to succeed.

H1053.3.r: (Comes with one leg on animal’s back, one on ground.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 188.
H1053.3.p: A further variant of the task of arriving neither on horseback nor on foot, another impossible condition set for the hero.

H1053.4.r: (Coming drawn by an animal on net, trough, or sledge.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 189.
H1053.4.p: A further variant of the task of arriving neither on horseback nor on foot, another form of the same paradox.

H1053.5.r: (Walks on a stick horse.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 190.
H1053.5.p: A further variant of the task of arriving neither on horseback nor on foot, another form of the same paradox.

H1053.6.r: (Crawls on all fours.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 190.
H1053.6.p: A further variant of the task of arriving neither on horseback nor on foot, another form of the same paradox.

H1054.r: *Type 875; *De Vries FFC LXXIII 181; BP II 349ff.; Fb “klæder”; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg.
H1054.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must come neither naked nor clothed, a test that seems impossible to satisfy.

H1054.1.r: (Comes wrapped in net or the like.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 182; Missouri French: Carrière.
H1054.1.p: A variant of the task of coming neither naked nor clothed, another form of the same clothing paradox.

H1054.2.r: (Comes clothed in own hair.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 181.
H1054.2.p: A further variant of the task of coming neither naked nor clothed, another form of the same clothing paradox.

H1054.3.r: (Comes with part of body clothed.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 181.
H1054.3.p: A further variant of the task of coming neither naked nor clothed, another form of the same clothing paradox.

H1054.4.r: (Comes clad in garments of mountain down.) Irish myth: *Cross.
H1054.4.p: A variant of the naked-or-clothed paradox in which the hero must come neither in softness nor in hardness, a contradictory condition to meet.

H1055.r: (Comes with one shoe on, one off; or in soleless shoes.) Type 875; *BP II 362; De Vries FFC LXXIII 200.
H1055.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must come neither barefoot nor wearing shoes.

H1056.r: (Lets bird fly as the reaches it toward king.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 205.
