H1056.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must come neither with nor without a present, here a gift for a game.

H1057.r: (Comes at twilight.) *De Vries FFC LXXIII 202; *BP II 362; Irish myth: Cross.
H1057.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must come neither by day nor by night, a test that seems impossible to meet.

H1058.r: (Stands between wagon and sleigh.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 213.
H1058.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must stand in a place between summer and winter, a seasonal contradiction to resolve.

H1061.r: (Comes with an animal.) Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; De Vries FFC LXXIII 212.
H1061.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must bring something that comes neither alone nor accompanied by another. The impossible wording is the test, and it is solved by a clever loophole.

H1062.r: (Comes partly washed.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 211.
H1062.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must bring something that arrives neither washed nor unwashed. The impossible wording is the test, and it is solved by a clever loophole.

H1063.r: (Eats a thin soup, a leaf, a single grain, or the like.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 210; Icelandic: Boberg.
H1063.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must bring something that arrives neither hungry nor full. The impossible wording is the test, and it is solved by a clever loophole.

H1064.r: (Rubs eyes with a twig to simulate crying.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 212.
H1064.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must bring someone who comes laughing and crying at the same time. The impossible wording is the test, and it is solved by a clever loophole.

H1065.r: (Brings dog, wife, ass, little son respectively.) Köhler-Bolte I 415, 455; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 423; Herbert III 201; Ward II 231; Oesterley No. 124; *Chauvin VIII 199 No. 244; *BP II 365; cf. Type 875; *De Vries FFC LXXIII 220ff.; *Anderson FFC XLII 357 and n. 2; *Wesselski Märchen 237 No. 48; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
H1065.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must bring four things at once: a best friend, a worst enemy, a best servant, and a greatest giver of pleasure. The impossible wording is the test, and it is solved by a clever loophole.

H1066.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must sweep the floor and at the same time not sweep it. The impossible wording is the test, and it is solved by a clever loophole.

H1067.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must light a fire but without actually lighting it. The impossible wording is the test, and it is solved by a clever loophole.

H1068.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must make a bed but not make it. The impossible wording is the test, and it is solved by a clever loophole.

H1071.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must eat bread and yet bring it back whole. The impossible wording is the test, and it is solved by a clever loophole.

H1072.r: (Sheep fed but kept near wolf where it is afraid and does not fatten.) *Chauvin VIII 181 No. 213; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H1072.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must take good care of a sheep but keep it from getting fat. The impossible wording is the test, and it is solved by a clever loophole.

H1073.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must fill glasses with water that comes neither from rain nor from a spring. The impossible wording is the test, and it is solved by a clever loophole.

H1074.r: Countertask: send for it when it is neither night nor day. American Negro (Georgia): Harris Friends 118 No. 15.
H1074.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must provide beef that is neither male nor female. The impossible wording is the test, and it is solved by a clever loophole.

H1075.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must bring four kinds of things: one that always grows (ambition), one that always shrinks (life), one that neither grows nor shrinks (one's fated lot), and one that both grows and shrinks (the universe). The impossible wording is the test, and it is solved by a clever loophole.

H1077.p: A paradoxical task in which the hero must build a house neither on the ground nor in the sky. The impossible wording is the test, and it is solved by a clever loophole.

H1090.p: A category of tests in which the hero must finish a task with superhuman, almost miraculous speed.

H1091.r: *Types 313, 554; *BP II 28, 517; *Köhler-Bolte I 397; *Fb “fugl”, “gryn”; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 322 No. 87; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “pois”; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 68 No. 513; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: Dixon 226; Chinese: Graham; N. A. Indian (Thompson River): Teit JE VIII 392 No. 100.
H1091.p: A test in which a huge quantity of grain, beads, or beans must be sorted in a single night. The hero usually cannot do it alone and needs help.

H1091.1.r: Clouston Tales I 238f.; Köhler-Bolte I 397; French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 130; Italian: Basile Pentamerone V No. 4; India: *Thompson-Balys; Indonesia: Dixon 217; Japanese: Ikeda; Korean: Zong in-Sob 17.
H1091.1.p: A sorting test in which the grain is sorted with the help of grateful ants who do the work for the hero.

H1091.2.r: *Fb “fugl”; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1091.2.p: A sorting test in which the grain is sorted with the help of grateful birds who do the work for the hero.

H1091.3.p: A suitor's test in which a huge mountain of mustard seed must be scattered in one watch, gathered together in another, and its oil pressed out in a third.

H1092.r: (Cf. H1022.2.) *Types 500, 501, 708; BP I 109ff., 490ff.; *Fb “spinde” III 492a; Hoffmann-Krayer Zs. f. Vksk. XXV 120 nn. 7, 8; Köhler-Bolte ibid. VI 71; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 4; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1092.p: A task in which the hero must spin an impossibly large amount of thread or yarn in one night.

H1092.0.1.p: A test in which the hero must spin and weave an enormous quantity of thread or cloth within a set time, far more than any person could manage.

H1092.1.r: (Cf. B571.) Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 71; Lithuanian: Balys Index Nos. 453*, 481*.
H1092.1.p: An animal helper performs the spinning task on the hero's behalf, completing the impossible amount of work.

H1093.r: B571.) N. A. Indian (Crow): Lowie PaAM XXV 121, Simms FM II 309, (Blackfoot): Wissler and Duvall PaAM II 130ff.
H1093.p: A test in which the hero must embroider a blanket in a single day, a task too large to be done that quickly without help. Animals often provide the help.

H1094.p: A test in which the hero must unravel something, such as cloth or a net, in a very short time.

H1094.1.p: A test in which the hero must quickly unravel a fishing or other net within a short time.

H1095.r: (Cf. H1115.) *Type 313; Fb “skov” III 300a; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg (H322.5); Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “forêt”; Italian: Basile Pentamerone II No. 7.
H1095.p: A test in which the hero must cut down an entire forest in a single night.

H1095.1.p: A test in which the hero must gather enough firewood in a short time to last the rest of his or her life.

H1095.2.p: A test in which the hero must stack all the wood from a felled forest within one day.

H1096.p: A test in which the hero must wash an enormous number of clothes and other articles in a short time.

H1097.p: A test in which the hero must drain land that the sea covers, all in a single night.

H1097.1.p: A test in which the hero must dry up a lake in a single night.

H1097.2.r: Italian: Basile Pentamerone II No. 7; India: Thompson-Balys.
H1097.2.p: A test in which the hero must clean an enormous cistern within one day.

H1101.r: *Type 313; Breton: Sébillot Incidents “butte”; Missouri French: Carrière.
H1101.p: A test in which the hero must remove a mountain or mound in a single night.

H1102.r: Type 313; Köhler-Bolte I 170; *Fb “stald” III 534a; Greek: Fox 82, Frazer Apollodorus I 195 n. 2; New Zealand: Dixon 71.
H1102.p: A test in which the hero must clean the Augean stable, which has gone uncleaned for years, in a single night. A river is turned through it to do the job.

H1102.1.p: A test in which the hero must clean a cowshed, a version of the Augean stable task.

H1102.2.p: A test in which the hero must empty a barn full of manure within a single day.

H1103.p: A test in which the hero must plant a vineyard in a single night.

H1103.1.r: Kabyle: Frobenius Atlantis II 32 No. 4; Africa (Benga): Nassau 215 No. 33.
H1103.1.p: A test in which the hero must quickly make a garden in a forest where nothing has been planted.

H1103.1.1.p: A test in which the hero must make a garden in an unplanted forest within three days.

H1103.2.r: Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 72, 73; Italian: Basile Pentamerone II No. 7; India: Thompson-Balys.
H1103.2.p: A test in which the hero must plow an enormous area of land within one day.

H1103.2.1.p: A hero must plow and sow an impossibly large area of land in a single night or day.

H1103.2.2.p: A hero must plant a crop and bring it to full growth in a single night.

H1103.3.p: A hero must cover a whole grove of mango trees with ripe fruit in a single night.

H1104.p: A hero must build a castle in a single night as a test of skill or speed.

H1104.0.1.p: A hero must build a castle in three days instead of one night.

H1104.1.r: S. A. Indian (Carib): Alexander Lat. Am. 264.
H1104.1.p: A hero must build a lodge made entirely of bird feathers in one night.

H1104.1.1.p: A hero must cover a barn with feathers in one day, with each feather coming from a different kind of bird.

H1104.1.2.p: A hero must thatch a roof with bird feathers, but the wind blows half away while the other half must be searched for.

H1104.2.p: A hero must build an entire village in a single night.

H1104.3.p: A hero must build a house made of iron in a single night.

H1104.4.p: A hero must erect a marriage hall in a single night.

H1104.5.p: A hero must build a granary already full of grain in a single night.

H1105.p: A hero must dig a pond very quickly as a test of speed.

H1106.r: N. A. Indian (Zuñi): Boas JAFL XXXV 77 No. 4.
H1106.p: A hero must shear an entire flock of sheep in a single day.

H1107.p: A hero must bring documents from a distant city within a single day.

H1108.p: A hero must pave a great road in a very short time.

H1109.p: A hero faces other tasks that demand miraculous speed and are not covered by the preceding headings.

H1109.1.p: A hero must bring water from a distant fountain faster than a witch can.

H1109.2.p: A hero must haul a huge number of things from one farm to another in a single day.

H1109.3.p: A hero must kill enough birds in one day to cover a mountain, with every bird belonging to a different species.

H1109.4.p: A hero must rid a city of mice infesting it within three days, a task that demands miraculous speed.

H1110.p: A general category of dull, endlessly repetitive jobs that a hero is set as a test of endurance.

H1111.r: *BP II 209; cf. Type 2300; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
H1111.p: A hero is set the endless job of carrying hundreds of sheep across a stream one at a time.

H1112.p: A hero is set the tedious job of herding rabbits.

H1112.1.p: A hero must keep four dogs together as a herd, a difficult and tiresome job.

H1112.2.p: A hero must pasture a cow that keeps running all day, so the job never ends.

H1113.r: Type 313; German: Grimm No. 113; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “étang”; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 369, 377; Africa (Benga): Nassau 216 No. 33.
H1113.p: A hero is set the endless job of emptying a pond by bailing out its water.

H1113.1.p: A tedious task set as a test: bailing out a whole pond with a thimble.

H1114.p: A hero must climb a mountain made of glass, where each attempt slides back down.

H1114.1.p: A hero must climb a tall glass tower to fetch three eggs from its top.

H1114.2.p: A hero must carry a burden up a mountain, and the burden keeps growing heavier.

H1115.r: (Cf. H1095.) Type 313; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “arbres”; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 208; Jamaica: Beckwith MAFLS XVII 251 No. 29.
H1115.p: A hero must chop down a large tree using blunt or fragile tools, which makes the job nearly impossible.

H1115.1.p: A hero must cut down a huge tree that grows back again as fast as it is felled.

H1115.2.p: A hero must saw through a tree made of iron, cutting it in two.

H1115.3.p: A hero must cut down a giant tree, a task far beyond ordinary strength or tools.

H1116.p: A hero must break a huge rock into pieces, a laborious task set as a test.

H1116.1.p: A hero must cut firewood from rocks using a brass axe, and a rock is shattered to splinters by lightning to make this possible.

H1116.2.p: A hero must break iron with a wooden axe, an impossible task.

H1116.3.p: A hero must tear down a huge wall.

H1117.r: (Brings one for each week-day.) Anderson FFC XLII 227 n. 1.
H1117.p: A hero must bring as many horses as there are days in the year, a tedious and large-scale task.

H1118.p: A hero must count the hairs on a pig's back (or the feathers on a bird), an impossibly tedious task.

H1118.1.p: A test task in which the hero must count every seed in a package of mustard. The task is tedious and nearly impossible, used to test a character's prowess.

H1118.2.p: A test task in which the hero must count, day after day, how many leaves fall from a tree. The endless counting is meant to prove the hero's endurance or skill.

H1118.3.p: A test task in which the hero must count all the palm trees visible from the king's palace. The impossible counting is set as a challenge.

H1121.p: A test task in which the hero must pick every nut from a very tall tree. The labor is tedious and seemingly impossible.

H1122.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “grain”; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 71—74; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H1122.p: A test task in which the hero must prepare an enormous quantity of grain. The sheer amount of work is the challenge.

H1122.1.p: A grain-preparation task in which the hero must supply an amount of grain beyond any human capacity, usually with supernatural help.

H1123.p: A test task in which the hero must feed a ravenous beast until it is completely satisfied. The beast's appetite makes the task very hard.

H1124.p: A test task in which the hero must gather every stone from a brook or field. The tedious labor is the challenge.

H1125.r: *Type 425; *BP II 272; Köhler-Bolte I 317, 512, 573; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 114.
H1125.p: A test task in which the hero must travel until a pair of iron shoes wears completely out. The long journey is the challenge.

H1125.1.p: A travel task in which the hero must journey until two skeins of thread have been completely unwound along the way.

H1127.p: A test task in which the hero must carry off a huge quantity of money. The load is so large that the task is tedious and difficult.

H1128.p: A test task in which the hero must keep a certain work going through the whole night without rest.

H1129.p: A general heading for other tedious tasks set as tests of a character's prowess that do not fall under the more specific headings.

H1129.1.p: A task in which the hero must fill a whole yard with manure, a large and disagreeable labor.

H1129.1.1.p: A manure-related task in which the hero must bring twelve cartloads of mud without using any buffaloes to haul it.

H1129.2.r: German: Grimm No. 186; Italian: Basile Pentamerone V No. 4.
H1129.2.p: A task in which the hero must fill twelve bed-ticks with feathers. Birds help the hero do it.

H1129.3.p: A task in which the hero must carry soil to cover a stony ground so it can be planted or used.

H1129.4.p: A task in which the hero must fill a pot with dew, a practically impossible job.

H1129.5.p: A fire-making task in which the hero must build a fire, but a whole tree burns up before the hero returns with another one.

H1129.5.1.p: A firewood-gathering task in which the hero must collect a bundle of wood, but the bundle is continually swept away by a swimming man.

H1129.6.p: A hero is set a tiresome, enormous labor such as building a causeway or clearing a whole tract of land. The task is a test of endurance and strength.

H1129.7.p: A hero must gather a whole bed-tick (mattress case) full of harp strings. The task is a test of patience and skill in an absurd, laborious chore.

H1129.8.p: A hero must collect a whole vessel full of nail clippings or scrapings. The task is a tedious, nearly impossible chore used as a test.

H1129.9.p: A hero must fill a crow's house with wrens' eggs. The task is an absurd, laborious test set to see whether he can do the impossible.

H1129.10.p: A hero must gather a fistful of fleas. The task is a tedious, tiny-scale chore set as a test.

H1129.10.1.p: A hero must assemble a huge number of fleas of many colors, which is impossible. It is a harder version of the flea-gathering task.

H1129.11.p: A hero is set the tedious job of carrying fuel, such as wood or firewood, as a test of his strength and willingness.

H1130.p: A general heading for tests in which the hero must perform tasks beyond normal human ability, such as feats of superhuman size or scale.

H1131.r: (Cf. H359.1.) Irish myth: Cross; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1131.p: A hero is set the task of building an enormous bridge. The task is far beyond ordinary human ability.

H1131.1.p: A hero must build a bridge that spans both land and sea. It is an extraordinary construction task used as a test.

H1131.2.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3250, Legends Nos. 343f.
H1131.2.p: The devil, while courting a woman, is given the task of building a bridge or dam. It is a test set for a suitor who is the devil.

H1132.p: A hero is set the task of recovering lost objects, often from the sea or other unreachable places, as a superhuman test.

H1132.1.p: A hero must recover a lost object from the sea. The task is an impossible test of skill or power.

H1132.1.1.r: *Types 513, 554; *Saintyves Essais 381; BP I 134ff., II 19ff.; *Fb “guldring”; Irish myth: *Cross; Greek: Fox 101 (Theseus); Japanese: Ikeda; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 280 No. 91.
H1132.1.1.p: A hero must recover a lost ring from the sea, a specific form of the sea-recovery task.

H1132.1.1.1.p: A test in which the hero must recover a ring from water. It is a trial of skill set to see whether he can do it.

H1132.1.2.r: *Type 554; BP I 134ff., II 19ff.; Fb “guldnøgle” I 514; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 25, 35, Beal XXI 307, 312; Missouri French: Carrière; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1132.1.2.p: A hero must recover a lost key from the sea, a specific form of the sea-recovery task.

H1132.1.3.p: A hero must recover a lost strap from the sea, a specific form of the sea-recovery task.

H1132.1.4.p: A hero must recover a lost pen from the sea, a specific form of the sea-recovery task.

H1132.1.5.r: Done by Sea-king. Japanese: Anesaki 266, Ikeda.
H1132.1.5.p: A hero must recover a lost fish-hook, a specific form of the sea-recovery task.

H1132.1.6.p: A hero must recover a cooking-spit from the sea, a specific form of the sea-recovery task.

H1132.1.7.p: A test of strength or skill in which the hero must retrieve a lost crown from the sea.

H1132.2.p: A test in which the hero must recover an object from inside a large fire.

H1132.3.p: A test in which the hero must retrieve an object from the hole of a python (large snake).

H1132.3.1.p: The hero must retrieve a ring from a python's hole, and a python goddess gives him help.

H1133.p: A task in which the hero must build a castle or fort, usually by superhuman means.

H1133.1.p: The hero must build a castle by magic.

H1133.2.r: Fb “slot” III 377a; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 5.
H1133.2.p: The hero must build a castle in the air.

H1133.3.p: The hero must build a castle in the sea.

H1133.4.p: The hero must build a palace made of gold or crystal.

H1133.5.p: The hero must build a palace and a city together.

H1133.6.p: The hero must make an exact copy of a castle out of wax.

H1135.p: A task in which the hero must defeat or destroy an entire army alone.

H1136.p: A task in which the hero must bring together the winds from all over the world.

H1136.1.p: The hero must bring back flour that the wind has scattered.

H1136.2.p: The hero must gather the wind in his fists.

H1137.r: Indonesia: De Vries’s list No. 236; Filipino: Fansler MAFLS XII 62.
H1137.p: A task in which the hero must bind or hold back the waves of the sea.

H1138.p: A task in which the hero must bring water to a land that lacks it.

H1138.1.p: The hero must make a low stream turn and fill a high stream, reversing the water's course.

H1141.r: *Type 513; Missouri French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys; Africa: Werner African 153.
H1141.p: A task in which the hero must eat an enormous amount of food.

H1141.1.p: The hero must eat a whole mountain of bread.

H1141.2.p: A superhuman test in which the hero must eat three hundred fat oxen.

H1141.3.r: “He who has eaten with a friend as much salt as I have eaten and does not recognize the friendship will not do so though he eat ten rooms full of salt.”) *Bolte Reise der Söhne Giaffers 207.
H1141.3.p: A test in which the hero must eat a whole room full of salt. In the tale the trickster eats only a pinch, so the task is cleverly avoided.

H1141.4.p: A test in which the hero must eat an entire goat without leaving a single scrap.

H1142.p: A superhuman test in which the hero must drink an enormous quantity of liquid.

H1142.1.p: A drinking test in which the hero must drink all the wine in a cellar until it is empty.

H1142.2.r: *Anderson FFC XLII 139, 356; BP II 369; *Chauvin VIII 62 No. 26; Norse: MacCulloch Eddic 93 (Thor); Gascon: Bladé I 8 No. 1.
H1142.2.p: A superhuman task in which the hero must drink the whole sea until it is dry.

H1142.2.1.p: A version of the sea-drinking task in which magic makes the hero believe he is drinking from a spring, through an illusion created by a magic thread.

H1142.3.p: A countertask to the sea-drinking challenge: the opponent answers by stopping up all the rivers that feed the sea.

H1143.r: (Cf. H1113., H1142.3.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 251.—French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule (H1023.2.3.); Spanish Exempla: Keller.
H1143.p: A superhuman task in which the hero must scoop out the sea with a spoon. The countertask is to stop all the rivers that feed it.

H1143.1.p: A task in which the hero must empty a lake with a pail in a single day.

H1144.p: A superhuman task in which the hero must measure the ocean.

H1144.1.p: A task in which the hero must gather together every drop of water in the ocean.

H1144.2.p: A task in which the hero must count all the waves of the sea.

H1145.p: Superhuman tasks requiring other very difficult measurements that cannot really be made.

H1145.1.p: A task in which the hero must weigh fire.

H1145.2.p: A task in which the hero must measure a gust of wind.

H1146.p: A superhuman task in which the hero must carry a mountain on his head.

H1147.p: A superhuman task in which the hero must make a ladder that a whole army cannot set up.

H1149.p: Other superhuman tasks that do not fit the more specific categories above.

H1149.1.p: A task in which the hero must yoke a lion and a wild boar together to work as a team.

H1149.2.r: (Is serpent that embraces the earth.) Icelandic: Boberg (Thor and the Midgard serpent).
H1149.2.p: A hero is set the task of lifting a particular cat, which is a feat of superhuman strength.

H1149.3.r: (She is Old Age.) Hdwb. d. Märchens I 445b n. 432; Icelandic: Boberg.
H1149.3.p: A hero is set the task of defeating an old woman, a test of superhuman prowess.

H1149.4.p: A hero must gather an enormous quantity of some rare or precious objects as a superhuman task.

H1149.5.p: A hero must perform a feat balanced on the point of a spear, set as a task by a woman from the otherworld who is an amazon.

H1149.6.p: A hero must break a pigeon's egg lying on a castle parapet, where the pigeon is in fact a fierce serpent.

H1149.7.p: A hero must thrust a spear through seven iron plates, drawing it back out again, as a superhuman task.

H1149.8.r: (Countertask: measure river and weigh mountain.) Chinese: Graham.
H1149.8.p: A girl is required to bring back a piece of cloth as long as a river and to raise a pig as big as a mountain.

H1149.9.r: Countertask: placing it on my shoulders. India: Thompson-Balys.
H1149.9.p: A hero is set the superhuman task of lifting a mountain.

H1149.10.p: A hero must leap across a river in a single bound as a superhuman task.

H1150.p: A hero is set the task of stealing something, capturing someone, or killing a creature, as a test of skill or courage.

H1151.r: *Type 1525; BP III 379ff.; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 123; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H1151.p: A hero is given the task of stealing something as a test of skill.

H1151.1.r: *Fb “guldæble” I 516, “æble” III 1135b; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 179, *Boberg Greek: Fox 87, Frazer Apollodorus I 220 n. 1.
H1151.1.p: A hero is set the task of stealing golden apples.

H1151.1.1.p: A hero is set the task of stealing a golden lotus flower.

H1151.2.p: A hero is set the task of stealing twelve horses from their stall.

H1151.2.1.p: A hero must steal a horse even though its owner has been warned in advance that the theft will happen.

H1151.2.2.p: A hero must steal the king's horse while the king is riding on it.

H1151.3.p: A hero must steal the sheet from the bed of a sleeping person.

H1151.3.1.p: A hero must steal a tray from beside the sleeping king's bed.

H1151.4.p: A hero must steal a ring off someone's finger as a test.

H1151.5.p: A hero must steal a belt from a queen as a test.

H1151.5.1.p: A hero must steal a girdle (belt) belonging to a goddess as one of the tasks he must complete to win a test.

H1151.6.r: Africa (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 123 No. 22, (Ekoi): Talbot 208.
H1151.6.p: A hero must steal the tail or tusks of an elephant as one of the tasks set to test his prowess.

H1151.6.1.p: A hero must steal a huge diamond from the forehead of an elephant, which is part of a task of stealing from the elephant's tusks or tail.

H1151.7.p: A hero must steal the two horns of a fierce wild bull as one of the tasks set to test him.

H1151.7.1.p: A hero must steal the gold-filled horn of a wild three-horned ox as part of a task of stealing a bull's horns.

H1151.8.p: A hero must steal cattle that are guarded by a marvelous dog as one of the tasks set to test him.

H1151.9.p: A hero must steal a golden horse belonging to a troll as one of the tasks set to test him.

H1151.10.p: A hero must bring back a branch from a tree that is guarded by ghosts, as one of the tasks set to test him.

H1151.10.1.p: A hero must steal pears from a garden that is cleverly guarded, as part of a task of bringing a branch from a tree guarded by ghosts.

H1151.11.p: A hero must bring back the tail of a baby lion to be used as a broom, as one of the tasks set to test him.

H1151.12.r: Type 653; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa: Weeks Jungle 43, (Madagascar): Renel II 118f. No. 91.
H1151.12.p: A hero must steal eggs from under a bird as one of the tasks set to test him.

H1151.13.p: A hero must steal something from a king as one of the tasks set to test him.

H1151.13.1.p: A hero must steal a king's pigskin as part of a task of stealing from a king.

H1151.13.2.p: A hero must steal a king's spear as part of a task of stealing from a king.

H1151.13.3.p: A hero must steal a king's horses, together with the chariot, as part of a task of stealing from a king.

H1151.13.4.p: A hero must steal a king's hound (hunting dog) as part of a task of stealing from a king.

H1151.13.5.p: A hero must steal three pearls from a king's treasury, which is heavily guarded, as part of a task of stealing from a king.

H1151.14.p: A hero must steal a sword from a giant as one of the tasks set to test him.

H1151.15.p: A hero must steal the necklace of the goddess Freya as one of the tasks set to test him.

H1151.16.p: A hero must steal the mead of poetry (a magic drink that gives inspiration) as one of the tasks set to test him.

H1151.17.r: S. A. Indian (Tupinamba): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 132.
H1151.17.p: A hero must steal the bait belonging to a demon named Añan as one of the tests he must pass.

H1151.18.p: A hero must rescue his wife's sister, who is held captive by an elephant and lives inside a box in the elephant's ear.

H1151.19.p: A hero must eat only food that he has stolen, and must do so without committing a sin.

H1151.20.r: (Cf. H1323.) French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule.
H1151.20.p: A hero must steal magic apples that heal illness and injury.

H1151.21.r: (Cf. D1500.1.18.) French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule.
H1151.21.p: A hero must steal magic water that has healing powers.

H1151.22.p: A hero must steal a laborer's pajamas as a test of his skill.

H1151.23.p: A hero must steal the beautiful clothing belonging to a witch.

H1151.24.p: A hero must steal the drum belonging to an ogress.

H1151.25.p: A hero must steal grain belonging to an ogre.

H1151.26.p: A hero must bring back a ruby taken from inside the head of a destructive serpent.

H1152.p: A hero must sell an animal but then keep it for himself, so the task is accomplished through trickery.

H1152.1.r: (Shears and sells wool; brings animal back.) De Vries FFC LXXIII 43ff., 157; Irish: Cross, Baughman.
H1152.1.p: A hero must sell a sheep or goat and then bring the animal back to his master together with the money.

H1153.r: (Devil finds that no one wants them.) *Type 1170; BP III 16.
H1153.p: A hero must sell three old women as part of a test.

H1154.p: A hero must capture certain animals as a test of his prowess.

H1154.0.1.p: A hero must bring back the head or heads of certain animals as proof of a task.

H1154.1.p: A hero must capture a magic pig that carries scissors, a comb, and razors between its ears.

H1154.2.p: A hero must capture a deer from a herd that is watched over by a giant.

H1154.2.1.p: A hero must capture ninety pigs, ninety horses, and one hundred wild oxen as a task.

H1154.3.p: A hero must bridle a wild animal as a test of his skill.

H1154.3.1.r: Finnish: Kalevala rune 14; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 74.
H1154.3.1.p: A hero must bridle a wild horse as a test.

H1154.3.2.p: A hero must tame and bridle a fierce, dangerous bear as one of the tasks set by a test of strength or skill.

H1154.3.3.p: A hero must capture and tie up a fierce wild boar as one of the tasks set by a test of strength or skill.

H1154.3.3.1.p: A hero must kill a wild boar, measured by its size or simply slain, as a task in a test of strength.

H1154.3.4.p: A hero must catch a wild elephant as one of the tasks set by a test of strength or skill.

H1154.3.5.p: A hero must load fierce, wild camels as one of the tasks set by a test of strength or skill.

H1154.3.6.p: A hero must yoke wild stags, harnessing them to work as one of the tasks set by a test of strength.

H1154.3.7.p: A hero must bring back tigers as one of the tasks set by a test of strength or skill.

H1154.3.7.1.p: A hero must obtain four full-grown tigers to stand guard at the four gates of a king's palace.

H1154.4.p: A hero must catch a huge fish without using nets or fishing tackle, as one of the tasks set by a test.

H1154.5.p: A hero must capture an elk as one of the tasks set by a test of strength or skill.

H1154.6.p: A hero must capture a squirrel and a rattlesnake as one of the tasks set by a test.

H1154.7.p: A hero must catch a bird as one of the tasks set by a test of skill.

H1154.7.1.p: A hero must retrieve a king's falcon as one of the tasks set by a test.

H1154.7.2.p: A hero must capture a blackbird, a task that is repeated each year.

H1154.7.3.p: A hero must bring four full-grown peacocks to sit one on each of four golden pinnacles of a palace room.

H1154.8.p: A hero must capture a magic horse as one of the tasks set by a test.

H1154.9.p: A hero must capture one pair of every wild animal in the land as a task.

H1154.10.p: A hero must capture badgers as one of the tasks set by a test.

H1154.11.p: A hero must obtain the marrow of a wild pig, the lard of a wild boar, and a water bird (possibly a coot) as tasks.

H1154.12.p: A hero must bring in a fierce lion alive as one of the tasks set by a test.

H1155.p: A hero is set the task of taming or subduing wild animals as a test of his strength and skill.

H1155.1.p: The hero must ride and tame a wild horse as one of his tasks.

H1155.1.1.p: The hero must groom a wild, unruly mare to make her tame and manageable.

H1155.2.p: The hero must milk a wild, unruly cow as a test.

H1155.3.p: The hero must feed a dangerous, man-eating sow.

H1155.4.p: The hero must care for a mad, wild elephant.

H1155.5.p: The hero must ride wild buffaloes as a test of his skill.

H1156.p: The hero must provoke the anger of a fierce wild animal as a task.

H1156.1.p: The hero must set fire to brushwood near the home of a sacred cobra, angering the snake.

H1161.r: Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 126, *Cross; English: Wells 115 (Sir Eglamour of Artois); Icelandic: *Boberg; Finnish: Kalevala rune 14; Missouri French: Carrière; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 184 n. 2, 187 n. 3, 191 n. 3, 197 n. 3, 199 n. 2, 200 n. 1, 210 n. 1 (Hercules), II 59 n. 1 (Cychreus); Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 3 No. 1.
H1161.p: The hero is set the task of killing a fierce, dangerous beast.

H1161.1.p: The hero must kill a murderous bird.

H1161.2.p: The hero must overcome a savage buffalo.

H1161.2.1.p: The hero must kill an ox as part of the task of overcoming a savage buffalo.

H1161.2.2.p: The hero must kill a fierce bull as part of the task of overcoming a savage buffalo.

H1161.3.p: The hero must overcome an elephant as a task.

H1161.3.1.p: A mouse must fight alone against the king's state elephant and destroy it.

H1161.4.p: The hero must kill a golden pig as a task.

H1161.5.p: The hero must kill a lion that is causing great destruction.

H1161.6.p: The hero must kill a tiger that is causing great destruction.

H1162.r: (Cf. H335.3, H335.5, H335.6.) Icelandic: Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
H1162.p: The hero is set the task of killing a certain particular man.

H1162.1.p: A hero must overcome a band of robbers as a task set before he can win a reward or marriage.

H1162.2.p: The hero is required to kill a king's son, on the condition that doing so will keep the father from dying.

H1163.p: The hero must pull up by the roots a tree that devours people.

H1165.p: The hero must take part in a bullfight, using buffaloes as the animals to be fought, as a set task.

H1166.p: The hero must fight a duel as a required task or test.

H1166.1.p: The hero must wrestle or otherwise struggle with a giant warrior as one of the set tasks.

H1172.p: The hero must capture an ogre and bring it to court.

H1173.p: The hero must lure the god Thor into the power of giants.

H1174.p: A suitor must kill a monster as a test of worthiness to win the princess's hand.

H1174.1.p: As the suitor's test, the hero must bring back two heads of a giant.

H1174.2.p: The suitor must overcome a dragon as his test before winning the bride.

H1177.p: The hero must bring fairies to court as a set task.

H1177.1.p: As a suitor's task, the hero must make fairies dance before the princess.

H1180.p: A grouping of various set tasks that heroes must perform, not fitting the other categories.

H1181.p: The hero must raise a buried treasure from the ground as a task.

H1182.r: (Reads a letter from a foreign king demanding a loan.) Chauvin VI 39 No. 207.
H1182.p: The hero must let the king hear a sound or thing that neither the king nor his subjects have ever heard before.

H1182.1.p: The hero must recover money that a foreign king owes, as a task.

H1182.2.p: The king asks his favorite minister to show him a trick he has never seen before.

H1183.p: The hero must carry a wagon axle that has broken a wheel, as a task.

H1184.r: (Scratches surreptitiously while gesticulating.) *Jamaica Beckwith MAFLS XVII 250f. No. 29.
H1184.p: The hero must cut down a tree without being stung by the stinging insects living in it.

H1185.r: (Needle put in food which causes eater to say “Oh my!”) De Vries FFC LXXIII 250.
H1185.p: A test in which the hero must prepare a food while crying out "Oh my" in the process, as a trick to make the task absurd or comic.

H1185.1.p: A test in which the hero must buy eggs for one coin and another item for another coin, and the master cries "ay, ay" when touching nettles hidden in the bag of eggs.

H1186.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “cochons”. Cf. Type 850.
H1186.p: A test in which the hero must make pigs dance.

H1187.r: Köhler-Bolte II 647ff. *Liungman Två Folkminnesundersökningar 25 n. 1; FSS 7ff. (H922); India: *Thompson-Balys; Icelandic: Boberg.
H1187.p: A task left by a departing husband for his virgin wife: she must have a son whose true mother she is and whose true father is her husband, which she accomplishes by disguising herself as a girl.

H1188.r: (Puts on iron boots.) Finnish: Kalevala rune 19.
H1188.p: A test in which the hero must plow a field full of vipers.

H1191.p: A test in which the hero must blind a witch.

H1191.1.p: A test in which the hero must behead a witch and bring her head to the king.

H1191.2.p: A test in which the hero must catch a witch who is ruining the king's best garden by haunting it.

H1192.r: Type 480; Roberts 168; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 10.
H1192.p: A test in which the hero must comb the hair of fairies.

H1193.p: A test in which the hero must make a dry spring flow again.

H1194.r: Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H1194.p: A test in which the hero must make a certain person laugh.

H1194.0.1.p: A test in which the hero must make a silent person speak.

H1194.1.p: A man whose laughter brings rain refuses to laugh, and is finally made to laugh when two people who do not know each other, sleeping in the same dark room, frighten one another.

H1194.2.p: A test in which the hero must make a jackal laugh or weep.

H1195.p: A test in which the hero must have a shirt made by a woman who is free from trouble and worry.

H1196.p: A hero is set the task of freeing a king from a magic doll that holds him. The one who succeeds will marry the king's rescuer if that rescuer is a girl.

H1197.p: A test in which the hero must cross a stream choked with weeds; the hero spreads a cloth on the weeds and floats across.

H1198.p: A test in which the hero must pick out one ruby from a tray full of identical rubies.

H1199.p: A miscellaneous test of prowess involving tasks not classed elsewhere in this section.

H1199.1.p: A test in which the hero must plant a beautiful garden.

H1199.2.r: Types 551, 610—12; Africa (Tanga): Nassau JAFL XXVIII 30ff. No. 5.
H1199.2.p: A test in which the hero must heal a sick person.

H1199.2.1.p: A hero is given the task of causing sickness to come upon a certain tribe or people. The task is set as a test of his prowess.

H1199.2.2.p: A hero is set the task of curing an ulcer that is considered impossible to heal. Success proves his skill.

H1199.3.p: A hero is ordered to shout from a place he is forbidden to enter or stand in. The task tests his daring or skill.

H1199.4.p: A hero is required to engrave a shield with a design no one else has ever made. The task tests his craftsmanship.

H1199.5.p: A hero is set the task of breaking an enchantment or magic spell. Success frees the person or thing under the spell.

H1199.6.p: A hero must get swine to shake the trunk of a certain tree. The task is an impossible-seeming test of his skill.

H1199.7.p: A hero must make swine eat the fish from a certain body of water. The task is set as a test of his prowess.

H1199.8.p: A hero defends himself alone against fifteen ships carrying sixty men. The task tests his courage and strength.

H1199.9.p: A hero is given the task of ridding a city of its thieves. Success proves his worth.

H1199.9.1.p: As part of ridding a city of thieves, the hero must find out who stole a ring. He succeeds by discovering the ring-thief.

H1199.10.p: A hero is required to jump over a fire. The task tests his bravery and agility.

H1199.11.p: A hero is set the task of going to bed with Odin, king of the underworld. The task is a test of his daring.

H1199.12.p: A hero is given an unusual task of herding or pasturing animals. The task is a test of his skill.

H1199.12.1.p: A hero is given the task of tending sheep for God, following wherever they go. On the way he sees many wonderful things.

H1199.12.2.p: A hero is set to pasture a witch's cattle, which are really her daughters. Grateful animals help him complete the task.

H1199.13.p: A hero must square a log of lumber on a stone without blunting his axe. A woman is purposely sent to distract him from the task.

H1199.14.p: A hero is required to climb an extraordinarily high and thin cliff. The task tests his prowess.

H1199.15.p: A hero is set the task of securing dishes that have been locked up in a vault. The task tests his skill.

H1199.16.r: seven coats of lacquer.) Chinese: Graham.
H1199.16.p: A hero must produce seven pairs of chopsticks in seven plates. The note describes a lacquered plate and pair of chopsticks as part of the task.

H1199.17.p: A hero is given the task of guarding something. The task tests his vigilance and strength.

H1199.17.1.p: A task in which the hero must guard the palace at night so that no one can get in or out.

H1199.17.2.p: A task in which the hero must guard six sisters-in-law so that they neither joke nor speak to anyone.

H1199.18.p: A task in which the hero must knock a single fruit off the king's tree.

H1200.p: A general heading for quests, journeys a hero undertakes to win something or accomplish a difficult goal.

H1210.p: A quest is given to the hero by someone else rather than chosen by him.

H1210.1.r: *Types 402, 550; Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 105; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chile: Pino Saavedra 399, 403, 404; Africa (Ekoi): Talbot 350.
H1210.1.p: The hero's father gives him a quest to carry out.

H1210.2.r: French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H1210.2.p: A king gives the hero a quest to carry out.

H1211.r: *Type 650; Dickson 51; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 116, 139—141; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H1211.p: Quests are assigned to the hero in order to get rid of him, usually because others want him gone or dead.

H1212.r: *Type 590; BP III 1f; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 14; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 49 No. 17.
H1212.p: A hero is sent on a quest because someone pretends to be ill; the cure is said to require something nearly impossible to get, such as lion's milk.

H1212.1.p: A hero is sent on a quest because someone pretends to have had a dream that requires a dangerous object or deed to fulfill.

H1212.2.p: A wife persuades her husband to undertake a quest by appealing to his love for her, sending him to get the liver of a dangerous animal.

H1212.3.p: A prince sulks and refuses to be cheered until his quest has been accomplished.

H1212.4.p: A quest is set because a pregnant woman has a craving that can only be satisfied by something difficult to obtain.

H1213.r: *Type 550; BP I 503ff., *III 33; *Chauvin VI 5 No. 182 n. 1; Köhler-Bolte I 411; Missouri French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys.
H1213.p: A hero sets out to find a remarkable bird after seeing just one of its feathers.

H1213.1.r: *Chauvin VI 5 No. 182 n. 1; *BP III 31, 33; *Cosquin Contes indiens 369ff.; Chavannes III 258f. No. 470 (cf. Wesselski Archiv Orientální I 6); Icelandic: *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1213.1.p: A hero sets out to find a princess after seeing one of her hairs, dropped by a bird or floating on a river.

H1213.1.1.p: A princess sets out to find a man after seeing one of his hairs, dropped by a bird or floating on a river.

H1213.1.2.p: A hero sets out to find the original of a picture after seeing the picture.

H1213.2.p: A hero sets out to find a strong man after seeing evidence of that man's work.

H1214.p: A hero is sent on a quest because he knows the languages of animals.

H1214.1.p: A hero is sent to find a beautiful girl because he hears parrots speaking about her.

H1215.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Greek: Fox 33 (Perseus).
H1215.p: A hero is sent on a quest because he has boasted that he can do something difficult or dangerous.

H1216.r: (Cf. H1385.7.) English: Wells 134 (Sir Degare); India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1216.p: A mother sends her son off to search for his father, whom he has never met and whose identity is unknown to him.

H1217.p: A hero is sent on a quest because of a dream that he or someone else has had.

H1217.1.p: A hero sets out on a quest to find someone who can explain the meaning of a dream.

H1218.p: A king who owns one marvelous object sends the hero to find another just like it.

H1219.p: A general heading for quests assigned for various other reasons not covered by the more specific entries.

H1219.1.r: (Cf. H942.) Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg.
H1219.1.p: A man is sent on a quest as the payment for a debt he incurred by losing a wager or game of chance.

H1219.1.1.p: A man is sent on a quest as the price of a magic object he has obtained or been given.

H1219.2.p: A man is sent on a quest as punishment for committing a murder.

H1219.3.p: A girl's father, whose daughter has been carried off, sends a man on a quest as punishment.

H1219.4.p: A fairy sets someone a quest.

H1219.5.p: A prisoner is given a quest, usually as the condition of his release or fate.

H1219.6.p: Someone is sent on a quest because another person has slandered or falsely accused him.

H1219.7.p: A host sends a guest on a quest as a way of repaying the hospitality he received.

H1219.8.p: Someone is sent on a quest as punishment for being curious, such as opening a forbidden door or looking where he was told not to.

H1220.p: A general heading for quests that the hero chooses to undertake on his own initiative rather than being sent on.

H1221.r: *Type 650; Irish myth: *Cross; English: Wells 66 (Ywain and Gawain), 134 (Sir Degare); Icelandic: *Boberg; Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “aventures”; Arabian: Burton Nights VI 1—83, S IV 420, 509ff. This motif is prominent in Romances of Chivalry.
H1221.p: A hero sets out on a quest simply in search of adventure.

H1221.1.r: Chauvin II 152 No. 16, 157 No. 37; cf. Tennyson’s “Ulysses.”
H1221.1.p: An old warrior, unwilling to settle down, keeps seeking new adventures instead of resting in his old age.

H1222.p: A prince, while out hunting, sets off on a quest.

H1223.p: Someone sets out on a quest in order to perform brave or heroic deeds.

H1223.1.p: A hero sets out on a quest to win back his honor by performing daring deeds.

H1224.p: A hero travels a long way to a distant king to ask for soldiers or help in battle.

H1225.p: A hero sets out deliberately to find a worthy, powerful opponent to fight.

H1226.p: A hero chases a cake that rolls away from him and is led into a quest.

H1226.1.r: Hindu: Keith 196; N. A. Indian: Matthews MAFLS V 108, Goddard PaAM VIII 196 No. 3 and numerous other references in Thompson Tales 320 n. 156.
H1226.1.p: A hero chases a hoop that rolls away from him and is led into a quest.

H1226.2.p: A hero follows a magic arrow that leads him into a series of adventures.

H1226.3.p: A hero chases a golden apple that rolls away from him and is led into a quest.

H1226.4.p: A hero chases a ball of yarn that rolls away from him and is led into a quest.

H1227.p: A hero must complete a quest before he is allowed to marry.

H1228.p: A hero sets out on a quest to take revenge on someone.

H1228.1.p: A hero sets out to avenge the death or wrong done to his king.

H1228.2.p: A son leaves home to avenge the killing of his father.

H1229.p: A miscellaneous group of quests that the hero chooses to undertake on his own initiative.

H1229.1.p: A hero sets out on a quest in order to keep promises he has made.

H1229.2.p: A queen writes a message on a stone; the hero finds it and sets out to search for her.

H1229.3.p: A hero sets out to find a marvelous object he saw in a dream.

H1230.p: A hero successfully completes his quests.

H1231.r: Italian: Basile Pentamerone V No. 4; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 358 n. 287k.
H1231.p: A hero must prepare so many pairs of boots for his journey that many are worn out, because the quest will be extremely long.

H1232.r: *Types 425, 451; *Tegethoff 44; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 71 No. 551, Espinosa Jr. Nos. 106, 114; India: Thompson-Balys.
H1232.p: A hero on a quest is given directions by the sun, moon, wind, and stars.

H1232.1.p: A hero on a quest is given directions by herdsmen or peasants.

H1232.2.p: On a quest, the hero is told which way to go by a queen.

H1232.3.p: On a quest, the hero is told which way to go by a maiden or woman living in a castle.

H1232.4.p: On a quest, the hero is told which way to go by a peasant and his wife.

H1232.5.r: S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 484.
H1232.5.p: On a quest, the hero receives directions from children who are still unborn in their mother's womb.

H1233.p: A hero undertaking a voluntary quest receives help from one or more helpers.

H1233.1.p: An old person helps the hero on a quest.

H1233.1.1.r: Type 400, 425; English: Wells 68 (The Weddynge of Sir Gawen and Dame Ragnell); India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1233.1.1.p: An old woman helps the hero on a quest.

H1233.1.2.p: An old man offers help to a hero who has set out on a quest.

H1233.2.p: A family member helps the hero on a quest.

H1233.2.1.p: The hero completes the quest with the help of his wife.

H1233.2.2.p: The hero completes the quest with the help of his brother, who is disguised.

H1233.3.p: A holy man helps the hero on a quest.

H1233.3.1.p: A holy ascetic gives the hero directions on his quest.

H1233.3.2.p: A fakir, an ascetic holy man, helps the hero on a quest.

H1233.3.3.p: The hero completes the quest with the help of a prophet, sage, or druid.

H1233.4.p: A supernatural creature helps the hero on a quest.

H1233.4.1.p: Fairies help the hero on a quest.

H1233.4.2.p: The hero completes the quest with the help of a giantess.

H1233.4.3.p: A griffin, a winged creature with a lion's body and eagle's head, helps the hero on a quest.

H1233.4.4.p: A demon helps the hero on a quest.

H1233.5.p: A god helps the hero on a quest.

H1233.5.1.p: A goddess (a deity) comes to the aid of a hero undertaking a quest.

H1233.6.r: *Type 550; Malone PMLA XLIII 444; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 187; Missouri French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1233.6.p: Animals come to the aid of a hero undertaking a quest.

H1233.6.1.p: A horse helps the hero during a quest.

H1233.6.2.p: A bird helps the hero during a quest by giving advice.

H1233.6.3.p: A porpoise (dolphin-like sea animal) helps the hero during a quest.

H1235.r: (Cf. H1241.) Types 400, 425, 516, 756B; *BP II 400; *Wesselski Archiv Orientální IV 1; Clouston Tales II 96; W. R. Halliday Indo-European Folk-Tales and Greek Legend (Cambridge, 1933) 132f.; Gaster Oldest Stories 51; Tegethoff 44; Rösch FFC LXXVII 110; *Andrejev FFC LXIX 225 n.—Irish: Cross, Beal XXI 326, O’Suilleabhain 74; Icelandic: *Boberg; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian: Basile Pentamerone Introduction, IV No. 8, V Nos. 4, 9; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 336 n. 211.
H1235.p: A hero on a quest is passed along from one helper to the next, each one sending him on to another who gives further help.

H1235.1.p: The helpers on a quest charge a price before they will give the hero advice.

H1236.r: English: Wells 55 (Gawayne and the Grene Knight); India: *Thompson-Balys.
H1236.p: The hero on a quest must cross a dangerous route full of perils.

H1236.1.r: ). Irish myth: Cross; Finnish: Kalevala rune 17.
H1236.1.p: The hero must cross a path covered with sharp points such as knives or axes.

H1236.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys; Am. Indian (Quiche): Alexander Lat. Am. 174.
H1236.2.p: The hero must cross a path guarded by dangerous animals.

H1236.3.p: The hero must cross a path guarded by hags (ugly old witches).

H1236.4.p: The hero must cross a path guarded by a giant.

H1237.p: On a quest to recover a lost wife, the hero uses magic to make obstacles disappear.

H1239.p: Miscellaneous ways in which a quest is brought to a successful end.

H1239.1.p: A prince promises to marry a servant girl if she will help him on his quest.

H1239.2.p: The objects sought on a quest are found in an empty castle where the hero is waited on by invisible hands.

H1239.3.p: The quest is completed using objects that helpers have given to the hero.

H1239.4.p: A man with magic knowledge beats his rivals in a quest by misleading them about the land ahead: he has them carry wood for a dry land and water for a wet one.

H1239.5.p: Seductive women try to lure the quester away from his goal.

H1240.p: Other circumstances that attend quests, not covered by the more specific headings.

H1241.r: (Cf. H1235.) *Type 550; BP I 503ff.; Wesselski Mönchslatein 91 No. 77; Irish myth: *Cross; Welsh: MacCulloch Celtic 187; Scotch: Campbell II 344; Icelandic: Lagerholm 58—63, 115—118, *Boberg; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H1241.p: A hero must complete a chain of quests, where finishing one quest makes the next one possible.

H1241.1.p: A hero who has come back from a successful quest is immediately sent out on another one.

H1241.1.1.p: A hero returns carrying berries and is sent back to fetch the tree they grew on.

H1242.r: *Type 402, 471, 550, 551, 577; BP 260, 503; Irish myth: Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 398; Chile: Pino Saavedra 402—405.
H1242.p: Only the youngest brother manages to succeed on a quest that his older brothers fail.

H1242.1.p: A hero who seems unpromising or unlikely to succeed nonetheless completes the quest.

H1243.r: *Type 461; **Aarne FFC XXII 165; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1243.p: A hero gains great wealth as a reward for answering questions or solving problems met on quests.

H1244.p: Forgiveness, such as pardon for a past wrong, is the reward for completing a quest successfully.

H1245.p: A quest must be finished within a single day.

H1247.p: The hero is forbidden to sleep until the quest is finished.

H1248.p: The object the hero is sent to fetch brings about the death of the person who sent him.

H1250.p: A hero travels to the other world, the realm of the dead or supernatural beyond ordinary life, on a quest.

H1250.1.p: The hero is tested before setting out on a journey to the other world.

H1251.p: A hero is sent to the other world to bring back samples of food eaten by magical animals.

H1252.p: A hero is sent to the other world to bring back a relative.

H1252.1.p: A hero is sent to the other world to bring back an ancestor.

H1252.1.1.p: A hero travels to the other world to get news of an ancestor.

H1252.1.2.p: A hero travels to the other world to find out whether his father is in heaven or hell.

H1252.2.p: A hero is sent to the other world carrying letters to dead relatives.

H1252.3.p: A hero goes to the other world to recover relatives who have been sold there.

H1252.4.p: A king sends a hero to the other world to deliver a message to the king's dead father.

H1254.p: A hero must travel to the otherworld to fetch magical objects.

H1256.p: A hero must journey to the otherworld in order to win a wife.

H1257.p: A hero sets out on a quest to find where paradise is located.

H1260.r: Type 465c; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; West Indies: Flowers 462.
H1260.p: A hero must travel to the upper world, the sky or heaven, on a quest.

H1261.p: A hero must go to heaven to bring back a crown.

H1262.p: A hero must go to heaven and bring God back to earth.

H1263.p: A hero travels to God to ask for good luck or fortune.

H1264.p: A hero must journey to the upper world to get fire.

H1265.p: A hero must travel to Paradise to get oil to anoint his dying father's body.

H1266.p: A hero goes on a quest to find or reach a god.

H1267.p: A pregnant woman craves fish, so her husband goes to heaven to get a lucky fishhook.

H1270.r: Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 323; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (z-G. 13/276).
H1270.p: A hero must travel to the lower world, the underworld or hell, on a quest.

H1271.p: A hero must go to hell to capture Cerberus and bring him up to earth.

H1272.p: A hero goes to hell to get devils and brings them back with him.

H1273.p: A hero goes to the devil in hell to get back certain objects.

H1273.1.r: *Type 756B; BP III 465; *Plenzat Die Theophiluslegende in den Dichtungen des Mittelalters (Berlin, 1926); Irish: Beal XXI 311, O’Suilleabhain 33.
H1273.1.p: A hero goes down to hell to get back a contract held by the devil.

H1273.1.1.p: A hero goes to hell to recover the contract of a rich man who has died and is held there.

H1273.2.p: A hero must go to the devil and bring back three hairs from his beard as part of a quest.

H1274.p: A hero must go to hell to get three dragon feathers.

H1275.r: Fb “gjedebuk” I 440, “helvede” I 589a; Icelandic: Egils saga ok Ásmundar 391, Boberg; Indonesian: De Vries’s list 161.
H1275.p: A hero must go to hell to obtain money or treasure.

H1276.p: A hero must go to the lower world to recover lost words.

H1277.p: A hero must travel to the outermost regions of hell to obtain blood belonging to a sorceress.

H1278.p: A hero must travel to the devil to get answers to riddle-like questions.

H1280.p: A general heading for tests in which a hero undertakes journeys to other realms beyond the ordinary world.

H1281.r: *Type 460B; Aarne FFC XIII 124; India: *Thompson-Balys. Cf. Patch PMLA XXXIII 630.
H1281.p: A hero sets out on a quest to Fortune in order to seek his fortune.

H1282.p: A hero must travel to the morning star to get answers to questions.

H1283.r: Type 702*; S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 143.
H1283.p: A hero must travel to the moon to get answers to questions.

H1284.r: *Type 460, 461; BP I 292; **Aarne FFC XXIII 115ff.; N. A. Indian (Thompson River): Thompson CColl II 387ff.
H1284.p: A hero must travel to the sun to get answers to questions.

H1284.1.p: A hero must travel to the place where the sun sets in order to reach the sun and ask it questions.

H1285.p: A hero must travel to the Mother of Time to get answers to questions.

H1285.1.p: A hero must bring a wizard woman named Soma from across the seven seas to attend a wedding.

H1286.p: A general heading for tests in which a hero journeys to the land of fairies.

H1286.0.1.p: A hero must travel to fairyland, which is located at the bottom of a lake.

H1286.1.p: A hero must travel to fairyland to obtain a precious jewel.

H1286.2.p: A hero must travel to fairyland to obtain a magic object.

H1287.p: A general heading for quests in which a hero travels to an underwater monastery.

H1287.1.p: A hero must travel to an island that lies beneath the water.

H1288.p: A hero must travel to a marvelous plain full of wonders.

H1289.p: A general heading for quests in which a hero travels to various other realms of different kinds.

H1289.1.p: A hero must travel to the realm of animals.

H1289.1.1.p: A hero must travel to the land of lions, elephants, and serpents to obtain a green stone.

H1289.1.2.p: A hero must travel to the land of snakes.

H1289.2.p: A hero must make a journey to the land of Bjarmaland, a remote realm in the north, as the test of a quest.

H1289.3.p: A hero must set out to reach the land of giants as the test of a quest.

H1289.3.1.p: A hero must travel to a land ruled by giants who eat human flesh, as a test of a quest.

H1289.4.p: A hero must go on a quest to see a god in person.

H1289.4.1.p: A hero must seek a thread made from lotus stalks growing from the navel of the god Vishnu.

H1289.5.p: A hero must travel to a land where every king dies, as a test of a quest.

H1289.6.p: A hero must travel to the world of the rakshasas, demonic man-eating beings of Indian lore, as a quest.

H1290.p: A general heading for miscellaneous motifs about quests to the other world that do not fit the more specific headings.

H1291.r: *Type 461; Irish: Cross Beal XXI 318f., O’Suilleabhain 50—52; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
H1291.p: On a journey to the otherworld, the hero is asked a series of questions that must be answered before passing.

H1292.r: (Cf. H1278, H1282, H1283, H1284.) *Type 461; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham.
H1292.p: A hero on a quest to the other world gets answers to questions he asked along the way, the answers being given there.

H1292.1.r: Answer: Animal to be removed from its water-vein. Types 460, 461; *Aarne FFC XXIII 144f.; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 345b. n. 120; Icelandic: Boberg.
H1292.1.p: On the way to the other world, the hero is asked a question about why a spring has gone dry, and receives the answer there.

H1292.1.1.r: Answer: In their last birth they had been two Brahman women and whenever they wanted to give alms they gave only to each other. India: Thompson-Balys.
H1292.1.1.p: On the way to the other world, the hero is asked why no one ever drinks from two particular wells, and learns the answer in the other world.

H1292.2.r: Answer: Gold is hidden under it (or a serpent is under its roots). Types 460, 461; *Aarne FFC XXIII 133, 136; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 256a n. 13; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 8; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1292.2.p: On the way to the other world, the hero is asked why a certain tree does not flourish, and learns the answer there.

H1292.2.1.r: Answer: Tree in its last birth had been a very learned man who gave his knowledge away. India: Thompson-Balys.
H1292.2.1.p: On the way to the other world, the hero is asked why no one wants to eat the fruit of a certain tree, and learns the answer there.

H1292.3.r: (Various answers.) Types 460, 461; Aarne FFC XXIII 150; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1292.3.p: On the way to the other world, the hero is asked why livestock keep dying, and learns the answer there.

H1292.4.r: Answer: He must remove stone which he has spit out in the church. Types 460, 461; *Aarne FFC XXIII 142f.
H1292.4.p: On the way to the other world, the hero is asked how a prince can be cured, and learns the cure there.

H1292.4.1.r: Answer: She must recover consecrated wafer which rat has stolen from her first communion. Types 460, 461; *Aarne FFC XXIII 142f.; Irish: Beal XXI 308f., O’Suilleabhain 27f.; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1292.4.1.p: On the way to the other world, the hero is asked how a princess can be cured, and learns the cure there.

H1292.4.2.r: Answer: By giving away his gem. India: Thompson-Balys.
H1292.4.2.p: On the way to the other world, the hero is asked how a snake can be cured of blindness, and learns the answer there.

H1292.4.3.r: Answer: He must distribute his knowledge. India: Thompson-Balys.
H1292.4.3.p: On the way to the other world, the hero is asked how a cripple can be healed, and learns the answer there.

H1292.5.r: (Various answers.) Types 460, 461; Aarne FFC XXIII 149; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 50, Beal XXI 318.
H1292.5.p: On the quest, the hero is asked how a girl whom suitors have so far failed to win can marry, and learns the answer in the other world.

H1292.6.p: On the quest, the hero is asked where a lost key is, and learns the answer in the other world.

H1292.7.p: On the quest, the hero is asked where a lost princess is, and learns the answer in the other world.

H1292.8.r: Answer: When he is able to get out of the boat and leave the oar in another’s hand. Types 460, 461; *Aarne FFC XXIII 136ff., 139; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1292.8.p: On a quest to the other world, the hero is asked to find out when a ferryman will be released from his duty, and must bring back the answer.

H1292.9.r: (Various answers). Types 460, 461; *Aarne FFC XXIII 136ff.; Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 8; India: *Thompson-Balys.
H1292.9.p: On a quest to the other world, the hero is asked to learn how a certain water creature can be freed from some annoyance, and must bring back the answer.

H1292.10.r: (Answer: tie on bell.) Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 8.
H1292.10.p: On a quest to the other world, the hero is asked how mice can get rid of cats, and must bring back the answer.

H1292.11.r: (Answer: by doing without wings.) Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV No. 8.
H1292.11.p: On a quest to the other world, the hero is asked how ants can live longer, and must bring back the answer.

H1292.12.p: On a quest to the other world, the hero is asked where a named character called Bras-de-Fer (Ver-sous-Terre) lives, and must bring back the answer.

H1292.13.p: On a quest to the other world, the hero is asked whether the questioner has seen his prince, and must bring back the answer.

H1292.14.p: On a quest to the other world, the hero is asked why the dragon king cannot rise into the sky, and must bring back the answer.

H1292.15.p: On a quest to the other world, the hero is asked why a child cannot talk or a dog cannot bark, and must bring back the answer.

H1292.16.r: Answer: in her last birth she had been the young of her present calf and had treated it the same way. India: Thompson-Balys.
H1292.16.p: On a quest to the other world, the hero is asked why a calf beats its mother cow every day, and must bring back the answer.

H1292.17.r: Answer: He had been a very generous god-fearing person in his last birth and God had not forgotten him. India: Thompson-Balys.
H1292.17.p: On a quest to the other world, the hero is asked whether a poor shepherd is known to God, and must bring back the answer.

H1292.18.r: Answer: When king’s daughter marries. India: *Thompson-Balys.
H1292.18.p: On a quest to the other world, the hero is asked when a certain building or structure can be finished, and must bring back the answer.

H1292.19.p: On a quest to the other world, the hero is asked how a man and a woman can be freed from some annoyance, and must bring back the answer.

H1292.20.p: On a quest to the other world, the hero is asked why a kingdom prospers by day but burns by night, and must bring back the answer.

H1300.p: Heroes set out on quests to find something unique or unmatched in the world.

H1301.r: *Fb “kone” II 263a; BP II 19, 34; Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 21; West Indies: Flowers 466.
H1301.p: The hero sets out to find the most beautiful woman in the world.

H1301.1.r: Type 402; BP III 18, Fb “brud” IV 65a; Irish myth: *Cross; English: Wells 151 (Richard Coer de Lyon); Missouri French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G 3/109, 3/404, z-G. 13/317); Chile: Pino Saavedra 402—405.
H1301.1.p: The hero searches for the most beautiful bride possible.

H1301.1.1.p: The hero seeks a bride who is as handsome as he is.

H1301.1.2.p: The hero seeks a princess who lives far away, in a distant land.

H1301.1.3.p: The hero travels to every island to see whether any woman can rival the beauty of his wife.

H1302.p: A quest for the most beautiful bouquet or bunch of flowers.

H1303.p: A hero is sent on a quest to find the finest chain in the world. The task tests his prowess by demanding something unique and hard to find.

H1305.p: A hero must search for the best bread in the world. Quests of this kind test the hero by requiring something rare and superlative.

H1305.1.p: Within the bread quest, the hero must search for the best meat. It is another superlative quest test.

H1305.1.1.p: Within the quest for the best meat, the hero must instead search for the worst meat. The test is a reversed superlative.

H1305.2.p: Within the bread quest, the hero must search for the best-cooked dish. It is a superlative quest test about cookery.

H1306.r: Type 402; BP II 34; *Hdwb. d. Märchens II 150b nn. 452—502; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 21; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 72 No. 557, Espinosa Jr. No. 105; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chile: Pino Saavedra 402—405.
H1306.p: A hero is sent on a quest to find the finest linen cloth in the world. The task is a superlative test of prowess.

H1306.1.p: Within the linen quest, the hero must find the best-worked handkerchief. It is a superlative test of fine needlework.

H1307.p: A hero is sent on a quest to find the smallest dog in the world. The task is a superlative test of prowess.

H1308.p: A hero is sent on a quest to find the finest horse in the world. The task is a superlative test of prowess.

H1311.p: A hero or king sets out to find the richest person in the world. It is a superlative quest test.

H1311.1.r: (Cf. H1395.) English: Child I 275—283 passim, III 17n., 503f.; Pélerinage de Charlemagne; Huet 146; Thien Motive 7; Russian: Andrejev No. 650b*; India: Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Chavannes 500 Contes I 374 No. 107.
H1311.1.p: A king searches for someone richer or more magnificent than himself. The quest tests whether any rival can be found.

H1311.2.p: A man seeks a bride who is both the richest and the poorest woman. The paradoxical quest is the test.

H1312.r: *Oesterley Gesta Romanorum No. No. 74; Herbert III 191; Christensen DF L 91.
H1312.p: A hero is sent on a quest to find the greatest fool in the world. The quest is a superlative test of prowess.

H1312.1.r: *Type 1384; BP I 335, II 440; Christensen DF L 35.
H1312.1.p: Within the quest for the greatest fool, the seeker must find three persons as stupid as his wife. It is a comic variant of the fool quest.

H1313.p: A hero must find a person who can draw a particular sword out of its place. Only the right person succeeds, which tests the hero.

H1315.p: A hero is sent to find the spring at the source of the biggest of three rivers east of Gardariki. The quest is for a unique place.

H1316.p: A hero is sent on a quest to find the strongest being or person. It is a superlative test of prowess.

H1317.p: A hero must find an ornament, such as a jewel, that matches one he already has. The quest tests his ability to find an exact match.

H1318.p: A liar escapes from the devil by setting him a quest to find a greater liar. The tale turns on who can lie most.

H1319.p: This heading gathers quests for unique things that do not fit the other categories of quests for the unique.

H1319.1.p: A hero must search for the one person who is able to cure a particular illness.

H1319.2.p: A hero must set out to find the best cap in the world.

H1319.3.p: A hero must set out to find the most beautiful rug.

H1319.4.p: A hero must set out to find the most beautiful ring.

H1320.r: *Type 550; Dickson 39, 50, 51; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
H1320.p: A hero must go searching for some wondrous object or creature with magical qualities.

H1320.1.p: A hero must search for a magic object that has supernatural powers.

H1320.2.p: A hero must search for something that he or she has seen in a dream.

H1321.p: A hero must search for some miraculous water with magical powers.

H1321.1.r: *Types 550, 707; *BP II 394; MacCulloch Childhood 52ff.; Italian Novella: Rotunda; India: *Thompson-Balys; Hawaii: Beckwith Myth 72, 257.
H1321.1.p: A hero must search for the Water of Life, a water that can bring the dead back to life.

H1321.2.r: Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 59 No. 425D, Espinosa Jr. No. 75; Arabian: Burton Nights S VI 213; India: Thompson-Balys.
H1321.2.p: A hero must search for water that has the power to heal.
