H1397.1.p: A hero goes on a quest to find and deal with a witch who is his stepmother.

H1397.2.p: A hero goes on a quest to find and deal with the children of an enemy.

H1400.r: *Type 326; *BP I 22ff.; Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Japanese: Ikeda.
H1400.p: A person is subjected to a series of tests meant to make him show fear. If he stays calm, he passes.

H1401.p: A god takes on frightening forms to try to scare a child, testing whether the child is fearless.

H1401.1.p: The ruler of the dead takes on terrifying shapes to frighten people who come to visit his realm.

H1401.2.p: An ogress takes on terrifying shapes to frighten messengers who come to her.

H1405.p: A test of courage in which someone pretends an enemy is approaching, to see who flees and who stays to fight.

H1406.p: A suitor is tested by being made to believe his own life is threatened, to see whether he is brave enough.

H1407.p: A fearless youth is tested by unknowingly kneading a serpent into dough, to see whether he will flinch.

H1408.p: A hero passes a test by crossing a wilderness full of all kinds of wild beasts without showing fear.

H1410.p: A person is tested by being required to stay in a frightening place, to see whether he shows fear.

H1411.r: Type 326; Irish: Cross, O’Suilleabhain 53, Beal XXI 319; England: Baughman; North Carolina: Brown Collection I 686; India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen II 73.
H1411.p: A person is tested by being required to spend a night in a haunted house, to see whether he is frightened.

H1411.1.r: Dead man’s members call out to hero, “Shall we fall, or shall we not?” *Type 326; *Taylor MPh XVII 321 n. 1; Scott “Marmion” note H; BP I 30 n. 1; Köhler-Bolte I 130; Fb “menneske” II 577b; Cape Verde Islands: Parsons MAFLS XV (1) 241 n. 1.
H1411.1.p: A person spends a night in a haunted house where a corpse falls down the chimney in pieces, as a test of fearlessness.

H1411.1.1.r: *Taylor MPh XVII (1919) 321 n. 1; Scott “Marmion” Note H; Finnish: Aarne FFC XXXIII 41 No. 46**.
H1411.1.1.p: A person spends a night in a haunted house where the carcass of a horse drops down the chimney, as a test of fearlessness.

H1411.2.p: A man proves he is not afraid by spending a night in a haunted house that is overrun with cats.

H1411.2.1.p: As a fear test, a person keeps watch through the night in a haunted house where the cats are magical.

H1411.3.p: A person proves fearless by spending the night in an enchanted castle, where the devil delivers a moral lecture and makes prophecies.

H1411.4.p: A person proves fearless by spending the night in a house or hall haunted by a demon or monster.

H1412.p: A person proves fearless by spending the night in a church.

H1412.1.p: As a fear test, a person goes into the church at night and rings the bell.

H1415.p: A person proves fearless by staying through the night under a gallows.

H1416.p: A person proves fearless by spending the night beside a grave.

H1418.p: A boy is taken into a frightening enemy's tent as a test of fearlessness.

H1420.p: A person proves fearless by dealing and associating with devils without being afraid.

H1421.r: Type 326; BP I 22f.; Christiansen Norske Eventyr 42.
H1421.p: A person proves fearless by playing cards with the devil in a church.

H1421.1.p: The hero proves fearless by playing skittles (a bowling-like game) with demons.

H1422.r: Type 326; BP I 22ff.; Christiansen Norske Eventyr 42.
H1422.p: A person proves fearless by cutting the devil's fingernails.

H1423.p: A person proves fearless by fighting with spirits.

H1423.1.p: As a fear test, a person passes through a door guarded by a fierce hound and an armed soldier.

H1423.2.p: A person proves fearless by going through a terrifying experience outdoors on Hallowe'en.

H1423.3.p: As a fear test, a person brings back the fattest goat from a hill, though a demon tries to seize him.

H1430.p: A person proves fearless by dealing and associating with ghosts without being afraid.

H1431.p: A person proves fearless by stealing clothes from ghosts.

H1433.p: A person proves fearless by playing a game with a dead man who has been reassembled.

H1434.r: Irish myth: Cross; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 47 No. 326.
H1434.p: A hero must prove he is fearless by eating and drinking from skulls. Passing this test shows he has no fear of the dead or of ghosts.

H1435.p: A hero must prove he is fearless by fetching skulls from a charnel house, a place where bones of the dead are kept. Doing so shows he is not afraid of the dead.

H1436.r: Irish: Read FL XXVII 277f., Knortz Irländische Märchen (Zürich, 1886) 23.
H1436.p: A hero must prove he is fearless by keeping goal in a hurling match played with corpses. Succeeding shows he is not afraid of the dead.

H1440.p: A general heading for tales in which a character is taught or made to feel fear, usually as a test or lesson, and the fearless hero is frightened.

H1441.p: A hero who has never been afraid is frightened when he is awakened by having cold water thrown on him.

H1441.1.p: A fearless hero is frightened when he is awakened by eels being put down his back.

H1450.p: A general heading for tests of staying awake and alert, where a character must keep watch without sleeping.

H1450.1.r: Type 513; *De Vries FFC LXXIII 311 n. 2; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 314 n. 137.
H1450.1.p: A contest in which the participants try to stay awake, and whoever sleeps first loses.

H1451.p: A test in which a person must keep silent and stay awake through a vigil in a church.

H1460.p: A test in which a person must keep watch by a tomb or grave.

H1461.p: A test in which a person must sit up through the night with a corpse.

H1462.r: *Type 530; *BP III 111 n. 3; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 365B*.
H1462.p: A vigil kept over a dead father, usually as a test a son must pass.

H1462.1.p: A vigil over a dead father in which only the youngest son endures the frightening events that happen during the night. The ceiling, floors, and walls knock together.

H1463.r: *BP III 420; Scotch: Campbell Tales I 220; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3365, Legends Nos. 693—697, 700f.; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 201.
H1463.p: A man keeps watch over a grave for three nights to protect himself from the devil.

H1470.p: A general heading for vigilance tests that do not fit the other categories of keeping watch.

H1471.r: *Types 301, 550; BP I 503, *514; MacCulloch Childhood 350; *Hdwb. d. Märchens I 207b; Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 148f., *Cross; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: Thompson CColl II 334ff.
H1471.p: A hero must keep watch against a monster that is causing great destruction. Only the youngest brother succeeds.

H1471.1.p: A hero must keep watch to catch thieves stealing from the king's garden.

H1472.p: A test in which a man must sleep beside a princess for three nights without looking at her or disturbing her.

H1480.p: A general heading for the ways a vigilance test is successfully completed.

H1481.p: A person cuts his own thumb and rubs salt into the wound to keep himself from falling asleep.

H1482.p: A person stabs a dagger into their own thigh to stay awake and avoid falling asleep during a vigil or watch.

H1483.p: A person keeps awake by slowly chewing grains, so the crunching and effort keep them from falling asleep.

H1484.p: A person repeatedly pricks themselves with a pin to stay awake.

H1484.1.p: A lover waiting for someone keeps awake by pricking with a pin, and uses a large fire and water to wash their eyes, a sign they are expecting a visit.

H1500.p: A heading for tales in which a character is put through tests of endurance.

H1501.r: English: Child II 102—110, IV 214f.; West Indies: Flowers 471.
H1501.p: A girl is tested by being made to dance for a long time, wearing out many partners.

H1502.p: A character is tested by being forced to endure hardship, such as serving a woman who has leprosy.

H1503.r: N. A. Indian (Iroquois): Alexander N. Am. 35.
H1503.p: A heroine endures a cruel test: scalding porridge is poured over her naked body, and dogs with rough tongues lick her wounds.

H1504.p: A character is tested by being made to sleep naked on the floor in the cold.

H1505.p: A boy is tested by having clothes sewn into his hands, and then the clothes are torn off along with the skin.

H1506.p: A hero passes an endurance test by staying silent while in a snake pit.

H1507.p: A hero chases and kills a fleeing enemy even though his own wounds are bleeding.

H1508.p: A test in which a character must pray for a very long time without stopping.

H1508.1.p: A test in which a character must repeat a magic incantation continuously for months.

H1510.r: *Types 461, 516 930; *Rösch FFC LXXVII 120ff.; Chauvin VIII 145 No. 145C; *Oesterley No. 20; *Herbert III 198.—Icelandic: Boberg; French Canadian: Barbeau JAFL XXIX 22; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Graham; S. A. Indian (Central Brazil): Ehrenreich International Congress of Americanists XIV 662; Africa: Werner African 214, (Ekoi): Talbot 208.
H1510.p: A heading for attempts to kill the hero that the hero survives, showing his power to survive.

H1511.r: Type 513; German: Grimm No. 71; Finnish: Kalevala rune 31; Chinese: Graham; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 311 n. 120; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 72 No. 11.
H1511.p: Attempts to kill the hero by burning him in a fire, which he survives.

H1511.1.p: A heat test in which the hero is made to swallow red-hot stones and survives.

H1511.1.1.p: A heat test in which the hero swallows heated brass or iron ornaments and survives.

H1511.2.p: An attempt to kill the hero by feeding him burning food, which he survives.

H1511.3.p: An attempt to kill the hero by smothering him with smoke, which he survives.

H1511.4.p: A hero is given a pipe to smoke that is meant to kill him. He survives the attempt.

H1512.p: Someone tries to freeze the hero to death as a test of his endurance. The hero survives.

H1515.r: Type 516; *Rösch FFC LXXVII 123; Hertz Gesammelte Abhandlungen “Die Sage vom Giftmädchen”; BP I 42ff.; Herrmann Saxo II 139; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 314 n. 140.
H1515.p: Someone tries to kill the hero by feeding him poisoned food. The hero survives the test.

H1515.1.p: Druids try to poison the hero with food. The attempt fails.

H1515.2.p: Someone tries to kill a saint by giving him a poisoned drink. The saint survives.

H1515.3.p: The hero is given food with thorns hidden inside it as a test.

H1516.p: Someone tries to kill the hero by poisoning his clothing. The hero survives.

H1517.p: The hero is tested by being bitten by a poisonous snake. He survives the bite.

H1521.p: The hero is sent to capture a giant clam, with the hidden purpose of getting him killed.

H1522.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Tahiti: Dixon 64; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 322 n. 160.
H1522.p: Trees that are meant to kill the hero threaten him as a test.

H1522.1.p: A bent tree is let go so that it snaps back and tears the hero to pieces. The hero escapes.

H1525.r: S. A. Indian (Tupinamba): Métraux BBAE CXLIII (3) 132.
H1525.p: The hero must pass between two rocks that clash together, as a test of his skill or courage.

H1531.p: Someone tries to kill the hero by throwing him onto a sharp spine or spike. The hero survives.

H1531.1.p: The hero is made to dance on sharp instruments, such as blades or spikes, as a test.

H1531.2.p: An attempt to kill the hero on a stairway set with razors fails.

H1532.p: The hero gets caught in the split of a tree as a test.

H1533.r: Irish: O’Suilleabhain 44, 50, Beal XXI 316, 318; Finnish: Kalevala rune 31.
H1533.p: Someone tries to kill the hero by hanging him, but the attempt fails.

H1534.p: Someone tries to kill the hero by letting a plank fall on him. The hero survives.

H1535.r: Irish myth: Cross; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 312 n. 122, (California): Gayton and Newman 95; Africa (Basuto): Jacottet 72 No. 11.
H1535.p: The hero is pushed over a cliff or precipice as a test. He survives the fall.

H1535.1.p: The hero is thrown into a pit as a test.

H1536.p: A hero is tricked onto a dangerous toboggan by someone who tries to kill him on the ride down.

H1537.p: A hero must survive a game played with a fierce wild beast, where the beast's game is a test of the hero's ability to stay alive.

H1537.1.p: A bear orders the heroine to play Blindman's Buff with it, making the game a dangerous test for her.

H1538.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Finnish: Kalevala rune 31; Eskimo (Greenland): Rasmussen III 85; N. A. Indian: *Thompson Tales 312 n. 124.
H1538.p: Someone tries to drown the hero as a test, but the attempt fails and the hero survives.

H1540.p: Contests in which characters are tested on how long they can endure hardship and suffering.

H1541.p: A contest in which characters try to endure cold longer than the others.

H1541.1.r: Hare tries to deceive frost by lying on frozen snow and saying, “Oh, how warm!” *Type 71; Dh III 23.
H1541.1.p: A contest of endurance against cold in which frost and a hare compete to outlast one another.

H1541.2.p: A cold-endurance contest in which the wind proves stronger than the frost.

H1542.r: Hdwb. d. Märchens I 194a n. 14; Icelandic: *Boberg; Melanesia: Wheeler 66.
H1542.p: A contest in which characters try to endure great heat longer than the others.

H1542.1.p: A contest in which a character must cross a river of fire, testing endurance of heat.

H1543.r: (Cf. H1538.) Jewish: Neuman; Africa (Madagascar): Renel I 168ff. No. 30.
H1543.p: A contest to see who can stay under water the longest.

H1544.p: A contest to see who can endure thirst the longest without drinking.

H1545.p: A contest to see who can go longest without eating.

H1550.r: Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “épreuves”; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
H1550.p: Tests that reveal whether a person's character is good or bad.

H1550.1.p: A person's bad character is revealed by looking at their eyes.

H1552.p: Tests that check whether a person is generous.

H1552.1.r: *Type 976; *Köhler-Bolte I 214—216; *Chauvin VIII 123f. No. 110; Penzer VII 7ff.; Chaucer’s “Franklin’s Tale”; India: Thompson-Balys.
H1552.1.p: A wife who promised to go to her lover on her wedding night is let go by her husband, meets robbers, and then is taken to her lover, who sends her back to her husband. The tale asks which of the three men was most generous.

H1552.1.1.p: A variant of the generosity test in which the question is which was most generous: the husband, the lover, or a magician.

H1552.2.p: A generosity contest between a ruler and his minister; the minister loses, is sentenced to death, and is pardoned once he admits defeat.

H1553.r: Gaster Exempla 202 No. 84; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 37, Beal XXI 314.
H1553.p: Tests that check whether a person has patience.

H1553.1.p: A philosopher trains his son in patience by having him beg before stone statues, which give nothing back, so that he learns to endure being ignored.

H1553.2.p: A king is tested for patience by being given strong reproof and harsh criticism, and he accepts it calmly without anger.

H1553.3.p: Those who want to enter a city gate must first put up with mocking insults from the old men sitting there, as a test of their patience.

H1553.4.p: A man shows his patience by calmly taking a blow to the face from a stool thrown by his superior in a monastery.

H1553.5.p: A monk who tries to test his patience by living alone loses his temper when a cup overturns, and he smashes it, failing the test.

H1553.6.p: A patience test in which the tester keeps asking pointless, irrelevant riddles to see whether the subject will stay calm.

H1554.p: A general test of curiosity, in which a person is tempted to pry into something they have been told not to investigate.

H1554.1.r: The new Eve. A woman has boasted of a lack of curiosity and blamed Mother Eve. The king entertains her in his castle. She may see everything but must not look into a certain silver jug. She does so and finds a mouse in it. (Cf. H1557.2.) *Type 1416; *BP III 543 n. 1; *Crane Vitry 139 No. 13; Alphabet No. 575; *Fb “Adam” IV 3b; H. C. Andersen “Krøblingen”, Danish Fairy Tales and Legends; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: *Neuman.
H1554.1.p: A curiosity test in which a mouse is shut inside a jug, and the person is tempted to look in to see what is there.

H1554.2.r: He does. The giver tells him he is the second man who almost made sure of getting the clock. The man asks how the other missed getting it; he loses the clock himself. England: Baughman.
H1554.2.p: A man is promised a beautiful clock if he can mind his own business for a whole year, and his curiosity is tested over that year.

H1554.3.p: A plowman is promised a horse if he can say the Paternoster without thinking of anything else, but he loses the bargain when he interrupts to ask whether he will also get the saddle and bridle.

H1555.p: A general heading for tests that check whether a person is honest, meaning whether they can be trusted with what is not theirs.

H1555.1.p: A man is entrusted with a treasure as a test of his honesty, to see whether he will keep it safe and not steal it.

H1556.r: Irish myth: Cross; Hindu: Tawney I 86 n., 196, 357, II 57, 71, 606; Arabian: Burton Nights V 144, IX 325.
H1556.p: A general heading for tests that check whether a person is faithful and loyal to someone they serve or love.

H1556.0.1.p: A servant's loyalty is put to the test to see whether he remains faithful to his master.

H1556.0.2.p: A guard's loyalty is tested to see whether he will stay faithful to his duty.

H1556.1.r: English: Wells 129 (Sir Orfeo); Italian: Basile Pentamerone II No. 4; India: Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 473.
H1556.1.p: Someone's loyalty is tested by pretending to be dead, to see how those close to them react.

H1556.1.1.p: A cock pretends to be dead to find out what the hens will say about him when they think he is gone.

H1556.2.r: Kittredge Gawain and the Green Knight 6ff.; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
H1556.2.p: The hero's loyalty is tested by subjecting him to temptations to see whether he will betray his trust.

H1556.3.p: A man suspected of being an assassin is tested by being given a chance to commit the murder, to see whether he will take it.

H1556.4.p: A person's faithfulness in love is put to the test to see whether their affection holds up.

H1556.4.1.p: A lover's loyalty is tested by putting him in bed with his mistress, and he only kisses her and goes no further.

H1556.4.2.p: A lover's loyalty is tested by having him make love to a maid.

H1556.4.2.1.p: A wife checks her husband's faithfulness by disguising herself as another woman and tempting him.

H1556.4.3.p: A lover's loyalty is tested by secretly putting a maid in the mistress's bed at a planned meeting; he must refuse her to pass.

H1556.4.4.p: An old uncle tests his nephew's faithfulness by sleeping with the nephew's beloved.

H1556.4.5.p: A husband or wife who swears to die for their mate loses that willingness when Death seems to come for them.

H1556.4.5.1.p: An old woman who says she would die for her daughter loses that willingness when Death seems to come for her.

H1556.4.6.p: A supernatural wife gives her husband a rose that loses one petal each time he thinks of her while he travels home.

H1556.5.p: A falsely accused hero is tested for loyalty by a friend or lover who pretends to sleep, either in the same bed or alone with him in the forest.

H1557.p: Tests in which a person's willingness to obey orders is checked.

H1557.1.r: (Cf. H1558.0.1.1.) *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 368; *Crane Vitry 187 No. 123; BP III 236; Wesselski Mönchslatein 8 No. 3; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 93a n. 7.
H1557.1.p: Sons are tested for obedience by being offered a slice of apple and told to open their mouths to receive what is given; the youngest obeys and is rewarded with the kingdom.

H1557.2.p: Someone blames Adam or Eve for disobedience, then immediately disobeys an order themselves.

H1557.3.r: Immediately disobeys. *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 319; Wesselski Märchen 220 No. 33.
H1557.3.p: An old man is content until he is forbidden to leave the city, and then he wants to leave.

H1557.4.r: (Cf. H1554.1.) They do so and are not allowed to hear confession. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 398.
H1557.4.p: A pope tests women's obedience by forbidding them to look into a box.

H1557.5.p: A king tests his subjects' obedience by asking whether they will let a spear be carried crosswise into their houses; the answer is that the way must be hewn open to allow it.

H1557.6.p: A king tests his gardener's obedience by pretending to be a thief.

H1558.p: Tests in which a person's friendship is checked to see whether it holds up.

H1558.0.1.p: A test of whether someone is worthy of being a friend.

H1558.0.1.1.r: (Cf. H1557.1.) *BP II 39 n. 2, III 236; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 92b. n. 3.
H1558.0.1.1.p: A father sends his son out with three apples to offer to people he meets. A man who eats all three is to be avoided, while one who divides them is a good candidate for friendship.

H1558.1.r: *Type 893; *Basset RTP XXII 10; *Crane Vitry 185f. No. 120; Herbert III 10, 55, 205; *Penzer V 87 n. 1; Alphabet No. 59; Chauvin IX 15f.; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 94b; Oesterley No. 129; Scala Celi 9a, 11b Nos. 60, 69.—Icelandic: Sveinsson FFC LXXXIII p. xix, *Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 32, *274.
H1558.1.p: A man pretends he has killed someone and asks his friends where to hide the body; all but his father's half-friend abandon him, and only that half-friend stays loyal.

H1558.1.1.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas IV 32, 275; India: Thompson-Balys.
H1558.1.1.p: Of three friends, the one least loved turns out to be the most reliable in an emergency.

H1558.2.r: *Chauvin IX 16 No. 2; Schiller’s “Burgschaft”; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
H1558.2.p: A miserable man confesses to a murder he did not commit so he can escape his suffering, and his friend offers to take the guilt in his place. The real murderer is moved by this loyalty and confesses.

H1558.3.r: Everyman. He calls in Riches, Family, etc. Only Good Deeds remains with him. *Chauvin III 101 No. 7; Jewish: *Bin Gorion Born Judas IV 226, 275; Icelandic: *Boberg.
H1558.3.p: A friend is tested by being asked whether he would be willing to die alongside the other person.

H1558.4.p: A hare with many friends is tested, and when she asks them for help in the final trial none of them come, so only her own legs save her.

H1558.5.p: A man pretends to be dead to see which of the friends he owes money to will show up to mourn or help him.

H1558.6.p: A man imagines that his friend has refused a request to borrow his horse, and grows cold toward him. When the horse's owner asks why, he explains, and the friend lends the horse and they are reconciled.

H1558.7.p: A spendthrift who wastes his money loses his friends when he becomes poor.

H1558.7.1.p: A sultan disguises himself as a beggar to find out which of his friends remain loyal to him.

H1558.7.2.p: When a man reports that he has lost his money, his friends desert him.

H1558.8.p: Friends refuse to fight each other, even when ordered or forced to.

H1558.8.1.p: A friend finds his sword too heavy to lift when he is asked to raise it against a friend.

H1558.9.p: A man leaves his pregnant wife in the care of a friend while he is away, and the friend is tested for loyalty.

H1558.10.p: A friendship between two men continues unbroken even when their sons are jealous of each other and quarrel.

H1558.11.p: A friend must publicly accept a slap from the other man as a test of loyalty.

H1558.12.p: A mourner claims that her dead husband can be touched only by a sinless person and asks people to help cremate the body. Everyone who volunteers quickly leaves, which exposes them as false friends.

H1558.13.p: A man is tested by whether he stays loyal to a friend who has been condemned to death.

H1561.p: A general heading for trials that test a person's bravery or courage.

H1561.1.r: English: Hibbard 229, Wells 151 (Coer de Lyon); Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: Neuman.
H1561.1.p: A hero proves his courage by competing in a tournament.

H1561.2.r: *Chauvin V 21 n. 1; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman.
H1561.2.p: A person proves his bravery by fighting one opponent in single combat.

H1561.2.1.p: A duel to the death fought on an island, where the combat is settled between two men.

H1561.2.2.p: A youth must fight his father's old friend without knowing who he is, though simply saying who he is would have won him a friendly welcome.

H1561.2.3.p: A test of bravery in which two men fight each other in single combat at a river crossing (ford) to prove their valor.

H1561.3.p: A test of bravery in which a person must stand still and not flinch when struck a blow.

H1561.4.p: A test of courage in which a nobleman, hiring servants, snaps at them as if to bite; those who dodge away are rejected, and those who stand ready to fight are hired.

H1561.5.p: A test of valor deciding who is worthy to be king: the candidate must seize the royal regalia placed between two fierce lions.

H1561.6.p: A test of bravery in which a hero must fight a giant.

H1561.7.p: A test of bravery in which a warrior and a hound attack the person being tested.

H1561.8.p: A test of valor in which a group of warriors fights against their own leader to see whether he stands firm.

H1561.9.p: A prince, given a choice of roads, deliberately takes the shorter but more dangerous one as a test of courage.

H1561.10.p: A master tests his disciple by asking whether he would be willing to plunge into the Indus River with him.

H1562.p: A test of physical strength used to show whether a person is strong enough for a task or worthy of a role.

H1562.1.p: A strength test in which a person must pull up a tree by its roots.

H1562.1.1.p: A strength test in which a person must cut a tree down with a single stroke.

H1562.2.r: ) English: Wells 59 (The Turke and Gowin), 114 (Sir Isumbras); Icelandic: *Boberg; Danish: Schmidt DF XXXIX 55.
H1562.2.p: A strength test in which a person must lift a heavy stone, such as one used as a fireplace stone.

H1562.2.1.p: A strength test in which a person must lift a sword.

H1562.2.2.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 95.
H1562.2.2.p: Before setting out on a rescue, a bat tests its strength by trying to lift a stone.

H1562.3.p: A strength test in which a person breaks a heavy glass bottle by striking it over a loaf of rye bread.

H1562.4.p: A strength test in which a person performs an extraordinary jump.

H1562.5.p: A strength test in which a heavy stone is thrown at a boaster, who throws it back.

H1562.6.p: A strength test in which a person must break a spirited, wild horse.

H1562.7.p: A strength contest in which two contestants stand back to back against a rock on opposite sides, each with an iron ring around the neck, the rings joined by a chain; they pull until the ring cuts through the neck of one of them.

H1562.8.p: A strength test in which a person must break a witch's back. The challenge is to physically overpower or break the witch.

H1562.9.p: A strength test in which the contestant must wrestle an opponent to prove his power.

H1562.10.p: A strength test in which the contestant must push a heavy ferry boat out from the shore.

H1562.11.p: A strength test in which the contestant must pull two iron bars that pass through a hole, drawing them together or apart.

H1562.12.p: A task in which the hero must destroy an iron castle as a test of strength.

H1562.13.p: A strength test in which the contestant must shoot an arrow through seven iron plates.

H1562.14.p: Two strong beings, one strong in speech (Mighty-of-His-Mouth) and one strong in hands (Mighty-of-His-Hands), agree to live together to test their strength. The note says strength of mind wins in the end.

H1563.p: A general test of a person's skill, showing how well they can perform a task.

H1564.r: English: Wells 64 (Avowynge of King Arthur etc.); Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman.
H1564.p: A test of whether a person is hospitable, showing how well they welcome and treat guests.

H1565.p: A general test of whether someone is grateful for help or kindness they have received.

H1565.1.r: Wealth removed. Alphabet No. 62; Scala Celi 12a No. 72; Wesselski Mönchslatein 13 No. 7; Herbert 83 No. 7; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
H1565.1.p: A magician teaches a pupil and then makes him believe he is greater than his teacher. The pupil has promised the magician great rewards but forgets the promise, so the test shows his ingratitude.

H1566.p: A test a candidate must pass to be admitted into a warrior band or fighting company.

H1567.p: A general test to see whether someone is fit to lead others.

H1567.1.p: A leadership test in which the candidate must eat a frightful or disgusting meal.

H1567.1.1.p: A leadership test in which the candidate must swallow a live mouse without vomiting it up, showing obedience.

H1568.p: A test that determines who is the champion among contestants.

H1568.1.p: A championship test in which the contestant must sit on a pillow covering an egg without breaking it.

H1569.p: A miscellaneous category of tests of character that do not fit the more specific headings.

H1569.1.p: A test of whether a person is hardworking and diligent.

H1569.1.1.p: A man tests how hardworking a prospective servant girl is before hiring her.

H1571.r: (For details see F647.) *BP III 238; Penzer VII 10ff.; Köhler-Bolte I 64; Bolte Reise der Söhne Giaffers 120.
H1571.p: A test in which a person's sensitivity is checked, for example by how strongly they feel a small discomfort such as a pea under a mattress or a hair in a bed.

H1572.p: A test used to determine whether a woman or man is able to have children.

H1572.1.p: A stone placed under a woman reveals her fertility: if she is fertile it yields milk, and if she is barren it yields blood.

H1573.p: A test of a person's religious faith or holiness, usually set up through a miracle or ordeal.

H1573.0.1.p: In a religious test, angels come to help the person being tested.

H1573.1.p: A test of whether someone truly believes in Christianity.

H1573.1.1.r: Proof of his belief. Irish myth: Cross.
H1573.1.1.p: A non-Christian is tested and the earth swallows him up as punishment for his unbelief.

H1573.1.2.p: A person performs a disgusting or loathsome act to prove that his Christian virtue is real.

H1573.1.3.p: A druid tries to weaken a king's Christian faith by performing a magic display, but the attempt fails.

H1573.1.4.p: A saint orders a man to jump into a fiery furnace, and the man is not harmed.

H1573.2.p: A test of the holiness or worthiness of religious figures such as saints or bishops.

H1573.2.1.p: To prove a person is a saint, he must show a magic miracle as evidence.

H1573.2.2.p: A saint is tested when a deity visits him in disguise to see how he responds.

H1573.2.3.p: To test whether a man is worthy of becoming a bishop, he is asked to plow a field without a plowshare.

H1573.3.p: A test of whether the power of Christianity is real.

H1573.3.1.p: A saint drinks poison and is not harmed, proving the power of Christianity.

H1573.3.2.p: A saint's horse is miraculously kept safe before a fairy, as proof of Christianity's power.

H1573.3.3.p: A saint changes a shape or form to prove Christianity's power before a druid.

H1573.3.4.p: A wizard or druid is burned while a saint is saved, showing the power of Christianity.

H1573.4.p: A test of whether the power of other, non-Christian religions is real.

H1573.4.1.p: A test of whether the power of Judaism can defeat other religions is put to the one being tested.

H1573.5.p: A person is warned in a dream to give up a sacred stone, but refuses to part with it, which tests the steadfastness of his love for God.

H1573.6.p: A person is put to a test to prove that he is righteous.

H1573.6.1.p: A person proves his righteousness by being able to cross a bridge, which serves as the test.

H1573.7.p: A person is tested to see whether he has truly repented of a wrong he committed.

H1573.7.1.p: A wrongdoer is placed in the same situation in which he sinned, to see whether he has really repented.

H1574.p: A person's rank or status in society is decided through a test.

H1574.0.1.p: A person's social rank is decided by the size of the portion he takes from a cauldron of food.

H1574.1.p: A person's noble birth is tested to prove he has aristocratic blood.

H1574.2.p: Fertility of the land or nature is taken as proof that a person has the right to be king.

H1574.3.p: A king is selected by means of a test.

H1574.3.0.1.p: Young princes who want the throne must pass a test set for them.

H1574.3.0.2.p: Two deities test the virtues of a king to judge whether he is fit to rule.

H1574.3.1.p: At a burning forge, whoever manages to rescue the anvil will become king.

H1574.3.2.p: Whoever wins the maiden who is queen becomes king.

H1575.p: A test is made of a person's ability to see.

H1575.1.p: A test of sight in which captives are walked across stepping-stones; if they cross without stumbling they are blinded again.

H1576.p: A test used to check whether someone really possesses magic powers.

H1576.1.p: A magic power is tested by having the person name the sex of a goat that has not yet been born.

H1576.2.p: A fakir proves his skill by heating an iron and passing it through his hands without being burned.

H1577.p: A test is used to show whether a person has God's favor.

H1577.1.p: A husband throws away his wife's jewel-box to test whether she can get it back with help from a goddess, which shows whether the goddess favors her.

H1577.2.p: A husband drowns his son to see whether his wife's guardian goddess can bring the boy back to life, which tests the goddess's favor toward her.

H1578.r: *Dh I 329; Köhler in Gonzenbach II 216 No. 17.
H1578.p: A test for finding out whether someone is pretending to be the opposite sex.

H1578.1.r: BP II 57f., III 236; Italian: Basile Pentamerone III No. 6; India: Thompson-Balys.
H1578.1.p: A test that exposes a girl disguised as a man.

H1578.1.1.r: BP II 57 n. 2; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 92b. n. 6; *Zachariae Kleine Schriften 58.
H1578.1.1.p: Peas are scattered on the floor and the person is watched walking on them: men walk firmly, while a disguised girl slips and stumbles.

H1578.1.1.1.p: Nuts and corn are scattered on the floor instead of peas, and the disguised girl is exposed by how she walks on them.

H1578.1.2.p: A spinning wheel is brought in: a real man ignores it, but a disguised girl shows interest in it.

H1578.1.3.p: Flowers are offered and the one chosen reveals the sex: a girl picks a carnation, a man a rose.

H1578.1.4.p: A ball is thrown into the person's lap: a girl spreads her legs to catch it, while a man does not.

H1578.1.4.1.p: A woman in a dress throws an apple to a man, and he reveals himself by putting his legs together to catch it.

H1578.1.4.2.p: A man disguised as a girl is tested by having to jump over a pit; only the man manages it.

H1578.1.5.r: *BP II 58; Bolte Wickram’s Rollwagenbüchlein 384 n. 2; FL I 133, 354; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 92b. n. 6.
H1578.1.5.p: Nuts and apples are offered: men tuck them into their shirts, while girls put them into their handkerchiefs.

H1578.1.6.p: A parrot warns a disguised girl, and she picks only one flower, which gives her away.

H1578.2.p: A man disguised as a girl is tested by having weapons placed among baskets and a war-trumpet sounded; he snatches the arms, revealing himself.

H1581.p: A test used to determine who is the rightful heir.

H1582.p: A test used to determine whether a person is in good health.

H1582.1.p: A person's good health is recognized by hearing their voice.

H1582.2.p: A person's good health is recognized by smoke rising from the chimney.

H1583.p: Tests that measure how much time has passed.

H1583.1.p: The passage of time is measured by how much iron shoes have worn away.

H1583.2.p: A person's age or the passing of time is measured by how far a ring fits or slides on a finger or body part.

H1584.p: A general category of tests in which someone's skill or knowledge of measuring space or distance is checked.

H1584.1.p: Land is measured by how much of it a person can see from one spot.

H1584.2.p: Land is measured by how much of it can be covered or crossed within a set number of hours.

H1585.p: A person's cleanliness is tested by shaking them to see whether lice fall off.

H1588.p: Two opponents compete by setting their dogs to fight each other to see whose dogs are stronger.

H1588.1.p: A litter of puppies is tested by throwing each one at a hanging animal hide; the pup that grips the hide is kept, and it grows into a great hunting dog.

H1588.2.p: A man and a king compete by setting their domestic animals against each other in a fight.

H1591.r: N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 74.
H1591.p: A general category of contests in which participants test their skill at shooting at a target or with a missile.

H1591.1.p: A contest in which participants test their skill by throwing a spear.

H1592.p: A general contest in which participants test their skill at hunting.

H1593.p: A goal-scoring match between fairies and humans, played to decide which side is stronger.

H1594.p: A general contest in which participants test their speed by racing on foot.

H1594.0.1.p: The loser of a foot race is put to death as the penalty.

H1594.1.p: A foot race is run between a fairy and a human.

H1594.2.p: A foot race is run between a giant and a human.

H1595.p: A general test of how well a person remembers things.

H1595.1.p: Solomon asks Marchus a question and gets a correct answer. Fourteen months later he asks a second question based on the first and again gets it right; four months after that he asks a third question built on the first two, and again the answer is correct.

H1596.p: A general contest in which people are judged on their beauty.

H1596.0.1.p: A test of how attractive a woman is to men.

H1596.1.r: Judgment of Paris. Scala Celi 22b, 27a Nos. 146, 175; Greek: Fox 124.
H1596.1.p: A golden apple is offered as the prize in a beauty contest among women.

H1596.2.r: Africa (Madagascar): Sibree Madagascar before the Conquest (London, 1896) 239ff.
H1596.2.p: Strangers are chosen to judge a beauty contest, so that the contestants are not biased by their own acquaintances.

H1596.3.p: Women must appear naked in a beauty contest.

H1598.p: A man is set to compete against some non-human being, such as a supernatural creature, in a test or contest.

H1598.1.p: A man competes in a contest against an angel.
